#3364. Google DeepMind analysis proves Signal and WhatsApp encryption is secure

The Signal protocol has long been considered the gold standard for end-to-end encrypted messaging, with Edward Snowden a notable advocate. Now a Google DeepMind analysis has “formally verified” the security of the protocol.

In addition to its use in the Signal app, the same protocol is also used by WhatsApp and Google Messages, and the work has been described as “a landmark development” …

“Formal verification” is the term given to mathematically proving or disproving that a cryptographic algorithm or protocol satisfies its security claims under all conditions. It guarantees that there is no situation in which the protocol will fail. This is a far higher standard than traditional testing methods which seek to find vulnerabilities but cannot promise that others do not exist.

Using agentic AI to carry out formal verification is a huge breakthrough for cryptography and AI alike. It is, however, extremely computationally demanding, so Google told Wired it’s unclear as yet how practical it will be to use it more broadly.

DeepMind researchers emphasize that their findings are just one milestone in a larger process. “We are very excited by this result, but there is a long distance to go before we are able to scale this to all the software of the world, and we want to do that,” Swarat Chaudhuri, a DeepMind research scientist, tells WIRED.

It’s important to note that the validation is for the protocol itself rather than the Signal app as a whole. However, encouragement can be taken from the fact that when tested against older versions of Signal that contained known vulnerabilities, it identified those and flagged them as failing formal verification.

Also worth stating is that Google was able to build on some past formal verification work already completed without the use of AI. This analysis took four weeks, and the scale of resources required has not yet been disclosed, so we shouldn’t expect a whole array of other protocols to be validated overnight. All the same, this is a very big deal.

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

You've probably heard the term "MacBook killer," especially following the launch of Nvidia's first RTX Spark laptops. Now, Apple has raised the stakes with its latest MacBook Pro models featuring the PROLED XDR Displays, and I wanted to see how these new machines actually stack up.

So, I put my 16-inch MacBook Pro M3 Max away for two weeks and used the Lenovo Yoga 9n 2-in-1 as my only laptop. I wanted to find out whether Nvidia's new platform could replace an older MacBook Pro, how it compares with Apple's latest flagships, and what makes RTX Spark laptops worth considering.

The Yoga makes a strong impression. Its versatile design, vibrant OLED touchscreen, and support for local AI workloads give me plenty to like. But after two weeks, I found that while it's a capable everyday laptop, its high price and performance trade-offs make it a more specialized alternative to a MacBook rather than a true replacement.

Nvidia  RTX Spark N1X with 5120-core GPU and 18-core CPU

Nvidia RTX Spark N1X 6144 Core GPU, 20-Core NPU

Nvidia RTX Spark N1X 6144 Core Blackwell GPU

2x USB-A, 2x USB-C, 1x HDMI 2.1, 1x 3.5mm Headphone jack, 1x SD card slot

2x USB-A, 2x USB-C, 1x HDMI 2.1, 1x 3.5mm Headphone jack, 1x SD card slot

This Lenovo Yoga 9n 2-in-1 is a versatile machine. It features a 360-degree hinge for tablet use, pen support, and a striking design with speaker grilles flanking the screen and keyboard.

Tent mode is perfect for sitting on my sofa and streaming episodes of “King of the Hill.” Folding the screen flat lets me use the giant 16-inch display as a primary monitor in the lab at work with an external keyboard and mouse.

Of course, holding a 16-inch screen like a tablet can feel a bit unwieldy. However, the ability to use the included pen in photo-editing apps like Photoshop is a nice feature. I also give Lenovo credit for including a pen in the box. There's even a small cradle that magnetically attaches to the top of the laptop, so you don't have to worry about losing the stylus.

The Yoga’s “Ice Blue" finish and polished accents also give this laptop a glamorous look, making it feel like a jewel on my desk. My Space Black MacBook just looks plain and boring compared to this Yoga 9n.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

The keyboard and touchpad are also excellent. The dedicated number pad makes spreadsheet work far easier than on my MacBook, while the haptic touchpad matches Apple's gold standard. Clicks feel crisp, and special Windows-specific feedback for actions like closing windows and completing file transfers adds a nice tactile touch that my Mac lacks.

You can even use the pen on the haptic touchpad instead of writing directly on the screen. It can feel a bit strange, but it's another example of the flexibility this design offers. I could never imagine Apple doing that on a Mac.

Connectivity is another area where the Yoga has an advantage over my MacBook. In addition to HDMI and a full-size SD card reader, Lenovo includes two USB-A ports, which you won't find on a modern MacBook Pro.

Given the laptop's relatively thick 0.69-inch chassis and 4.28-pound weight, there's plenty of room for extra connections. During my two weeks with the Yoga, I left my dongles at home, which was a surprisingly refreshing change.

One of the biggest reasons I enjoy using the Yoga 9n 2-in-1 is the 16-inch OLED touchscreen. It's large, colorful, and bright enough to make everything from productivity work to streaming video enjoyable.

However, there's a new challenger in town. Apple's latest MacBook Pro, with its PROLED XDR display, has raised the bar for what we expect from a laptop screen. Although the numbers show that the Yoga 9n 2-in-1 doesn't quite match Apple's latest MacBook, that doesn't make it any less good.

Its 16-inch size gives me plenty of room to multitask with Google Chrome tabs and Slack while working in the lab. Brightness also reaches just over 1,000 nits in HDR, and one of my favorite shows, "King of the Hill," looks incredibly vibrant.

The episode where Bobby dresses up as the local college's mascot to help out Connie was a particularly good showcase. The oranges and other rich colors in the mascot suit practically jumped off the screen, making the animation look wonderfully alive.

In our lab tests, the Yoga's panel delivered a particularly high and oversaturated color volume, measuring 193.1% sRGB and 136.6% DCI-P3. It also ranked third in SDR brightness among the MacBook Pro 16-inch with M5 Max, Galaxy Book 6 Ultra, and HP Omnibook Ultra 16, reaching 449.8 nits and delivering an impressive 1,002 nits in HDR. Its 0.30 Delta-E result also placed it fourth in color accuracy among the laptops we compared.

However, the MacBook Pro 16-inch M5 Max PROLED XDR still comes out ahead in several important areas. It ranks first in brightness, reaching 549 nits in SDR and an impressive 1,949 nits in HDR. It also delivers the best color accuracy with a near-perfect 0.19 Delta-E.

However, Yoga is a more compelling matchup against my MacBook Pro M3 Max. As shown in the photo above, Lenovo's display produced particularly striking colors in the individual feathers of a parrot. Still, Apple's OLED display delivered more natural-looking detail and contrast, which I ultimately preferred.

Apple has also introduced touchscreen support on its new MacBook Pro and macOS, giving the Yoga serious competition in this category. If you're simply looking for the best touchscreen OLED laptop, Apple's latest MacBook Pro is hard to beat. However, choosing the MacBook means giving up the Yoga's 2-in-1 versatility and included pen.

Considering that the two laptops cost roughly the same in the configurations I tested, your choice will largely come down to pen support and whether you prefer Apple's ecosystem or Lenovo's more flexible design.

RTX Spark-powered laptops like this one aren’t really mainstream. They are more specialized notebooks focused on running local AI and taking advantage of native CUDA cores and the unified memory setup in this new chip from Nvidia. This makes them more of a laptop for developers and those who might want to run local agent platforms.

I tested this myself by downloading LM Studio and loading the Qwen 3.8-27b model. I took the Yoga 9n 2-in-1 offline and asked the model to write a 30-chapter novel about an earthquake in NYC and to describe the government falling apart and the city descending into chaos. The model produced an answer in 6 minutes and 20 seconds.

My final project for a college creative writing class was similar, so I was especially interested in seeing what the local model could produce. The chapters were relatively short and didn't include nearly as much detail as my own writing, yet the model still produced a coherent story. I was impressed by how much it could accomplish entirely on the laptop without an internet connection.

Out of curiosity, I also ran UL Procyon’s Text Gen benchmark. Across all the workloads, it scored 2,635, 2,346, 2,274, and 2,148. This was with the Phi-3.5-mini, Mistral 7B, Llama-3.1-8B, and Llama-2-13B LLM instruct models using CUDA acceleration.

We don’t run these tests on every Windows laptop and Mac, so I have no reference to compare them to, but those numbers look great. According to UL’s own scoring page, scores are in the lower 200s for Intel Core Ultra chips and in the 1,000s for Snapdragon X2 Elite chips. This shows that this first-gen ARM chip from Nvidia is in a great place for AI performance.

For now, the most compelling reason to buy an RTX Spark laptop is its ability to run local AI workloads. That's a much more specialized use case than everyday productivity or gaming, and it's something worth considering before spending this much on a laptop.

The Yoga 9n 2-in-1 isn't designed to be a conventional productivity laptop. Nvidia's RTX Spark platform places a strong emphasis on AI, but that doesn't mean you can't use it for everyday work, creative applications, or even gaming.

For my typical laptop workload, the Yoga is more than capable. I regularly juggle Chrome tabs, Slack, and other applications while working in the lab, and I have no major issues keeping everything running smoothly. Photoshop works well for photo editing, and I have no trouble using Wondershare Filmora on Windows 11.

In other words, for everyday tasks, the Yoga 9n 2-in-1 was a perfectly capable replacement for my MacBook. The raw performance benchmark results, however, tell a different story and are a downside of this laptop.

For raw processing power, the Yoga 9n 2-in-1 struggles to justify its premium price. I give Nvidia credit for delivering competitive performance from its first-generation Arm chip. However, there's still a noticeable gap in demanding creative applications.

The MacBook Pro 16-inch M5 Max PROLED XDR outperformed Lenovo’s laptop across our major productivity and creative benchmarks, with particularly large leads in Geekbench 6 and Premiere Pro.

The Yoga scored 13,437 in Photoshop and 85,779 in Premiere Pro. Apple's MacBook Pro was also considerably faster in both, completing the test in 7,75 minutes in Photoshop and 4,47 minutes in Premiere Pro.

Lenovo Yoga 9n 2-in-1 (RTX Spark, 64GB RAM)

MacBook Pro 16-inch M5 Max PROLED XDR (M5 Max, 128GB RAM)

HP OmniBook Ultra 16 (RTX Spark, 32GB RAM)

In Geekbench 6, the Yoga scored 3,076 single-core and 20,084 multi-core. That's ahead of the Samsung Galaxy Book 6 Ultra (2,852 and 16,655) and puts it almost neck and neck with the HP OmniBook Ultra 16, which has RTX Spark (3,165 / 20,056). However, the MacBook Pro M5 Max remains considerably ahead at 4,359 single-core and 30,327 multi-core.

The results are particularly interesting when comparing the Yoga against my older 16-inch MacBook Pro M3 Max. Apple's previous-generation high-end chip scored 3,162 in Geekbench 6 single-core and 21,250 in multi-core. While the Yoga comes surprisingly close, it still falls behind. Its HandBrake result of 2:00, however, comfortably beats my older MacBook's 2:37.

The takeaway is that Nvidia's first-generation RTX Spark platform delivers solid everyday performance and competitive results in certain creative workloads. However, the Yoga doesn't consistently outperform newer high-end, near-fully specced-out MacBooks, making it harder to justify spending $3,999 if raw processing power is your priority.

Gaming and Nvidia go hand in hand, and this Yoga can certainly run demanding games. However, RTX Spark isn't a ticket to high-end gaming performance. Developers need to optimize their games for the new Arm-based architecture, or the games won't run at all. That's why I found out that some games from our lab's catalog (like Red Dead Redemption 2) won’t run at all. Others, like Far Cry 6, also misbehaved and didn’t run properly.

I technically can't play Forza Horizon 6 on my MacBook, so the Yoga still has the edge for my gaming needs. I enjoyed playing it with extreme settings and ray tracing enabled, and it averaged 38 frames per second at 1080p. Increasing the resolution dropped it to 23 fps, though. That's playable, but hardly the kind of performance you’d expect from a $3,999 laptop.

Assassin’s Creed Shadows (Medium, 1080p, 1880p)

Cyberpunk 2077 (Ray Tracing Ulta, 1080p, 1880p)

The results are more mixed in other games. In Cyberpunk 2077, the Yoga managed 34.55 fps at 1080p with Ray Tracing Ultra enabled, putting it in the same general range as the other laptops we tested. At higher resolution, it actually outperforms the MacBook and Samsung, although the HP was slightly ahead. Assassin's Creed Shadows is less impressive, with the Yoga reaching just 25 fps at 1080p.

Our synthetic benchmarks tell a similar story. In 3DMark Wild Life Extreme, the Yoga scored 21,830, averaging 130.21 fps. That's slightly behind the HP OmniBook Ultra 16, which scored 22,978 and averaged 137 fps.

Compared to a MacBook, the Yoga can game, but these results put it closer to an RTX 5070 gaming laptop. It won’t be a compelling choice if gaming is your main priority. You can get a more capable gaming laptop for this kind of money.

The top reason I love my MacBook Pro is its battery life, since I only have to charge it at most three times a week. When I tried to replace my Mac with the Yoga 9n 2-in-1, I quickly learned that this system can’t match what my MacBook Pro delivers. Even lab results show that this Yoga is behind the competition.

I put the Yoga 9n 2-in-1 through my daily workflow and started the day fully charged. With the screen at a comfortable 33% brightness, I worked through spreadsheets in Google Sheets, talking to my coworkers on Slack, and taking the occasional Google Meet meeting. By the time 3:30 got around, the battery was down to 62%. That was more than enough for when I got home, but after two hours of watching YouTube videos and cartoons on Hulu, I got the recharge warning and had to plug the laptop into power.

In our lab tests, MacBook Pro 16-inch (M5 Max PROLED XDR) claims first place with a marathon runtime of 21:24, followed in second by the Samsung Galaxy Book 6 Ultra at a solid 15:11. The Lenovo Yoga 9i 2-in-1 takes third place with 12:20, leaving the HP OmniBook Ultra 16 (RTX Spark) in fourth at 10:52.

Lenovo’s RTX Spark 2-in-1 is ahead of HP’s, but the numbers don’t lie: the Yoga 9n isn’t the best for battery life.

Lenovo’s Yoga 9n 2-in-1 is an expensive proposition. As configured, our unit costs $3,999 directly from Lenovo. The same configuration is slightly cheaper at Best Buy for $3,749.99. If you want to save money, you can also pick up the entry-level model with the N1X 18-Core Processor, 32GB RAM, and a 512GB SSD for $3,199.99 from Lenovo or $3,099 from Best Buy.

Those prices are pretty wild, but the ongoing RAM crisis and the tough economy are what contribute to them. Apple’s MacBooks are around the same price and, frankly, arguably deliver better performance.

You can get a 16-inch MacBook Pro with the NanoTexture PROLED XDR display, M5 Pro chip, 24GB RAM, and a 1TB SSD for $3,549.99. That’s still cheaper than the Yoga 9n 2-in-1. If you remove the nano-texture display, you can also upgrade to an M5 Max chip with an 18-core CPU, a 32-core GPU, 36GB RAM, and 2TB of storage for $4,799.99. That’s about $800 more than the Yoga, but you’d get more storage and a better screen.

The point is that these RTX Spark machines are not cheap. Most people shouldn’t consider buying them, since their use case is more specialized for AI than anything else. You can take that money and put it toward a brand-new MacBook Pro instead. Or, if you’re really on a budget, invest that $3,999 in a better Windows laptop like the Samsung Galaxy Book 6 Ultra, known for its OLED screen and battery life.

The Lenovo Yoga 9n 2-in-1 is an intriguing, beautifully built hybrid that serves as an impressive canvas for Nvidia’s RTX Spark platform. Thanks to a stunning 16-inch OLED touchscreen, included stylus, versatile 360-degree hinge, and local AI power, there is plenty to like. During my two weeks with it, the Yoga easily replaced my MacBook Pro for everyday productivity tasks like web browsing, Slack, and multimedia consumption.

However, at $3,999 as tested, it doesn't quite earn the title of "MacBook Killer." For heavy creative professionals, it might not be a strong enough MacBook replacement, given its weaker raw processing power in demanding benchmarks and rendering tasks. Likewise, due to its poor battery life, it simply didn't fit into my lifestyle the way my long-lasting Mac does.

If your daily workflow hinges on running local AI models on a flexible 2-in-1 canvas, the Yoga 9n will be for you. But for most power users seeking maximum performance and all-day endurance, a high-end MacBook Pro remains the smarter investment.

#3361. Aura's Second E-Ink Picture Frame Is Much Improved, and Much Cheaper

Last year, Aura released the Aura Ink, its first digital photo frame using an e-ink display rather than the LCD screens common to the other devices that made them the major player in the market (Aura customers have already uploaded more than one billion photos this year alone). When I reviewed the original 13-inch Aura Ink last year, I recommended it, with a few major reservations. Today, Aura announced its second-generation 10-inch Ink frame, and while I wouldn't exactly say they've solved every one of my issues, the new device is significantly improved—and much cheaper.

Most digital photo frames will remind you of an iPad with a decorative border around it. They're great for displaying hundreds of your photos with vibrant color, but not everyone loves the look, or the fact that these frames always need to be plugged in. An e-ink frame, on the other hand, uses a variant of the sort of low-power screen you'd find in a Kindle Colorsoft—less bright, but more paperlike, and much closer to the look of a traditionally printed photo.The Aura Ink is a great choice if you want a digital frame that looks more like a "real" photo and doesn't need to be plugged in and doesn't light up like a tablet (though it does have a light, it's really to make up for the fact that color e-ink screens don't reflect light very well, and thus can make your pictures look way too dark without an additional boost). You'll still get all the benefits of an LCD frame like the Aura Aspen, including the ability to load photos from anywhere using the versatile Aura app (you can now even text them directly to the frame), but you'll only need to charge it once every few months.

Now for the downsides: Where most digital frames allow you to flick between photos with a swipe, the Aura Ink is much more sluggish—switching from one photo to another takes about 45 seconds. While an LCD can match the colors in your photo exactly, e-ink uses a "dithering algorithm" to blend tiny pixels together to create the illusion of different hues ("millions" of them, according to Aura). In practice, this means up close, your pictures will look rather grainy, and the colors won't be nearly as bright as what you see on your phone screen.

All of that said, the Aura Ink is a great product, provided you know what you're buying, and the new 10-inch model offers some big upgrades over the 13-inch original released in 2025:

Resolution has been bumped up from 150 ppi to 200 ppi, so your images look more detailed and less grainy. (Though the difference is hard to capture in a photo, I can definitely see the improvement when comparing them side-by-side.)

Instead of the six base colors available on the older frame, the 10-inch Aura Ink blends nine different hues to approximate the colors in your images, offering greater color accuracy and improved contrast.

The transition effect when you move between photos has been updated to look more intentional—like waves of color moving across the screen versus a series of increasingly intense flashes.

It's a heck of a lot cheaper: $349, versus $499 for the 13-inch model—though that's still significantly pricier than Aura's most popular offering, the 10.1-inch Aura Carver, which starts around $200 less.

I write a lot about e-ink devices, from e-readers to tablets, and my common refrain, especially with color devices, is that they're great at what they do, but you should understand what they do before you plunk down your money. The Aura Ink will never look as bright and colorful as an LCD frame, and if you want a frame that can switch between images every few minutes or even play video, you'll need to look elsewhere (to maximize battery life, Aura recommends swapping photos on the Aura Ink no more than 12 times per day).

But if you want to display photos that look more like the ones that hung on the walls of your childhood home, in a frame that doesn't need to be plugged in all the time, you'll probably dig it, provided you can stomach the $350 price tag.

#3358. Ring’s wheeled and flying robots will patrol your home

Some people use a whole bunch of fixed cameras to monitor their homes, but Amazon has just announced a more flexible solution through wheeled and flying robots.

Both the $250 Drone Cam and $1,000 Rover Cam can respond to alarms or door and window sensor alerts in order to go check out what’s happening and send live video …

Amazon says they are the first two Ring Robotics products, with more likely to follow. Both are autonomous.

Ring Drone and Ring Rover are both powered by AI Pilot, a custom-built system that uses the devices’ cameras, specialized vision models, on-device sensors, and cloud processing to see, think, and navigate autonomously.

AI Pilot simplifies the customer experience, starting with setup. Simply carry Ring Drone through your space or let Ring Rover autonomously explore, and it turns what it sees into a floor plan. It intelligently identifies rooms and suggests patrol points: spots worth extra attention. This could be a side door, windows, a register, or a long corridor, helping eliminate guesswork while also allowing you to add additional points customized to your space and security preferences.

When a patrol or flight is initiated, AI Pilot plans the most efficient route to get to a preset point based on the map it’s created. From there, it reacts in real time—autonomously navigating around furniture, shelving, and any obstacle it encounters.

You can set either device to patrol on a fixed schedule, as well as activate them manually, but they will also automatically respond to sensor alerts and alarms.

When a Ring camera, sensor, or alarm is triggered, [either device] automatically [moves] to previously set patrol points to investigate […] Continuous person motion detection means Ring Rover can alert you and start recording the moment it detects motion in its view—even when docked.

The Ring Rover Cam will begin shipping on December 16 for $999.99, but you can preorder it today. The Drone Cam starts shipping in late January for $249.99, but there’s no preorder yet.

#3355. Adobe unveils new AI tools for Photoshop, Premiere, and more, with MCP support coming in 2027

Adobe today announced a sweeping set of updates at its annual Adobe MAX conference, focused on giving users more ways to automate complex workflows, edit content, and work across its creative apps. Here are the details.

At the Adobe MAX event today, the company unveiled a series of features, many of them AI-powered or AI-assisted, that will begin rolling out across its suite of creative platforms as early as today.

In Photoshop, the new Relight tool offers a way to non-destructively and dynamically add, reposition, and resize light sources in the composition, while Generative Restylelets users** prompt the platform to generate variations of an image’s style and fine-tune the results using adjustable sliders.

Photoshop is also adding a Quick Compare slider to make it easier to track before-and-after results, and is getting several features in the beta app, including, per Adobe:

Following its acquisition of Topaz Labs, Adobe is also introducing two new AI image enhancement models: Wonder 4, which combines upscaling, denoising, deblurring, and sharpening into a single operation, and Image HDR, which converts standard images into HDR with improved brightness and detail.

Adobe Premiere is also getting generative tools that make it easier to prepare raw files for a project, including Enhance Audio, Separate Crosstalk, and Separate Sound Source. Adobe is also adding a Generative Remove tool to Premiere in beta, “bringing you the power to remove unwanted objects, like boom mics and logos or background distractions, directly on your timeline,” says the company.

Premiere is also getting Color Mode, a new color-grading tool starting today, which “supports everything from quick corrections to more advanced grades while keeping your video as the focus.”

Another interesting tool making its way into Premiere is Generative Media Tool. Here’s Adobe:

The Generative Media Tool brings Generate Video, Generate Sound Effects, Generate Soundscape and Generate Music directly into your timeline in Premiere. You can generate missing b-roll, background music or sound for a scene using context from your edit, then keep refining the result in your timeline. You can also choose from Adobe Firefly and models from partners including Google, Kling, Runway and Luma based on the creative needs of your project.

As for iPhone users who rely on Premiere Mobile, Adobe announced that its newly established partnerships with UMG and WMG will bring hundreds of thousands of licensed music tracks to the app (for non-commercial use) starting today, with users able to explore trending songs, discover featured artists, and create videos using artist-inspired templates.

Premiere mobile is also getting agentic tools soon, including Quick Cuts, which generates a first cut based on the user’s prompt and the materials they add, and an AI Assistant, which helps users find the right editing tools and execute tasks based on natural language instructions.

In Lightroom, the company is adding multiple new tools that make it easier to edit or more quickly fix small imperfections. That includes Glow, which “adds soft, cinematic light to your photos,” Blemish Removal for quick skin fine-tuning, Open Eyes in beta, and an improved and expanded Camera Tethering on Desktop and the iPad, with support for more cameras and advanced shooting controls, plus the ability to connect cameras directly to an iPad for live previews and photo editing.

Adobe is adding new brushes, gradients, patterns, and graphic styles to Illustrator, alongside new Blend controls, which “make it easier to develop and refine designs with a persistent control panel and live preview,” per the company.

As for InDesign, a new Co-editing feature, available in beta, streamlines collaborative work, while the new Flex Layout tool dynamically adjusts content based on the canvas size and artwork. InDesign is also getting Check Document and Rewrite that more quickly “help identify common editorial and accessibility issues while you’re still working.”

While it will not launch until 2027, this feature will enable users to connect Photoshop, Illustrator, Premiere, and After Effects to the AI tools and agents they already use.

In practice, this will mean connecting Photoshop to ChatGPT and having them work in tandem to adapt an entire campaign based on new artwork you develop and attach to your prompt.

This integration will also account for other connected tools, so the user can ask ChatGPT to make edits, add new files to a Google Drive folder, update the team on Slack, and so on.

Here’s Adobe on the upcoming MCP integration:

Because it runs locally on your computer, your agent works directly in your native project files, and your layers, vectors, bins and sequences stay editable.

The company notes that MCP integrations will enter private beta in early 2027, and users can sign up here to learn more.

According to Adobe, Firefly is getting even better at helping users organize and edit their raw material for tasks such as turning travel clips into a vlog, creating social media campaigns, or assembling videos from storyboards.

The new Firefly Video lets users organize scenes, assemble clips, add captions, and generate transitions and B-roll, while Firefly Design brings illustration, image editing, animation, and 3D tools into a single canvas.

Adobe is also adding Quick Actions for common editing tasks, Firefly Graph for creating reusable workflows, and Firefly Builder (in private beta) for prototyping websites and apps using natural language.

Firefly’s AI Assistant is also getting new capabilities, including Plan Mode, which lets users review and approve an agent’s proposed actions, and Model Selector, which lets them choose which AI model to use.

Adobe is also previewing Always-on agents, which can handle recurring tasks such as organizing assets, checking quality, and preparing content for different platforms in the background, even when users step away.

Adobe is also expanding its Creative Agent across Creative Cloud, with AI Assistants now available in beta in Illustrator, Premiere, InDesign, After Effects, and Frame.io, as well as the Photoshop beta app.

These assistants allow users to execute complex, multi-step tasks using natural language prompts. In Premiere, for example, users can ask the assistant to apply effects to an entire sequence, track subjects across frames, or adjust color and exposure across multiple clips.

To learn more about these and other features announced at Adobe MAX today, stay tuned to the company’s blog.

#3354. 'GTA 6' Runs Best on This Console

Grand Theft Auto 6 might just be the most anticipated game of all time. It's been 13 years since Rockstar dropped GTA 5, and after years of rumors, leaks, and official announcements, the sixth mainstream installment in the series is nearly here. In fact, anyone who pre-ordered the game digitally can now pre-load it onto their console, if you want to ensure you're ready to play the second the game comes out.

Now, few of us will buy a game console specifically for GTA 6—unless you don't already have a current-generation PlayStation or Xbox. (The PC version of the game isn't expected until at least early 2027.) But, as it turns out, there's one specific console that can run GTA 6 better than the rest.

Rockstar confirmed as much in a post on Tuesday, which was meant to spread the news about pre-loading the game. But, interestingly, it spurred a discussion about the performance of the game itself, as well as which consoles are best to run it.

No matter which console you play GTA 6 on, Rockstar says that the game will only target 30 fps (frames per second). That's decided slow for a mainstream game in 2026. GTA 5 also shipped at 30 fps in 2013, but newer consoles can run it at higher frame rates. In fact, most games that launch on the latest generation of consoles can run at 60 fps, if not higher. While it's certainly not a dealbreaker, it is interesting that Rockstar's latest game can't run at a faster frame rate even on the PS5 Pro or the Xbox Series X.

To that point, Rockstar called out the PS5 Pro specifically in its post, announcing, "The PlayStation 5 Pro offers breathtaking visuals, with improved clarity through PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (PSSR) and ray-traced shadows only available on PlayStation 5 Pro."

PSSR is Sony's AI upscaler, similar to options like DLSS from Nvidia, which uses AI to add extra graphical information to games in real time. That allows developers like Rockstar to run the game at a lower resolution to save on processing power, but still boost the visuals to reach a higher perceived resolution. As such, it's not as ideal as running the game at a higher resolution natively, but it can help improve the visuals without pushing the hardware beyond its limits. Meanwhile, ray-tracing offers realistic lighting effects and can also be graphically intense.

While PlayStation and Xbox players alike will be stuck at 30 fps, it seems only PS5 Pro gamers will be able to play the game with ray-tracing effects and AI upscaling. It's surprising that Xbox Series X players don't have similar benefits, as the hardware is more powerful than Xbox Series S. Rockstar didn't specify why only the PS5 Pro gets these upgrades.

In the post, Rockstar also announced that the PS5 version of GTA 6 takes advantage of other PlayStation-exclusive perks, like high-fidelity haptic feedback in the DualSense controller, spatial audio rendering using the PlayStation's Tempest 3D audio, as well as improved load times—though Rockstar didn't specify what those load times would be. These perks apply to all PS5 consoles, not just PS5 Pros. Rockstar goes so far as to say that GTA 6 plays best on PlayStation 5 consoles.

That's not to say that Microsoft's consoles are totally left out of the perks. Rockstar says that GTA 6 will be available on Xbox Cloud Gaming on both Xbox Series X and S, as well as Xbox One. In addition, both PlayStation and Xbox gamers can play GTA 6 using Remote Play, so no one has to physically play on their console if they want to game on the go.

Again, there's no reason to go out and buy a specific console for GTA 6, so long as you have something that can run the game. After all, PS5 Pros are difficult to find, especially without wildly overpaying. But it's interesting that Rockstar has managed to give Sony's consoles the extra perks here, particularly since the company hasn't explained why that is.

Following the recent update to the iPad mini, we’re expecting the iPad Air to be next in line to be upgraded to an OLED screen.

OLED screens were initially exclusive to the iPad Pro. That finally changed last month when Apple gave the iPad mini its biggest update in years. The new model is thinner and lighter and powered by an A20 Pro chip, while the headline news is the new OLED screen.

#3351. Lifehacker's Pick for the Best TV to Gift in 2026 Isn't Actually a TV

Welcome to Holiday Office Hours From the Labs, a collaborative multimedia project in which Lifehacker, CNET, ZDNET, and Mashable harness the power of our product testing laboratory and our editors' expertise to offer the best gift-buying recommendations possible. In this episode, we're talking televisions.

I recently did a deep dive into TV development history, checked out what was on shelves for 2026, and I concluded that the best gift TV you can give this year is, actually, a pair of sunglasses. The XBX by XReal video display glasses are basically a TV you can shove in your pocket. Check them out:

I looked past traditional sets for a couple of reasons. First, because as much as we all love a great show or movie, who actually buys someone a TV set as a gift? More importantly, there's the nature of television itself. Since it was invented in the late 1920s, television quality has been measured by how big the screen is and how clear and bright the picture is, but in 2026, a nothing-special 4K television delivers an image that is pixel-invisible to a typical viewer, and most of us don't have living rooms big enough to need a display bigger than 65 inches. I think the innovation in the space is going to come from the form factor and the use case, and what better form factor is there than a pair of sunglasses?

These glasses deliver the equivalent of a 142" TV viewed from across the room. It's hard to compare resolution to traditional TVs—technically, the display is 1080p in each eye, but because the TV is just millimeters from your eye, it looks much clearer than that. The peak brightness is 1,600 nits, bright enough for most rooms, and there's a totally opaque shield if you need it. The refresh rate is a crisp 120Hz. They support HDR10 and real-time SDR-to-HDR upscaling, offer billions of colors, and it's all in a package that weighs only 62 grams.

Then there are the use cases. It can act as a separate monitor for your computer; you can watch a different show than your roommate without bothering them; but most of all, these are great for flights. There is no situation in life that calls for a big screen TV more than a cross-country airplane flight. Slip these on with a pair of headphones, and you can fly to Boise in your own private, virtual theater.

They plug right into any device that supports USB-C video, there's no battery to remember to charge, and they cost less than $300. In other words: They're the perfect TV gift for the holidays, even if they aren't technically a TV.

#3350. Screens 5.10 adds two highly-requested remote desktop features

Screens, the remote desktop app for iPhone, iPad, Mac, and Apple Vision Pro, is adding two highly-requested features. Version 5.10 introduces remote Mac audio and automatic desktop resizing through Apple’s High Performance Screen Sharing technology.

The remote desktop can now adjust to your screen when you rotate your iPhone or iPad, change your multitasking layout, or resize a connection window on Mac and Vision Pro. You can also choose a fixed resolution.

Remote audio lets you hear sound from a compatible Mac, while HEVC streaming promises smoother video, scrolling, and animations.

The update also introduces a Metal-based renderer designed to improve performance across connections, including Windows, Linux, and Raspberry Pi.

Other changes include a Liquid Glass connection carousel and floating toolbar improvements on iPhone and iPad.

Edovia’s announcement has the full rundown. Screens 5.10 is available on the App Store as a free download with in-app purchases. Subscriptions start at $4.99/month or $29.99/year, with a $199.99 lifetime option also available.

#3348. Apple’s new HomeView to add two major features not yet announced, per leaks

Apple’s HomeView arrives this Friday (pre-order here), but leaks indicate there are already two major new features in the works that haven’t been announced. Here’s what to expect.

It’s been a busy product launch season for Apple, and the company isn’t done quite yet.

Two new Home products arrive in stores this Friday, November 13: Apple HomeView and the new Apple TV 4K.

Yet despite the HomeView still being days away from launch, leaks in Apple code have already revealed two unannounced features that are in the works.

Leaker pdfu discovered evidence in HomeView 27.2 software that Apple is preparing for the product to add security camera functionality.

Based on pdfu’s findings, much of the work has already been done for HomeView to integrate with HomeKit Secure Video.

However, Apple hasn’t announced any sort of security camera functionality, so there’s clearly still more work to be done and it’s always possible the feature is never enabled.

Additionally, pdfu found a key change in iOS 27.3’s beta that reveals support for third-party AI apps is coming to HomeView.

HomeView has a unique third-party app story. There’s no App Store, but the product can run CarPlay-compatible apps from your iPhone automatically. At launch, only audio and video apps will be supported.

But iOS 27.3’s beta code adds “conversational apps” as a third category of supported apps. That’s what AI chatbots like ChatGPT and Claude are classified as in CarPlay.

Nobody should buy a HomeView in the hope of these two features being added. But if you are interested in HomeView, it sounds like Apple has an ambitious set of software updates planned for its new product.

You can pre-order Apple’s HomeView here for $299.

#3347. What to Expect From Best Buy's 2026 Black Friday and Cyber Monday Sales

For all intents and purposes, Black Friday sales are already here. There are plenty of deals out already, even though we're weeks away from the actual event. One of the reasons for that is the competition retailers have with each other to be the first to get your money. One of the retailers that is making the biggest early splash is Best Buy, confirming their entire plan for the rest of the year. Here's what you need to know.

Best Buy has announced the following events:

DoorBoosters: A Halloween sale from Oct. 30 to Nov. 1.

Early Black Friday Deals and Doorbusters: The official start of early Black Friday deals on Nov. 6. New deals will drop every Friday.

Black Friday Doorbusters and Deals: Best Buy says this will be its main sale, starting on Thursday, Nov. 19 and running until Nov. 28 with deals on "computing, gaming, home theater, wearables, and more."

Cyber Sunday and Monday: Best Buy is extending Cyber Monday to five days and says you can find deals going up to 50% off select tech.

Last-minute savings: The Christmas sale will run from Dec. 18 until Dec. 24.

You don't need to be any kind of member to shop Best Buy's Black Friday in July sale; however, it is free to sign up for a My Best Buy membership, which will get you free shipping. If you join one of their paid subscriptions (My Best Buy Plus for $49.99 per year or My Best Buy Total for $179.99 per year), you'll get faster free shipping, exclusive prices and deals, an extended 60-day return window on most products, and access to select sales, like the Member Deals Days sale that is going on right now. Paid members will also earn extra rewards from both the current sale and the upcoming Black Friday in July sale.

You can find deals on TVs, laptops, headphones, video games, electric bikes, and more. There will be new deals every week in stores, on its website, and in the Best Buy mobile app. They'll offer price matching, meaning if the price drops further during the sale (Dec. 24), they will match it and offer a refund.

Here are the best deals I've found so far. I'll be updating these deals throughout the sale, so make sure to come back and see what's new. Remember that new deals drop every day.

Best Buy price matches its own products, so if a product drops in price later, you'd get those savings too, but it does not cover any deals coming from a competitor's Black Friday sale. There are some other important exceptions you can read in more detail here.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

The other major retailers doing Black Friday sales are Amazon, Target, and Walmart. Currently, Amazon has many early deals, seeing their lowest prices yet. Target has some week-long deals and a Deal of the Day. Walmart will have three Black Friday and Cyber Monday shopping events. Nowadays, large retailers and small businesses compete for Cyber Monday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, Nov. 30, 2026.

No. If you find the product you're looking for with a major discount right now, get it. It's not likely to drop any lower, but it could always run out of stock. Take advantage of price matching or guarantees instead of waiting. Remember, you can always return products later if you change your mind. For the majority of products, the deal from Black Friday will be the same one on Cyber Monday.

#3343. 10 Google Privacy Hacks Everyone Should Know

Your Gmail account doesn't just have one email address. In fact, it has unlimited addresses, but you need a hack to utilize them. When you're signing up for a new service, you can add another word to your email address, as well as the "+" symbol, to create an alias. For example, if your email is "[email protected]," and you're signing up for an Amazon account, you can use "[email protected]" as your email address. The email will still end up in your main inbox, as if you simply used [email protected]. Not only can this trick turn one Gmail address into an unlimited number of addresses, but it also helps you identify who sold your email address to spammers, because those emails will have the alias in the "To" field.

Gmail's web view has a crucial security feature that lets you view session logs. This feature is inexplicably buried at the bottom of the inbox, and the font size is tiny, so it's easy to miss. To find it, log in to Gmail on the web, and scroll to the bottom of your inbox. Click the Details button in the bottom-right corner, below "Last account activity." This will show you a pop-up that lists the devices, apps, and locations you've recently logged in from. This makes it easy to see if there's been any suspicious activity in your Google account, and you can click the Security Checkup link in the pop-up to review this data. Just note that if you use a VPN or a service like iCloud Private Relay, you might not recognize your own device's location. To check if unwanted apps have access to your Google account, you can visit this settings page.

Google wants to show you personalized search results, which initially feels very helpful, but it also ends up trapping you in an algorithmic bubble. The best way to break out of your search bubble is to periodically use other search engines, but if you wish to stick to Google, you can disable personalized search recommendations in Google Search and the Play Store on Android. Go to this settings page, and turn off Personalized Recommendations and Play Personalization.

Google tracks your web and app activity by default, which includes your search history, voice data (if you use the speak-to-search feature), and activity from sites, apps, and devices that use Google services. However, associated information, such as your location data, is also saved to your Google profile, which you might not assume gets included in "Web & app activity." Fortunately, you can disable this tracking by going to this settings page, scrolling down to "Web & App Activity," and turning off all options in this section.

Google's Timeline feature saves your location in Google Maps to create a map of places you've visited. This is useful if you want to keep track of your recent stops; however, Google can use Timeline data to help businesses see how effective their ads were, or how likely you are to visit nearby stores. Its confirmation page confirms this: "Depending on your settings, activity saved as history in your Google Account, including ad interactions, may also be connected to Timeline data to help nearby businesses estimate the likelihood that people will visit their stores. No personal information is shared with businesses."

Timeline isn't enabled by default, but in case you enabled it a while ago, and are no longer using it, you can turn it off by going to this settings page. Click Turn off, and delete your activity to remove Timeline data from your Google account.

You can't fully escape Google's ads or tracking, but you can disable personalized ads to stop the company from using your account data to show ads. To do this, go to this settings page, and turn off Personalized ads.

While Google claims that it isn't using your emails to train AI, the company does offer AI features that make your emails feel more robotic than human. One of these is "Smart Reply," which offers email reply suggestions such as "Got it. See you soon." I can type that on my own, and I feel uncomfortable with Gmail analyzing the contents of my emails and replies to offer suggestions that I wouldn't use anyway. You can disable this by going to Gmail Settings > General, or by visiting this settings page. Scroll down to "Smart features," and turn off the checkbox next to it. This will disable Smart Compose, Smart Reply, suggestions for pending replies and follow-ups, spelling, grammar, and autocorrect.

A physical security key is a great security upgrade. It's a physical barrier that prevents most ways to hack into your account remotely. Even if someone discovers your email ID and password, and has access to your two-factor authentication code, they won't get in without physical access to that key. You can check out Google's support page for physical security keys for more information on compatibility and setting up your security keys.

Google uses data from Gmail and Google Drive to target ads, which means that your emails, files, and photos could be used for monetization. To stop this, you'll need to disable Personal Intelligence. To turn it off, visit this settings page, and click Turn off Personal Intelligence.

#3342. Atomically Thin Materials Significantly Shrink Qubits

MIT researchers use 2D materials for capacitors in quantum circuits in an effort to scale processors

Superconducting quantum processor and its microwave packaging.

Quantum computing is a devilishly complex technology, with many technical hurdles impacting its development. Of these challenges two critical issues stand out: miniaturization and qubit quality.

IBM has adopted the superconducting qubit road map of reaching a 1,121-qubit processor by 2023, leading to the expectation that 1,000 qubits with today’s qubit form factor is feasible. However, current approaches will require very large chips (50 millimeters on a side, or larger) at the scale of small wafers, or the use of chiplets on multichip modules. While this approach will work, the aim is to attain a better path toward scalability.

Now researchers at MIT have been able to both reduce the size of the qubits and done so in a way that reduces the interference that occurs between neighboring qubits. The MIT researchers have increased the number of superconducting qubits that can be added onto a device by a factor of 100.

“We are addressing both qubit miniaturization and quality,” said William Oliver, the director for the Center for Quantum Engineering at MIT. “Unlike conventional transistor scaling, where only the number really matters, for qubits, large numbers are not sufficient, they must also be high-performance. Sacrificing performance for qubit number is not a useful trade in quantum computing. They must go hand in hand.”

The key to this big increase in qubit density and reduction of interference comes down to the use of two-dimensional materials, in particular the 2D insulator hexagonal boron nitride (hBN). The MIT researchers demonstrated that a few atomic monolayers of hBN can be stacked to form the insulator in the capacitors of a superconducting qubit.

Just like other capacitors, the capacitors in these superconducting circuits take the form of a sandwich in which an insulator material is sandwiched between two metal plates. The big difference for these capacitors is that the superconducting circuits can operate only at extremely low temperatures—less than 0.02 degrees above absolute zero (-273.15 °C).

Superconducting qubits are measured at temperatures as low as 20 millikelvin in a dilution refrigerator.Nathan Fiske/MIT

In that environment, insulating materials that are available for the job, such as PE-CVD silicon oxide or silicon nitride, have quite a few defects that are too lossy for quantum computing applications. To get around these material shortcomings, most superconducting circuits use what are called coplanar capacitors. In these capacitors, the plates are positioned laterally to one another, rather than on top of one another.

As a result, the intrinsic silicon substrate below the plates and to a smaller degree the vacuum above the plates serve as the capacitor dielectric. Intrinsic silicon is chemically pure and therefore has few defects, and the large size dilutes the electric field at the plate interfaces, all of which leads to a low-loss capacitor. The lateral size of each plate in this open-face design ends up being quite large (typically 100 by 100 micrometers) in order to achieve the required capacitance.

In an effort to move away from the large lateral configuration, the MIT researchers embarked on a search for an insulator that has very few defects and is compatible with superconducting capacitor plates.

“We chose to study hBN because it is the most widely used insulator in 2D material research due to its cleanliness and chemical inertness,” said colead author Joel Wang, a research scientist in the Engineering Quantum Systems group of the MIT Research Laboratory for Electronics.

On either side of the hBN, the MIT researchers used the 2D superconducting material, niobium diselenide. One of the trickiest aspects of fabricating the capacitors was working with the niobium diselenide, which oxidizes in seconds when exposed to air, according to Wang. This necessitates that the assembly of the capacitor occur in a glove box filled with argon gas.

While this would seemingly complicate the scaling up of the production of these capacitors, Wang doesn’t regard this as a limiting factor.

“What determines the quality factor of the capacitor are the two interfaces between the two materials,” said Wang. “Once the sandwich is made, the two interfaces are “sealed” and we don’t see any noticeable degradation over time when exposed to the atmosphere.”

This lack of degradation is because around 90 percent of the electric field is contained within the sandwich structure, so the oxidation of the outer surface of the niobium diselenide does not play a significant role anymore. This ultimately makes the capacitor footprint much smaller, and it accounts for the reduction in cross talk between the neighboring qubits.

“The main challenge for scaling up the fabrication will be the wafer-scale growth of hBN and 2D superconductors like [niobium diselenide], and how one can do wafer-scale stacking of these films,” added Wang.

Wang believes that this research has shown 2D hBN to be a good insulator candidate for superconducting qubits. He says that the groundwork the MIT team has done will serve as a road map for using other hybrid 2D materials to build superconducting circuits.

Dexter Johnson is a contributing editor at IEEE Spectrum, with a focus on nanotechnology.

#3341. Apple TV launches new sign language accessibility feature

Apple today launched a neat new accessibility feature for the Apple TV streaming service. Users will now have the option to watch with a sign language interpretation for some of Apple’s original movies.

The feature is launching this Friday with the debut of the new film Being Heumann, as well as F1: The Movie. Support for more titles will follow later.

Alongside those two films, Apple said that sign language options will be available for Greyhound and Way of the Warrior Kid later this year, with more to come.

To access the new functionality, you need to be using the Apple TV app on iPhone, iPad or Mac running 27.2 or later. The feature will also be available on some versions of the Apple TV app on other platforms.

By default, the Sign Language controls are hidden. If you want to use the feature, firstly go to the Settings app -> TV app, and enable the Sign Language display.

Then, on eligible titles, a new Sign Language button will appear in the player controls. You can simply toggle to enable, and choose from American Sign Language or British Sign Language modes.

When enabled, a signing interpreter then appears in the corner of the frame, synced with the video playback.

When browsing the catalog, sign language availability will also be shown next to the usual subtitle and audio language information. Users will also be able to search “with ASL” or “with BSL” to find compatible titles.

#3340. Latin Grammys 2026 Winners: The Complete List

On Thursday night, Latin music’s biggest stars took over Las Vegas’ MGM Grand Garden Arena for the Latin Grammys, celebrating the best of 2026.

It’s no surprise that Rosalía made Latin Grammys history when she took home her third Album of the Year award after a night of several wins. Before she opened the ceremony with operatic flair, the Spanish superstar took home four trophies: Best Alternative Album for her showstopping album Lux, Best Pop Song for highlight “La Perla,” and Best Short Form Music Video for “Sauvignon Blanc.”

“The truth is I know I have a lot to learn. I know that I’ve probably made my best work but I know there’s still a lot left to be the best,” Rosalía said in her AOTY acceptance speech. “Thanks, mama, for making me this way. I’m going to bring this Grammy to your house. I don’t know if another one is going to fit in your house, but I’ll bring it to you anyways and see if you make room.You always find a way for anything,” she added.

In another emotional highlight, Karol G took home Best Urban Music Album for her 2025 LP, Tropicoqueta after being award Best Reggaeton Performance before the ceremony. “I’m going to very honest because God willing I’ve been up here a couple of times but this one is special,” the Colombian superstar said in her acceptance speech. “People always hear the end result but making Tropicoqueta meant a lot to me that people can’t even imagine.”

Karol continued: “The most important part is to have an album that I can tour because I feel when I’m singing it, people feel proud to be Latina and to carry their flags with pride. That’s the most beautiful part.” Before she walked off, Karol let out an impassioned yell: “Latina forever!”

Milo J had a big night as well, earning his first Latin Grammys ever and eventually walking home with four awards total. The 20 year-old Argentine musician nabbed Song of the Year for his track “Solifican12” and Best Folk Album for La Vida Era Más Corta.

Argentine duo Ca7riel and Paco Amoroso were early winners of the night, nabbing awards for “Best Electronic Music Performance” and “Best Pop/Rock Song.” With their wins, they helped both Fred Again.. and Sting become first-time Latin Grammy winners. Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

Before the ceremony, superproducer Edgar Barrera led this year’s nominations with 13 nods. Barrera was recognized in the Producer of the Year category and in major categories like Album of the Year and Song of the Year for his work on albums like Karol G‘s Tropicoqueta and Carín León’s Muda, as well as Becky G and Santana’s powerful anti-ICE collaboration.

Trailing him were some of the biggest names in Latin music. Karol G, Rosalía, Ca7riel & Paco Amoroso and Jorge Drexler were all tied with seven nominations each, picking up nods in major categories.

#3339. Garmin Cyclists Can Now Make Themselves Appear on Waze in Real Time

Cyclists who ride with Garmin gear can now appear as live, moving icons on the Waze driving app, and nearby drivers will receive an alert to slow down and watch for them on the road.

For riders already using Garmin devices, opting in costs nothing and adds a new layer of safety, particularly on roads where drivers may not expect cyclists. The feature is rolling out now, but you should be aware of its limitations.

Riders can simply opt in once through Garmin Connect. After that, sharing starts automatically when an outdoor cycling activity begins and stops when the ride ends. While a ride is underway, Waze users near the cyclist see a cyclist icon move along the road and receive a Live Cycling Alert reminding them to slow down and stay aware.

The feature runs on LiveTrack, Garmin's existing live location-sharing tool, which lets friends and family follow a rider's real-time location, speed, course, and more. Garmin says this collaboration extends that peace of mind to motorists, giving them greater awareness of their surroundings.

Garmin notes its location sharing is temporary and session-based. The rider's name, identity, and route are hidden, and no personal information is shared or displayed in Waze. Drivers see only an anonymous icon and the alert.

You'll need a few things to get this feature up and running:

A compatible Garmin Edge bike computer or Garmin watch

A phone running Garmin Connect with a data connection

An outdoor cycling activity (the feature doesn't apply to indoor rides)

The good news is using the feature is free: LiveTrack costs nothing on compatible Garmin bike computers and watches, and Waze is free for drivers.

This new feature is a great safety perk, but there are real-world caveats worth considering:

This feature is for Waze only. Alerts reach drivers only when Waze is open on their phone. Google Maps, which has far more users, is excluded, so a large portion of the drivers you share the road with won't see you this way.

It depends on your phone's signal. Your position travels from the Garmin to your phone, then to Garmin's servers, then to Waze, and finally to the driver's phone. On a patchy rural signal, a few seconds of lag could put the icon on the wrong side of a bend from where you actually are. A rider who leaves their phone at home or whose phone loses signal simply won't show up on a Waze map, as a ride without a data connection is invisible to Waze.

Finally, remember to treat this safety feature as an extra perk, not a guarantee. At the end of the day, it isn't a replacement for bike lights, bright clothing, and defensive riding.

#3338. iPadOS 27.3 adds new iPad setting I instantly turned on

iPadOS 27.3 is currently available in beta, and it introduces a new iPad setting for app windowing that I instantly turned on. Here are the details.

I use the iPad Pro as my primary computer, and for the most part have found Apple’s software changes in iPadOS 26 and 27 to be great upgrades.

But with the powerful new windowing capabilities, there have definitely been some quirks that need refining. One of them involves resizing windows with the traffic light controls in the top-left corner.

For example, in iPadOS 27 the controls move locations and even disappear depending on the size of the window. It can be pretty frustrating.

I need to just get better about learning keyboard shortcuts for window controls. But in the meantime, iPadOS 27.3 adds a new optional setting that I instantly turned on and have been loving.

Inside Settings ⇾ Multitasking & Gestures, if you have ‘Windowed Apps’ enabled you’ll see a new option below it: ‘Double-tap Top of Window to Zoom’

If you use your iPad mostly with touch input, or simply haven’t used keyboard shortcuts enough to remember them, this new setting is a great way to quickly resize windows.

When the setting is enabled, two taps (or a double-click with the trackpad) will zoom the window to take up the full screen. Then you can double-tap again to revert it to its previous size.

I generally keep my app windows in specific size setups, but regularly find myself wanting to go fullscreen temporarily. The new setting provides a convenient way to do that quickly without needing the traffic light controls or my keyboard, and is a welcome refinement to iPadOS windowing.

Will you enable this new iPadOS 27.3 setting? Why or why not? Let us know in the comments.

#3337. Latin Grammys Celebrate 100 Years of José Alfredo Jiménez With Edgar Barrera, The Warning, More

Led by Edgar Barrera, stars at the Latin Grammys honored Mexico’s roots with a touching tribute celebrating the legacy of José Alfredo Jiménez. The late Mexican icon, considered a founding father of regional Mexican music, received a star-studded tribute featuring the Warning, Reik, Sofia Reyes, Yami Safdie, and Camila Fernández.

Barrera led the homage to José Alfredo Jiménez with Mexican rock group the Warning joining him for a stirring performance of “Te Solté la Rienda.” Reik, Reyes, and Yami Safdie took on the classics “La Media Vuelta” and “Si Nos Dejan.” Fernández, who is the granddaughter of another late Mexican legend, Vicente Fernández, brought down the house with a powerful take on “El Rey.” She put a fiercely feminine spin on a song that was written about celebrating a man.

Alfredo Jiménez earned the title of the “king of ranchera music” for his singular songwriting that set the gold standard for regional Mexican music. The Latin Recording Academy’s tribute coincides with the 100 year anniversary of Alfredo Jiménez’s birth. #3336. How AI Will Change Chip Design

Artificial intelligence’s promise and potential for the semiconductor industry

Rina Diane Caballar is a contributing editor covering tech and its intersections with science, society, and the environment.

An array of semiconductor wafers are ready to be made into chips.

The end of Moore’s Law is looming. Engineers and designers can do only so much to miniaturize transistors and pack as many of them as possible into chips. So they’re turning to other approaches to chip design, incorporating technologies like AI into the process.

Samsung, for instance, is adding AI to its memory chips to enable processing in memory, thereby saving energy and speeding up machine learning. Speaking of speed, Google’s TPU V4 AI chip has doubled its processing power compared with that of its previous version.

But AI holds still more promise and potential for the semiconductor industry. To better understand how AI is set to revolutionize chip design, we spoke with Heather Gorr, senior product manager for MathWorks’ MATLAB platform.

How is AI currently being used to design the next generation of chips?

Heather Gorr: AI is such an important technology because it’s involved in most parts of the cycle, including the design and manufacturing process. There’s a lot of important applications here, even in the general process engineering where we want to optimize things. I think defect detection is a big one at all phases of the process, especially in manufacturing. But even thinking ahead in the design process, [AI now plays a significant role] when you’re designing the light and the sensors and all the different components. There’s a lot of anomaly detection and fault mitigation that you really want to consider.

Then, thinking about the logistical modeling that you see in any industry, there is always planned downtime that you want to mitigate; but you also end up having unplanned downtime. So, looking back at that historical data of when you’ve had those moments where maybe it took a bit longer than expected to manufacture something, you can take a look at all of that data and use AI to try to identify the proximate cause or to see something that might jump out even in the processing and design phases. We think of AI oftentimes as a predictive tool, or as a robot doing something, but a lot of times you get a lot of insight from the data through AI.

What are the benefits of using AI for chip design?

Gorr: Historically, we’ve seen a lot of physics-based modeling, which is a very intensive process. We want to do a reduced order model, where instead of solving such a computationally expensive and extensive model, we can do something a little cheaper. You could create a surrogate model, so to speak, of that physics-based model, use the data, and then do your parameter sweeps, your optimizations, your Monte Carlo simulations using the surrogate model. That takes a lot less time computationally than solving the physics-based equations directly. So, we’re seeing that benefit in many ways, including the efficiency and economy that are the results of iterating quickly on the experiments and the simulations that will really help in the design.

So it’s like having a digital twin in a sense?

Gorr: Exactly. That’s pretty much what people are doing, where you have the physical system model and the experimental data. Then, in conjunction, you have this other model that you could tweak and tune and try different parameters and experiments that let sweep through all of those different situations and come up with a better design in the end.

So, it’s going to be more efficient and, as you said, cheaper?

Gorr: Yeah, definitely. Especially in the experimentation and design phases, where you’re trying different things. That’s obviously going to yield dramatic cost savings if you’re actually manufacturing and producing [the chips]. You want to simulate, test, experiment as much as possible without making something using the actual process engineering.

We’ve talked about the benefits. How about the drawbacks?

Gorr: The [AI-based experimental models] tend to not be as accurate as physics-based models. Of course, that’s why you do many simulations and parameter sweeps. But that’s also the benefit of having that digital twin, where you can keep that in mind—it’s not going to be as accurate as that precise model that we’ve developed over the years.

Both chip design and manufacturing are system intensive; you have to consider every little part. And that can be really challenging. It’s a case where you might have models to predict something and different parts of it, but you still need to bring it all together.

One of the other things to think about too is that you need the data to build the models. You have to incorporate data from all sorts of different sensors and different sorts of teams, and so that heightens the challenge.

How can engineers use AI to better prepare and extract insights from hardware or sensor data?

Gorr: We always think about using AI to predict something or do some robot task, but you can use AI to come up with patterns and pick out things you might not have noticed before on your own. People will use AI when they have high-frequency data coming from many different sensors, and a lot of times it’s useful to explore the frequency domain and things like data synchronization or resampling. Those can be really challenging if you’re not sure where to start.

One of the things I would say is, use the tools that are available. There’s a vast community of people working on these things, and you can find lots of examples [of applications and techniques] on GitHub or MATLAB Central, where people have shared nice examples, even little apps they’ve created. I think many of us are buried in data and just not sure what to do with it, so definitely take advantage of what’s already out there in the community. You can explore and see what makes sense to you, and bring in that balance of domain knowledge and the insight you get from the tools and AI.

What should engineers and designers consider when using AI for chip design?

Gorr: Think through what problems you’re trying to solve or what insights you might hope to find, and try to be clear about that. Consider all of the different components, and document and test each of those different parts. Consider all of the people involved, and explain and hand off in a way that is sensible for the whole team.

How do you think AI will affect chip designers’ jobs?

Gorr: It’s going to free up a lot of human capital for more advanced tasks. We can use AI to reduce waste, to optimize the materials, to optimize the design, but then you still have that human involved whenever it comes to decision-making. I think it’s a great example of people and technology working hand in hand. It’s also an industry where all people involved—even on the manufacturing floor—need to have some level of understanding of what’s happening, so this is a great industry for advancing AI because of how we test things and how we think about them before we put them on the chip.

How do you envision the future of AI and chip design?

Gorr: It’s very much dependent on that human element—involving people in the process and having that interpretable model. We can do many things with the mathematical minutiae of modeling, but it comes down to how people are using it, how everybody in the process is understanding and applying it. Communication and involvement of people of all skill levels in the process are going to be really important. We’re going to see less of those superprecise predictions and more transparency of information, sharing, and that digital twin—not only using AI but also using our human knowledge and all of the work that many people have done over the years.

Rina Diane Caballar is a writer covering tech and its intersections with science, society, and the environment. An IEEE Spectrum contributing editor, she's a former software engineer based in New Zealand.
