#3248. Why a Mathematician Is Chasing Eclipses With Algorithms and Cameras

With custom-built gear, his team seeks to solve a long-standing solar mystery

Advanced image-processing software developed by Miloslav Druckmüller combines scores of individual images, captured during a total solar eclipse and painstakingly calibrated. The techniques reveal fine details in the sun’s corona, which is white in this image. The tiny pink shapes seen along portions of the edge of the blacked-out solar disk are prominences, which are extensions of relatively cool plasma that can jut out hundreds of thousands of kilometers into space.

The sun hangs low over the plains of Castile and León, in the north-central region of Spain. But from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza, it appears that a few puffy white clouds have started to block the sun. That’s vexing.

A group of researchers, some wearing cardboard eclipse glasses, is clustered around sets of portable telescopes and cameras connected to laptops. All this gear is scattered on tabletops perched on the mountainside. On the computer screens, the sun’s disk looks like a deep orange crescent that is slowly waning. That’s because the moon began to crawl across it about half an hour ago. In 25 minutes, it will obscure the sun completely, producing an eerie and wondrous phenomenon—a total solar eclipse.

In the late-summer, late-afternoon heat, the researchers watch anxiously as those fluffy clouds linger around the sun. From an abandoned hut on the slope a few meters above, where the researchers have set up camp, one of the grad students emerges and nods toward the cloud formation. “Do you think it will dissolve?” he blurts out.

“It will.” Miloslav Druckmüller glances calmly at his group of doctoral candidates, now making final checks of the equipment in preparation for totality. Here in Spain, on this 12th day of August, Druckmüller is getting ready for his 19th solar eclipse. He knows from long experience that weather can turn quickly when the moon’s shadow suddenly pushes the temperature down. Plus, there’s no sense in riling up the grad students any more than they already are.

Miloslav Druckmüller led the design and construction of a unique optical instrument that incorporates eight astrocameras. Each is equipped with a spectral filter for sensing and recording specific emission spectra from the solar corona. Each of those spectra, in turn, is associated with a particular ionic species of iron atoms. Because the temperature needed to ionize iron varies depending on the ionic species, analyzing the locations and relative abundance of these ionic species offers valuable insights into the distribution of heat in the corona.Václav Široký

During totality, the moon blocks the overwhelming glare of the solar disk, revealing delicate structures in the sun’s outer atmosphere, the corona. Using custom-built telescope systems and image-processing techniques that Druckmüller has spent decades developing, the researchers aim to gain insights into the processes in this enigmatic region that is otherwise hard to study. In addition to imaging the visible coronal light, the team will try to track the dispersal of superhot ions of iron into interplanetary space, which could give rare insights into the pattern of heat emanating from the corona.

And they’ll have 107 seconds to do all that.

Druckmüller is a professor of mathematics and image processing at the Brno University of Technology in the Czech Republic and a leading figure in the Solar Wind Sherpas, an international team that studies the sun’s corona during total eclipses. In the solar eclipse world, he is nothing short of a legend, albeit a reluctant one.

An image from Miloslav Druckmüller’s first solar-eclipse expedition, to Hungary, vividly shows Baily’s Beads. These elongated white lights along a piece of the left edge of the blacked-out solar disk are caused by beams of sunlight shining through gaps in the irregular lunar surface during the eclipse. The pink shapes are solar prominences, which are jets of plasma extending out into space and held in place by the sun’s intense magnetic field.

He photographed his first solar eclipse in 1999, in what he thought would be a one-off lark. During that eclipse, the moon’s deep shadow missed Druckmüller’s native Czechia by just a few tens of kilometers, so he chased it to Hungary with a 30-year-old Soviet MTO 1,000-millimeter lens. All he remembers from that day is the rush of adrenaline he felt while trying to find the sun in the sky with the lens’s minuscule field of view and keep it in focus for the two minutes of the eclipse.

He insists that he has never enjoyed any of the eclipses he has photographed. “In fact, I have never properly seen any of those eclipses. You are just watching the screens, making sure that it’s all doing what it’s supposed to do. There are so many things that can go wrong and you can’t redo it.”

A composite sequence of photographs shows the 12 August 2026 solar eclipse as seen from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain.

Despite Druckmüller’s outward tranquility on this Spanish hillside, the stakes are high. Just 45 minutes ago, his group heard from their colleagues in Iceland, where viewing conditions had promised to be better than in Spain. But a vast low-pressure system had clouded the entire sky, leaving all three Iceland teams without a view.

On the Pico Trigaza mountain in Spain, two postgraduate researchers used a laser to get a rough, initial alignment for the tracking mount of an optical instrument. The alignment was necessary to precisely compensate for the Earth’s motion.

The corona has been a mystery for centuries. Though dimmer—by a factor of a million—than the sun’s visible surface, the corona is nevertheless extremely hot: about a million degrees Celsius compared to 5,500 degrees on the surface. Because the sun’s nuclear fusion engine churns at the star’s heart, it might seem that temperatures should fall farther from the core.

To observe the faint corona in visible light, researchers must block the sun’s ferocious glare. Specialized telescopes called coronagraphs do this with an opaque disk called an occulter. But because light bends around the occulter’s edges in an effect called diffraction, it must block an area much larger than that of the solar disk to prevent light from spilling over and ruining the images. But doing so means obstructing the inner part of the corona, which harbors the most important processes that underpin the puzzling phenomena of the sun’s upper atmosphere.

That’s why total eclipses matter so much to solar physicists. By sheer chance, the moon is exactly the right size and at just the right distance to completely cover the sun during a total solar eclipse. Because the moon is so far away from Earth, the view is not marred by diffraction, and the corona reveals itself nearly all the way down to the sun’s surface.

As astrocameras recorded spectral data about the sun’s corona, a laptop computer [on table, at left] displayed the phase of the eclipse.

Space probes can image the solar surface in other wavelengths, but those views have limitations, too. Spacecraft such as NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory do see the innermost parts of the corona in extreme ultraviolet light, explains Shadia Habbal, a solar physicist at the University of Hawaii and leader of the Solar Wind Sherpas project. “But it cuts off very quickly, so you don’t see its extension into space as well as we can see it in the visible emission lines” during an eclipse. “That’s the biggest advantage,” she says, of solar eclipse photography.

The European Proba-3 mission, launched in 2024, simulates total solar eclipses by flying two spacecraft in a formation 150 meters apart with one acting as an occulter and the other as the telescope. The instruments aboard that satellite, however, have limitations compared to the equipment used by the Solar Wind Sherpas team.

When Druckmüller developed the film from his 1999 eclipse expedition, the photographs didn’t do justice to the event’s eerie beauty. He spent countless evenings applying his expertise in numerical image processing in an attempt to re-create in his photographs the sights he witnessed in that Hungarian corn field.

It took two years, but eventually he succeeded. Where before there were dull views of the blackened lunar disk surrounded by the blunt wisps of the corona, Druckmüller revealed the subtlest details of the magnetic field lines stretching from the sun far into space. As his photographs circulated among solar physicists, invitations to eclipse expeditions began to arrive.

Solar researchers Miloslav Druckmüller and Shadia Habbal have been collaborating for two decades and 15 eclipses.

Habbal learned about the images from a Ph.D. student who had seen them at a conference presentation that didn’t credit Druckmüller. When Habbal’s team later published the images in a paper, they misattributed them to another researcher. Druckmüller found out through an astrophysicist friend. “I wrote her a rather disappointed email and she responded within 10 minutes,” Druckmüller recalls. “She really didn’t have a clue.”

The error was corrected, and within weeks, Habbal and Druckmüller began a collaboration that grew into a friendship. “Milos’s processing brings out details that nobody has seen before, and they tell you a lot about very tiny features in the corona that you don’t see otherwise,” says Habbal.

Capturing the corona’s delicate structures means finding a way to show its brightest and faintest features in the same image. “During the solar eclipse, the contrast between the darkest and brightest parts of the corona is enormous, possibly one to a million,” Druckmüller explains. “But a computer monitor only allows you to display a contrast ratio of one to about 800.” (Some modern monitors, particularly OLED ones, can deliver higher contrast ratios.)

The human eye can adjust to this enormous range of brightness, allowing an observer to see both the bright corona and the faint stars and planets that briefly emerge in the darkened sky. To bring those details together in a photograph, Druckmüller uses custom image-processing algorithms to combine exposures that capture different parts of that range.

Researchers Martin Šebek and Peter Urgoš make fine adjustments to the focus and alignment of the astrocameras on a key optical instrument before the 12 August solar eclipse.

To create a single image, Druckmüller’s teams need to take 200 individual frames during the eclipse at exposure times ranging from 0.001 second to two seconds. The data must then be calibrated against a vast number of reference images to filter out noise and imperfections. Flat fields, which depict a uniform light background, help correct for defects caused by telescope optics, dust spots, and variations in pixel sensitivity. Dark frames, taken with light blocked from the sensor, help correct for artifacts created by the camera’s image sensor itself. “It takes the computer more than two days to process one image,” Druckmüller says. Including the calibration data, a single finished image requires about 3,000 input frames.

Since 2008, teams directed by Habbal and Druckmüller have traveled to every total solar eclipse, spreading out across multiple locations to hedge against bad weather. About half of the teams return with usable data. For the others, it’s just a short and stressful voyage. For the 12 August eclipse, three groups deployed to Iceland and two to Spain.

The teams seek sites close to the center of the band of totality, where the moon blocks the sun for longest. In Spain, the 12 August band of totality cut across the north of the country; the center line of the shadow passed within 11 kilometers of Pico Trigaza, promising Druckmüller and his colleagues a precious 107 seconds of totality.

But duration is only part of the calculation. Totality on Pico Trigaza will commence 51 minutes before sunset, with the sun just 8 degrees above the horizon. That low, the rays must pass through a much thicker layer of the atmosphere than when the sun is higher in the sky, increasing the light distortion that complicates photography. At the researchers’ camp on Pico Trigaza, 1,600 meters above sea level, the thinner air should help a bit.

An abandoned hut on the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain was spruced up so that it could serve as a home base for the research team recording the 12 August solar eclipse.

“Iceland would have been a much better place for us than Spain because the sun was higher up, some 25 degrees above the horizon,” Druckmüller says wistfully. But Iceland’s notoriously unpredictable weather made Spain an essential backup.

If you pack a van with thousands of dollars’ worth of cameras and optical gear and then set out on a 2,351-kilometer journey, you shouldn’t be surprised if you finish the trip with a few striking photographs [top]. The sleeping arrangements for the grad students at the Pico Trigaza hut [bottom] were spartan, but the views were first-rate.Top: Martin Šebek; Bottom: Václav Široký

On the mountain, locals have spruced up a rustic, long-unused hut for the researchers, running power cables from a nearby telecommunication outpost and bringing in a water tank. Five Ph.D. students drove more than 2,000 kilometers from Brno and have spent nearly a week preparing the equipment. Druckmüller and his wife joined them two days before the eclipse. They cook on a small propane grill and sleep in sleeping bags on yoga mats. “We have plenty of space here to set up our telescopes, beautiful views, and a roof over our heads,” Druckmüller says with a grin. “It’s perfect.”

But even the best equipment and a carefully chosen site count for nothing if the clouds roll in. “So much work goes into the preparations and then, if you end up with nothing, you just feel terrible sadness,” says Jana Hoderová, an assistant professor of mathematics at Brno University of Technology and one of Druckmüller’s key collaborators.

As the moon continues to slide in front of the solar disk, the pesky cumulus cloud that kept everybody on edge begins to dissolve. It’s 10 minutes to totality. The relief is palpable.

The countdown on the computers that control the cameras has begun. The screens are now showing only a tiny orange sliver, and the evening is becoming perceptibly less bright.

Twenty astrophotography cameras, most of them drawing power from a car battery that was also buffering the cameras from any grid instabilities, are pointed at the sun. Alongside equipment capturing the corona’s visible light, the team has built an assembly of eight cameras to detect light emitted by various iron ions that arise in the corona.

Among the optical gear assembled at Pico Trigaza to capture the 12 August solar eclipse was a unique instrument designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona [at left]. Václav Široký

Those instruments looking for iron ions have been put together with resourcefulness and thrift. A colleague of Druckmüller’s laser-cut the aluminum plates holding the carefully aligned lenses in exchange “for two bottles of whisky.” The brackets and attachments were 3D-printed at Brno University of Technology. The lenses, produced for the defunct camera maker Contax, were bought at steep discounts on eBay. By far the most expensive elements are interference filters that isolate the wavelengths emitted by the iron ions.

Around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still.

“That’s something nobody else in the world can do,” Druckmüller says with visible satisfaction. The unique technology, codeveloped with Habbal’s Hawaii team, has already enabled researchers to map the distribution of temperatures across the entire corona and to discover previously unseen structures, dubbed “smoke rings,” in the coronal plasma. The photographs also revealed the boundary region where the solar plasma becomes so thin that its ions stop colliding.

The optical assembly designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona is outfitted with astrocameras, each of which captures spectra from a different ionic species. To do that, each astrocamera is equipped with a spectral filter whose bandwidth is so narrow—one nanometer—that the filter appears as a mirror.Martin Fornůsek

“Iron is the most abundant of the heavy elements that we see in the solar corona,” says Habbal. “And because the corona is so hot, the iron atoms lose electrons and get ionized. The larger the loss, the higher the temperature.”

For example, a temperature of around 1.6 million °C is necessary to produce an iron ion that has lost 12 electrons. But only 1.4 million °C is needed to strip an iron atom of 11 electrons. Once it’s in a particular electrical state, the ion retains its specific ionization, even as it travels outward with the solar wind. Each of those ions, whether +11 or +12, emits a different wavelength of light, allowing the researchers to map not just temperatures within the corona, but also how those iron ions spread into interplanetary space and distribute heat. Habbal and her colleagues had long been trying to image those iron ions during solar eclipses. But it wasn’t until Druckmüller entered the picture that they were able to develop the gear and the mathematical techniques to do it.

With just a minute to go to totality, the researchers begin removing protective filters from the lenses. It’s 50 minutes to sunset, and the waning sun has just begun to light up the clouds above the horizon with the first tinge of orange. Then, suddenly, the evening begins a rapid and premature descent into darkness. Along the edge of the fantastically thin solar crescent, the brilliant orange points known as Baily’s Beads flash and disappear—the last fragments of photospheric light visible through deep lunar valleys. As totality begins, observers remove their glasses. The hot air cools. The graduate students remain quietly and intently focused on their gear.

Druckmüller looks up from his camera toward the darkened plains. Around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still. The sky is ablaze with fiery colors all along the horizon where the deep lunar shadow drops off. Venus burns brilliantly in the southwest, a sharp white pinpoint in the darkened sky. The sound of camera shutters suddenly fills the air. Then, as quickly as it fell, the darkness begins to recede, bid farewell with another handful of golden Baily’s Beads.

The crowd erupts in cheers. The Ph.D. students throw themselves at each other and hug like they mean it.

“The students did most of the work this time, so I actually allowed myself to really look at it,” Druckmüller says. “It was beautiful. Pico Trigaza may not have been the best for science photography, but from the aesthetic point of view, it was extraordinary.”

The 2026 solar-eclipse team at Pico Trigaza in Spain included [from left] Magdalena Šrotířová, Peter Urgoš, Martin Fornůsek, Miloslav Druckmüller, Václav Široký, and Martin Šebek.Václav Široký

But for Druckmüller, this is just the beginning. While other eclipse chasers will race to release their images, he will take his time. He expects to publish the first visible-light images of the corona in about two weeks. Processing the iron-ion images, and uncovering whatever insights they may hold, will take months—maybe even a whole year.

“Probably until the next eclipse in 2027” in North Africa, Druckmüller says.

Who knows? Maybe he’ll even enjoy that one, too.

Tereza Pultarova is a London-based journalist specializing in aerospace and defense technologies. She is a native of the Czech Republic.

I enjoyed this piece very, very much, and I truly hope this team continues its work.

Those are some pretty impressive photos! It also seems like the iron ion filtering is pretty unique. I love seeing cases where people build something they want to see in the world with minimal outside support. Seems like it would be a solid return on more public money to seek out and support scrappy projects like this one.

There are also four new Siri AI languages supported in watchOS 27.3: Chinese (traditional), Norwegian, Turkish, and Vietnamese.

For the latest Apple Watch models, watchOS 27.3 adds a new Audio Intelligence feature called Live Rewind. Per Apple’s website:

Live Rewind recalls what was just said in the last 15 seconds by showing a text snippet on your Apple Watch when you double-press the Digital Crown, so you can catch something you missed or are less familiar with. You can ask Siri about the content of the snippet or simply save it to the Siri app.

I’m curious to see how useful this proves in everyday life. When Apple demoed the feature in September, it showed Live Rewind being used at a restaurant when an Apple Watch user missed part of the server’s menu explanation. Asking the server to repeat what they said seems like an easier solution, but perhaps there are other occasions Live Rewind will come in handy.

It won’t be for everyone, but I’ve been testing watchOS 27.3’s new Siri Recap feature and really love it.

Siri Recap only works on Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, and it’s off by default. But if you have one of those models and enable the feature, Siri can create automatic logs of what’s happening in your day-to-day life.

Most of the time, you won’t need to reference any of the recaps and they’ll be automatically deleted after a week. But based on my experience with the feature, Siri Recap definitely comes in handy at times when trying to remember key details from conversations.

Which of watchOS 27.3’s new features are you most interested in? Let us know in the comments.

#3245. Use Your Year-End Review to Reach for a Promotion

Maintaining a document of your successes throughout the year gives you a starting point

Brian Jenney is the owner of Parsity, a program that helps engineers through hands-on training.

This article is crossposted from IEEE Spectrum’s careers newsletter. Sign up now to get insider tips, expert advice, and practical strategies, written in partnership with tech career development company Parsity and delivered to your inbox for free!

When I landed my first job as a software engineer, I had a simple plan: Work hard and somebody would notice. Eventually a manager would tap me on the shoulder and hand me a promotion (probably with a nice little speech).

That plan stalled my career for about five years.

I switched jobs twice, kept my head down, read a stack of programming books, and sometimes pulled 12-hour days. I was never promoted. At my third job, out of frustration, I started interviewing at other companies and almost immediately got an offer for a senior engineer role.

So I went back to my job and quit. My team was blindsided. I liked my manager and the people I worked with, and they came back with a counteroffer. Then someone from HR asked me, “Why didn’t you just ask us?”

I took the counteroffer and stayed. Three jobs in, I finally got promoted, and all it took was asking (in the most dramatic way possible).

Today, I would take a different approach.

Year-end review discussions are a great time to push for a promotion. But at most companies, raises and promotions are largely settled before the formal review conversation happens. If the year-end review is the first time your manager hears you want a promotion, you’re usually too late.

Now is a great time to start the conversation.

Engineers tend to believe good work speaks for itself. It rarely does. Your manager is juggling a team, a roadmap, and their own boss. They see a fraction of what you do, and the work they don’t see might as well not exist when raises get decided.

Perception is reality, so you have to shape it. That means learning to brag a little.

A “brag document” is a running list of what you accomplished, when, and why it mattered. Add to it every two weeks or once a month, and write each entry so your manager’s manager would understand it.

Engineers tend to write things like “migrated the billing service.” A better entry reads “migrated the billing service, which cut failed payments by 30 percent and unblocked the Q3 pricing launch.” If there’s no number, name who benefited and how.

Include the work people forget to count, too: handling incidents, mentoring new hires, interviewing candidates, and writing the docs everyone else relies on. If you helped your team adopt AI tools this year, write that down. (It counts as leadership, whether or not anyone called it that.)

The document does two jobs. It gives you ammunition when you make your case, and it gives your manager something to ctrl + c then ctrl + v when they argue for you in meetings you’ll never attend.

Bragging builds the case. Asking forces action.

If your goal is a promotion or a raise, you might ask: “What would it take for me to get to [the next level] in the next year?”

A good manager will give you an outline that can turn into a plan. Push for specifics until you have deliverables you can work toward, then send a short recap email so the plan exists somewhere besides your manager’s memory. (Managers change jobs too.)

Sometimes the answer will still be “not this year,” and the reason may have nothing to do with you.

Budgets get frozen, promotion slots get capped, and decisions get made above your manager’s head where even a manager who wants to help can’t.

Don’t read too much into that. But be honest with yourself, too. Most of the time, a no means there’s something you aren’t doing yet. Find out what it is instead of guessing for five years like I did.

Asking costs you one slightly awkward conversation. Sitting back and waiting to be noticed can cost you years.

And the spam filter is getting clogged up…”

Policy change doesn’t just come down to paid lobbyists—lawmakers want to hear from working experts, too. One engineer shares what he learned from his first two visits to Capitol Hill.

Could community colleges help fill the coming talent shortage in the U.S. semiconductor industry? Alternatives to four-year university degrees are a promising option for the technicians who will be needed to run new fabs.

#3244. Who Will Replace Jensen Huang? Here's What Prediction Markets Think.

Jensen Huang has resigned as CEO of Nvidia.

Throughout the artificial intelligence (AI) revolution, Jensen Huang has been synonymous with Nvidia (NVDA -4.34%). As the company's co-founder and longtime CEO, Huang helped transform Nvidia from a graphics chip manufacturer into a dominant supplier of AI computing infrastructure.

Recent reports concerning Huang's personal relationships and potential exposure to foreign intelligence have prompted an independent board investigation and raised questions about his future. Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO on Nov. 12. As investors focus on leadership succession plans, prediction market platform Kalshi offers an interesting glimpse into who might lead Nvidia next.

According to Kalshi’s trading odds, Ian Buck is currently in the lead, with an implied probability of approximately 36% of becoming Nvidia's next CEO. Buck joined Nvidia in 2004 and helped develop CUDA, the software platform that allows developers to program GPUs for applications beyond graphics processing.

That's particularly relevant because hyperscalers like Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet, and Oracle account for most of the investments in AI infrastructure. During Nvidia's fiscal second quarter, hyperscalers accounted for $48.7 billion of the company's total data center revenue.

Nvidia's chief financial officer (CFO), Colette Kress, currently has a 19% chance to emerge as Nvidia's next CEO. For now, Kress has been named interim CEO.

Kalshi traders are also considering candidates from outside Nvidia. Rene Haas, CEO of semiconductor designer Arm Holdings, currently has 10% odds. Haas previously spent seven years at Nvidia, giving him familiarity with the company's operations and semiconductor strategy. His experience running Arm, whose chip processor designs are used across various devices, makes him a logical candidate.

Former Apple CEO Tim Cook is also among the possibilities, with recent odds around 4%. Of note, Cook's name may only be among the top ranks because President Trump floated the idea of Nvidia appointing him as its CEO.

While Cook's experience managing Apple's global supply chain and navigating international business relationships could be valuable, his candidacy seems speculative, as there's no confirmed indication Nvidia is pursuing him.

Prediction markets can offer useful insights into investor expectations, but they are hardly infallible. Kalshi's probabilities change in real time as they reflect trading activity rather than inside knowledge. Limited liquidity in niche markets can also cause outsize swings in the odds.

Nvidia's next CEO will inherit a business with enormous competitive advantages. The company's Blackwell and Vera Rubin computing platforms, proprietary networking technology, and CUDA software ecosystem have established robust barriers to competition.

These assets are not going to disappear because of a leadership change. Ultimately, investors should pay more attention to Nvidia's ability to execute its technology roadmap than to the latest fluctuations in prediction market odds or rumors.

#3242. OpenAI’s quarterly revenue reportedly hits $10bn as its losses grow

Its adjusted operating margin improved to -109%, according to the WSJ. But OpenAI revenue is still below Anthropic’s $17bn for the quarter, and Anthropic lists on Nasdaq next week.

OpenAI’s revenue reached $10bn in the third quarter, up almost 50% from the second, The Information reported. OpenAI shared the figures with investors on Tuesday. Demand for its newer models and enterprise products had picked up, Valida Pau and Jemima McEvoy wrote, citing a person familiar with the matter.

It is the first quarter in which OpenAI’s revenue has reached $10bn, Bloomberg reported, citing people familiar with the matter. Revenue was almost three times its level a year earlier, they said. OpenAI declined to comment to Bloomberg.

The Wall Street Journal’s Berber Jin saw documents on the results. They show OpenAI’s adjusted operating margin improved to -109% in the third quarter, from -150% in the second. Its adjusted operating loss still rose, to $10.9bn from $10.1bn.

In the second quarter, OpenAI’s revenue grew 18% to $6.7bn, the Journal reported at the time. That left it behind Anthropic on quarterly revenue for the first time.

Greg Brockman, OpenAI’s president, spoke on the investor call. So did Sarah Friar, its chief financial officer, and product leader Thibault Sottiaux, Bloomberg’s Rachel Metz and Rebecca Torrence reported.

OpenAI revenue has regained momentum thanks to new models, aggressive price cuts and a bigger push into AI agents, according to Bloomberg. The company told investors it ended September with roughly $50bn in annualised revenue. That matches the $50bn run rate reported in October.

Anthropic reported $16.96bn in revenue for the same quarter. It first disclosed it in its IPO filing on 2 November. Its operating loss was $567m, and its adjusted operating margin was 15%.

Anthropic’s growth has slowed. Its revenue rose about 47% from the second quarter to the third. It had jumped 144% the quarter before, its filing shows.

The two companies count revenue differently. Anthropic includes sales made through its cloud partners, while OpenAI counts only its share of some partner sales, TechCrunch noted.

#3240. Apple offers a military discount, here’s how to get it

If you’re a member of the U.S. military, Apple offers an easy way to save 10% on eligible products and accessories. It’s available to current and veteran members of the U.S. military and their immediate family members living in the same household. While you’ll need to verify your eligibility to access the discount, the process is simple. There are also a few limitations you’ll want to know about before placing an order. Here’s everything you need to know.

A 10% discount is available to current and Veteran members of the US Military, National Guard and Reserve. Immediate family members who reside in the same household are also eligible.

Verification is handled through ID.me. Creating an ID.me account is free, and current military members can verify their service using their .mil email address. Veterans can enter details of their service information for ID.me to verify, or upload images of official documents (such as a DD-214) for ID.me to review and confirm their eligibility. Once you’re verified, your ID.me account can also be used to access military discounts from other retailers and services that support ID.me verification.

Once verified, you can start shopping by visiting Apple’s Store for Veterans and Military. The discount only applies to Apple products and accessories (including Beats) so third-party products aren’t eligible. Apple services, such as Apple Music and iCloud+, are also excluded. Orders can be shipped directly to you, or you can choose in-store pickup if the product is available at a nearby Apple Store.

This is probably the biggest catch. Apple specifically says ACMI isn’t available when shopping through the Veterans and Military Store. You can still earn 3% back in Daily Cash with Apple Card, but you lose the option to finance your purchase at 0% interest over several months. Apple Upgrade also isn’t available when purchasing through the military store.

The only way to get the military discount is to make your purchase through Apple’s website in a browser. The Apple Store app isn’t an option, which means you also can’t take advantage of Apple’s “Get Ready” feature to select your iPhone model, color, storage capacity, and carrier ahead of pre-orders opening. Instead, you’ll have to navigate Apple’s website on launch day, when demand is high and server traffic can make checkout more challenging. Whether the 10% savings is worth giving up the convenience of a potentially quicker checkout is ultimately up to you.

The military discount can’t be combined with carrier promotions or discounts on iPhone purchases. You can still trade in your existing iPhone through Apple and receive the applicable trade-in value, but you can’t take advantage of carrier-specific trade-in offers, like promotions that give you a larger credit when you trade in an eligible device and activate or upgrade a line.

These purchase limits reset on January 1 each year.

Apple’s military discount is a useful perk, especially if you’re buying a product at launch and want to save 10% right away. However, it’s worth comparing prices with other retailers before you buy, since sales and promotions can sometimes beat Apple’s discount. The military store also comes with a few limitations, so you’ll want to weigh the savings against the features and payment options you’re giving up. Even with those caveats, 10% off can make a real difference on an expensive Apple purchase.

#3239. IEEE Program Schools Preuniversity Educators On Tech Topics

The TryEngineering workshops help teachers deliver engaging STEM lessons

An educator constructs a microchip model during the IEEE Making a Microchip lesson plan demonstration.

Now in their third year, the IEEE TryEngineering educator sessions continue to empower preuniversity teachers with specialized professional development programs on engineering topics and classroom-tested lessons.

This year’s sessions, held across the United States, have focused on educating teachers about artificial intelligence and semiconductor technology. One session was held in Egypt.

In all, 54 educators learned about the engineering design process this year. They received an overview of TryEngineering resources including the Making of a Microchip and Train Your Tree lesson plans.

Workshops are scheduled this year in Greece and Guatemala.

The TryEngineering program is administered by IEEE Educational Activities.

These teachers and guest speakers attended the two-day session held at the Florida Semiconductor Institute and SkyWater Technology chip manufacturing facility.IEEE Educational Activities

Central to the educator session program’s success is its university network. Host campuses welcome teachers into their facilities, where faculty provide background information about some of the technologies being taught, as well as possible engineering career paths and job opportunities for students.

This year’s sessions involved the educators in hands-on projects. Facilitators at each location were selected based on their experience in engineering education, and they worked with the TryEngineering staff on their presentations.

Sixteen teachers from nine schools participated in the session, held in Cairo. It was facilitated by Marwa Soudi, an IEEE member, and Senior Member Stamatis Dragoumanos. Both are past chairs of the IEEE preuniversity coordinating committee. GEMS provided outstanding STEM facilities for teachers, Saudi and Dragoumanos said. Participants received an overview of the Working With Wind Energy and Tall Tower Challenge lesson plans.

Another educator session is scheduled for later this year.

Educators from across the state gathered at the university’s Florida Semiconductor Institute, headquartered in Gainesville, and FSI’s NeoCity high-tech manufacturing campus near Orlando. The session was hosted by Roseanne Perez, an FSI workforce development program specialist, and Sophia Watson, FSI’s assistant director of workforce development. The two-day experience featured an inside look at microelectronics through a guided tour of a SkyWater Technology chip manufacturing facility.

Engineering instructor Mary Acken facilitated hands-on lesson demonstrations for the 15 attending teachers.

Reflecting on the workshop’s impact, one participant said the SkyWater tour was excellent, the instructors were great, and the teachers enjoyed learning from like-minded educators.

Michael Kozicki, an IEEE member, and Stefan Myhajlenko from the university’s engineering school welcomed 11 Arizona teachers to the Tempe campus.

The session was facilitated by Janet Hartkopf, an Arizona school leader and a former TryEngineering educator session participant. Hartkopf highlighted collaborative learning, the need for diverse perspectives in engineering education, and career paths.

The teachers received instruction on how to implement the hands-on lessons in their classrooms, and they toured the university’s NanoFab facility to observe microelectronics research.

“This training was amazing!” said a participant who leads an elementary after-school STEM club. “I loved the hands-on lessons and e-books, which I will definitely be using with my students. I am excited to explore all the resources on the TryEngineering website. The experts from ASU were great.”

Sixteen STEM educators attended this session, held at the university’s International Institute for Biosensing in Minneapolis. Its director, Patricia Khashayar, an IEEE member, introduced participants to the capabilities of the university’s Supercomputing Institute and Nano Center.

Under the guidance of Claire Dietz, an education and outreach coordinator, and Pam Schumacher, an instructor at St. Paul College, the teachers completed classroom-ready lessons including a photonics experiment using the Nano Center’s equipment. Schumacher attended last year’s TryEngineering educator session.

Nano Center Director Sarah Swisher, an IEEE senior member, provided an overview of semiconductor operations and highlighted growing job opportunities for the state’s young people.

The experience inspired all 16 teachers to plan student field trips to the Nano Center during the upcoming academic year, they said.

“Great class!” one participant said. “I’m excited to bring some of the TryEngineering materials back to our school.”

This year’s sessions built on the momentum from last year when, with financial support from Onsemi’s Giving Now program, nearly 80 teachers attended sessions across five U.S. states and Mexico.

Driven by that success and the demand for more, the IEEE Educational Activities Board continued its support. Upcoming global sessions are expected to expand the program’s international footprint.

“I appreciated the time to collaborate with peers on how to implement hands-on lessons,” one participating teacher this year said. Some participants said they planned follow-up visits with the experts and campus tours.

You can learn more about the sessions by emailing TryEngineering.

#3238. SpaceXSI’s Grok Build left 35,000 apps open, security firm Claroc says

Grok Build proposes ‘Anyone with the link’ when users publish an app, and app addresses land in public DNS records. SpaceXSI says apps stay private until their creator shares them.

Anyone who found the address of a Grok Build app could open more than 35,000 of them, security firm Claroc found in research published on 10 November. Two dozen belonged to staff at SpaceXSI, the company that makes Grok. They held a confidential onboarding plan, a sales territory map and advertising proposals.

SpaceXSI took its own 24 apps offline after the report, Claroc said. It left the apps of other Grok users open. Ars Technica’s Dan Goodin reported that SpaceXSI started removing them within hours of his email asking about the findings.

Grok Build turns a description typed into a chat into a working app. The user can then publish it at its own address on grok.me. Claroc tried more than 43,500 of those addresses. Of the 37,571 still online, 35,578, or 94.7%, opened without any sign-in.

Most were games, landing pages and calculators. About one in ten held internal business or personal data. Claroc estimates that 650 to 800 apps held private data.

Claroc confirmed some cases by hand. They included one intensive care patient’s lab results, a hospital group’s roster of more than 3,500 staff, and a fire department’s shift board. One contractor’s timesheet app carried 18 accounts with their passwords in plain text, in code that every visitor’s browser downloads.

Besides SpaceXSI and X, Claroc identified 30 organisations, six of them in the Fortune 500. It named none. Ars Technica listed more. They include a Tesla service-centre scorecard naming 22 technicians and a roster for a US Navy logistics contract.

SpaceXSI’s own open apps included a map of 594 strategic sales accounts and eight X advertising proposals. Claroc said one proposal, to a US federal agency, carried a confidential label.

Grok gives every published app its own hostname of random words, such as name.grok.me. Nobody needs to guess one. When a visitor opens an app, its name reaches passive DNS services. These commercial databases log internet lookups, and anyone with an account can search them.

Shared chats from Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini keep the secret part of the link in the path, Claroc said. DNS never sees it. Last month, the same method exposed Meta’s Muse links.

In the paid account Claroc used, the publish screen proposed “Anyone with the link” as the access setting. It also offered “Invited users” and “Only you”.

“AI app builders turned publishing into a few clicks, and the default answer to who can see it is everyone,” Asaf Aprozper, Claroc’s co-founder and chief technology officer, said in the firm’s report.

Claroc also built two test apps of its own. In a team customer list, Grok’s code added anyone who signed in with Google to the team before checking membership. An outside account could then read, edit and delete records, the firm said.

A representative for Cursor, the coding company SpaceX bought in August, responded in an email to Ars Technica.

“Apps are private by default and nothing goes public unless the creator chooses to share it,” the representative said, according to Ars Technica.

SpaceXSI also told a reporter that publishing takes several steps, including a legal notice, and that employee accounts start on “Only you”, Claroc said. Claroc’s answer is that the people who published the 35,578 open apps went through every one of those steps.

The representative said ChatGPT, Lovable and Bolt also make shareable links. Aprozper agreed that apps on Lovable, Bolt and Replit have the same exposure.

“However, Grok is where we found by far the most sensitive company data,” Aprozper told Ars Technica.

Claroc sells security tools for AI-built apps. It asked SpaceXSI to make “Only you” the default, move shared apps onto hard-to-guess paths, and warn builders when an app has a database but no sign-in. It is now notifying the affected organisations itself.

It is not the first data problem for Grok Build. In July, the tool sent entire Git repositories to xAI’s servers. In October, Musk said the merged company would be renamed SpaceXSI.

#3237. iCloud+ has new perk in iOS 27 if you pay for more storage

The tentpole feature of iCloud+ is cloud storage, but Apple keeps improving and expanding the service to include other perks too. And in iOS 27, iCloud+ has a new benefit for high-storage tiers: AI features for HomeKit cameras.

With iOS 27, iCloud+ has added a new perk if you pay for more storage: Apple Intelligence features for compatible Home cameras. Per Apple’s website:

With Apple Intelligence in the Home app, you can automatically generate video descriptions for recorded clips from compatible Home cameras. You can then search your recordings using natural language

These AI-generated video descriptions provide a convenient summary of what’s happening in your home, let you browse important clips at a glance, and search the camera’s recent history of recordings.

The price ladder requirement for the 12TB plan in order to get 5 cameras is WAY TOO HIGH. I rather dedicate a local mac running some sort of AI model that can do this locally instead of paying that.

All of this is available with a camera that supports HomeKit Secure Video (I recommend this Aqara camera for $35). But because AI features depend on Private Cloud Compute, Apple only offers them on the following iCloud+ plans:

Apple charges $9.99, $29.99, and $59.99/month for each of these plans, respectively. So most users probably won’t find the monthly cost worth it for AI camera features alone. But if you already need a lot of iCloud storage, now you’ll get these new features thrown in too.

Note: these AI features have additional requirements too. You’ll need a home hub like a HomeView, Apple TV 4K, or HomePod, and your iPhone must support Apple Intelligence.

Have you used iOS 27’s new AI features for Home cameras? How are they working for you? Let us know in the comments.

iCloud is built into every Apple device, so that…

#3236. Pelthos (PTHS) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Zelsuvmi growth accelerates as a gene therapy deal takes shape.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Pelthos Therapeutics Inc. (PTHS -14.48%) reported a 114% year-over-year increase in net product revenue for Zelsuvmi during the third quarter of 2026. Management detailed a strategy to expand its dermatological portfolio through the upcoming launches of Xepi and Xeglyze while diversifying into the rare disease gene therapy market via the acquisition of Castle Creek Biosciences. The company reported improved formulary access and high prescriber adoption for its lead product despite seasonal headwinds in molluscum contagiosum claims. The strategic merger, which is targeted to close in the first quarter of 2027, adds a Phase III cell therapy candidate to the company's existing platform of FDA-approved products.

Pelthos issued a press release today announcing its financial results for the quarter ended September 30, 2026. A copy can be found in the Investor Relations tab and on the company's corporate website at www.pelthos.com. As a reminder, this conference call is being recorded and will remain available for 90 days.

I'd now like to turn the call over to Scott Plesha, Chief Executive Officer. Scott, you may begin.

Scott Plesha: Thank you, Mike, and good morning, everyone. We're pleased to be here with you today to share our third quarter 2026 financial and operational results and highlights. I'm joined today by Peter Greenleaf, our Executive Chairman; John Gay, Chief Financial Officer; and Sai Rangarao, our Chief Commercial Officer. The third quarter of 2026 was a successful one for Pelthos with progress made in several key areas. During Q3, we generated Zelsuvmi net revenue of $15.2 million, which represents a year-over-year increase of 114% from Q3 of 2025. In 5 quarters since commercial launch, we have dispensed over 40,000 units of Zelsuvmi and treated over 31,000 patients.

In early October, we announced that we had signed an agreement with a major PBM to open access to Zelsuvmi covering 24 million commercial covered lives and received a formulary update enhancing access to Zelsuvmi with a regional health plan that covers approximately 3 million lives. We believe that these improvements in formulary access will be important to the continued growth of Zelsuvmi. With these improvements, Zelsuvmi now has formulary coverage across 127 million or approximately 70% of commercially covered lives and strong Medicaid coverage of more than 70 million or 100% of covered lives. We continue to make progress in establishing the manufacturing of our 2 other highly complementary products, Xepi and Xeglyze.

We are currently building launch inventory for Xepi for the treatment of impetigo and expect to begin promoting it to our current customer base by the end of Q1 2027. With Xeglyze, for head lice, we have initiated the manufacturing of API and expect to commercially launch it by the end of Q3 2027. We're excited about the impending launches of Xepi and Xeglyze as we expect they'll have a meaningful call overlap for our existing field force which we expect will provide the company with greater operational and financial leverage from our existing team and infrastructure.

Before we cover our commercial and financial results, I want to spend a few minutes on the exciting Castle Creek Biosciences transaction we announced on October 30. While I'm limited in what I can say given that the S-4 has not yet been filed, I believe it's important to comment on why we have such strong conviction in this acquisition and the long-term opportunity it creates for Pelthos and our shareholders. Since our formation in July of last year, our strategy has been focused on building a strong commercial organization in dermatology with the physician relationships, commercial infrastructure and manufacturing expertise necessary to succeed in bringing innovative therapies to market.

Having made substantial investments in establishing that foundation, we see great synergy and opportunity to leverage these capabilities across a broader portfolio, expanding our potential future revenue base and generating greater revenue on the investments we've already made. Castle Creek represents a particularly strong fit with that strategy. Its lead candidate is D-Fi, an investigational redosable gene-modified cell therapy being developed for dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa or DEB, a rare lifelong disease characterized by extremely fragile skin, chronic wounds and serious complications. D-Fi has been granted orphan drug designation. And once the transaction closes, we expect to continue development of its Phase III clinical trials.

Patients who suffer from DEB live with intense wound burden, frequently accompanied by serious complications, including a greatly increased risk of developing squamous cell carcinoma, which is the leading cause of death in DEB patients. The wound burden never goes away, creating sustained demand for multiple therapies that can close wounds and keep them closed. The market for DEB therapies has already proven its commercial potential. The first gene therapy approved for DEB, a weekly topical treatment launched in 2023, generated $127 million in global net revenue in the third quarter of this year, up 30% from a year ago and more than $1.1 billion since launch with over 760 U.S. reimbursement approvals to date.

The pace of this launch demonstrates that payers recognize the severity of this rare disease. Coverage has been broad. Revenue per patient is high and gross to net adjustments have been modest relative to many specialty markets. We also believe there remains significant unmet need in this disease state. And so far, our conversations with KOLs and health care providers who treat DEB have consistently highlighted the need for further treatment options. We believe D-Fi, upon approval, can leverage this need and capture a meaningful share of the market because it offers a differentiated approach. It uses the patient's own skin cells engineered to produce Type 7 collagen and delivered by intradermal injection directly into the wound.

It is designed to be redosed with treatment sessions every 8 weeks in the planned Phase III trial. We expect the treatment paradigm with DEB to increasingly evolve more than one therapy across different wounds and stages of the disease. And we see a clear role for D-Fi as a stand-alone first-line treatment as well as being used alongside existing treatment options. This opportunity is also not limited to the U.S. We believe that approximately 1/2 of the market for DEB treatments is outside the U.S. and our agreement with Castle Creek includes rest of the world rights to D-Fi as well.

This is exactly the kind of high-value specialist-driven market where we believe our commercial model provides a great deal of synergy. It is concentrated. It is served by dermatologists we already have relationships with, particularly in pediatric dermatology and the economics per patient support an efficient, focused launch. Beyond D-Fi, Castle Creek's proprietary fibroblast-based technology adds a cell and gene therapy capability to Pelthos' existing Nitricil manufacturing platform. Together with our 3 FDA-approved products, Zelsuvmi, Xepi and Xeglyze, the combined company will offer a more diversified portfolio spanning marketed, launch stage and late-stage assets across multiple therapeutic modalities. This combination of complementary capabilities is central to the strategic rationale of the transaction.

By leveraging our existing manufacturing expertise and commercial infrastructure, we believe we may be able to accelerate the development, and if approved, launch of this product candidate. If successful, we believe this program has the potential to expand our revenue base and create long-term value for our shareholders. But the potential of this transaction extends beyond the addition of a single development asset, no matter how great D-Fi potential. This transaction positions Pelthos to be a stronger, more diversified biotech company, poised to pursue additional pipeline opportunities, build a broader commercial portfolio and expand its long-term earnings potential. A disciplined capital allocation approach remains central to this strategy.

And we intend to focus on translating these opportunities into sustainable revenue while maintaining the financial discipline necessary to generate attractive long-term returns. In short, we are extremely enthusiastic about the potential of D-Fi and are confident that the Castle Creek transaction can be a foundational pillar of the next phase of Pelthos' growth. I'll now turn it over to Sai to provide more specifics on the results of our commercial performance. Sai?

Sai Rangarao: Thank you, Scott. Good morning, everyone. I'm pleased to provide an update on our Q3 2026 Zelsuvmi performance and our progress to date. Zelsuvmi continues to deliver strong utilization and adoption among HCPs and patients. We continue to receive very positive feedback from prescribers regarding Zelsuvmi's clinical profile and ease of use. According to our latest data, we now have more than 10,000 unique HCP prescribers. This reinforces our confidence that Zelsuvmi is transforming the treatment of molluscum or MC as evidenced by its strong HCP adoption. Since our commercial launch in July 2025 to date, more than 34,000 patients have received Zelsuvmi.

This milestone is a testament to the strong demand among HCPs and patients for Zelsuvmi as an optimal treatment option for MC. Turning to prescription details for Q3 2026. The number of prescriptions increased by 4% from 11,925 in Q2 to 12,384 in Q3. This represents 365% year-over-year growth. The number of unique prescribers also increased from 4,571 in the second quarter to 4,942 by the end of the third quarter. Both metrics are reported in Symphony Metys data. Prescribed units in October totaled an estimate 4,231 compared with 4,063 in September. Despite seasonal trends and summer scheduling dynamics among HCPs and patients, performance between July and August remained stable and in line with expectations.

In fact, we surpassed 1,000 weekly TRx units in early October, further affirming HCP and patient demand for utilization of Zelsuvmi, even during a quarter that historically experiences lower MC claims volume. Our coverage for Zelsuvmi has continued to grow. Most notably, we executed a contract with a large PBM to help patients gain access to Zelsuvmi. This formulary agreement effective October 1, 2026, provides open access to approximately 24 million covered lives without a prior authorization requirement. This agreement has already helped many patients gain rapid and seamless access to Zelsuvmi. We also announced that Pelthos received a formulary update from a regional health plan covering approximately 3 million lives, further enhancing access to Zelsuvmi.

As of October 2026, Zelsuvmi has formulary coverage across 127 million commercially covered lives, representing approximately 70% of the market, along with strong Medicaid coverage of more than 70 million lives, representing 100% of covered lives. Zelsuvmi continues to gain adoption as a first-line treatment option and is being well received by coverage providers. A large number of states still do not require a prior authorization for Medicaid coverage. In other states where prior authorization is required, Medicaid only requires a PA written in accordance with the product to label. This means that patients over one year of age presenting with MC qualify for coverage. We continue to maintain very favorable gross to net performance.

As a reminder, our GTNs are driven by distribution costs, Medicaid discounts, payer contracts and our co-pay voucher program. Our goal is to offset the prescription costs through the co-pay card program, so that the out-of-pocket cost to patients is 0 or close to 0 for the majority of prescriptions. For the third quarter of 2026, our GTNs were 31.5%. Going forward, we expect our GTNs to move into the mid-30s range, in line with our expectations, considering additional formulary coverage. Our hardworking sales teams continue to ramp up their efforts to educate HCPs across the nation.

Despite expected seasonal fluctuations, the team's efforts have continued to drive increased utilization of Zelsuvmi, along with growth in the number of new prescribers. Awareness and utilization of Zelsuvmi as the first and only at-home prescription treatment option for MC are further supported by our comprehensive promotional strategy. We believe our Zelsuvmi YouTube commercial and patient testimonial videos continue to serve as highly educational resources, encouraging caregivers and patients to ask their HCPs about Zelsuvmi. With more than 9.2 million total views of our Zelsuvmi YouTube commercial and more than 1.7 million views of our patient testimonial videos, our continued awareness and conversion initiatives have developed momentum.

Throughout Q3 into early Q4, we participated in several key conferences, including the American Academy of Pediatrics meeting and one of the largest clinical dermatology meetings in the country. Our participation in these meetings generated numerous leads and helped HCPs initiate treatment for new patients through education provided at these venues. These engagements translated into meaningful interest in both continued and new use of Zelsuvmi, reinforcing its utilization among HCPs. We continue to strengthen our differentiated commercial platform, leveraging a strong foundation and the outstanding execution capabilities of our sales team to drive continued growth of Zelsuvmi. Lastly, here in Q4, our commercial leadership team has begun planning for the March 2027 launch of Xepi.

Extensive strategic brand and tactical planning is underway to align our go-to-market strategy to meet our customers' needs and position us for a successful launch of Xepi for the treatment of impetigo. I am proud of the strong performance we have delivered to date, which reflects the passion, commitment and outstanding execution of our exceptional commercial team. With that, I'd like to turn the call over to John to walk us through our financials. John?

John Gay: Thank you, Sai. Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us on today's call. As Scott and Sai have already touched on, we continue to focus on driving growth for our lead product, Zelsuvmi, and look forward to launching Xepi in the first quarter of next year. With today's filing of our quarterly report on Form 10-Q for the period ending September 30, 2026, we have now completed and reported 5 fiscal quarters of commercialization efforts for Zelsuvmi. While these quarters straddle 2 fiscal years, we have reported in aggregate $57.5 million of net product revenue since the commercial launch of Zelsuvmi. Turning to the operating results of our business.

Please note that my comments will focus on our third quarter 2026 results as compared to the second quarter of 2026. For the third quarter of 2026, we reported $15.2 million of net product revenue as compared to $15.4 million in the second quarter of 2026. As Scott and Sai mentioned, we signed a major PBM agreement to unlock access for patients seeking Zelsuvmi with no prior authorization. While overall gross revenue increased, the gross to net increase in Q3 reflects the formulary agreement, which we believe will contribute to future incremental revenue growth.

Cost of goods sold was $1.7 million for the third quarter of 2026 as compared to $3.6 million in the second quarter of 2026. As discussed in our last quarterly earnings call, cost of goods sold for the second quarter of 2026 also included a $900,000 write-off of commercial API inventory identified through the company's quality control process. We had no such write-offs of inventory during the third quarter of 2026. Absent the impact of inventory write-offs in the second quarter of 2026, the key driver of the quarter-over-quarter reduction in COGS was primarily due to an approximate 39% reduction in the U.S.

GAAP per unit cost of goods sold during the third quarter of 2026 as compared to the second quarter of 2026. As we have previously discussed, the component of our cost of goods sold includes fair value adjustments associated with the July 2025 merger. At the time of the merger, all finished goods and active pharmaceutical ingredient inventory on hand was fair valued as prescribed under U.S. GAAP. At the end of the second quarter of 2026, we had sold through all of the stepped-up finished goods inventory. And we expect to consume the remaining stepped-up ATI inventory within the next 12 to 15 months.

Once we have sold all inventory with a base of step-up, we expect to have a normalized per unit cost of goods of approximately a mid- to high single digit of our WAC price. For the third quarter of 2026, we reported $18.8 million of SG&A expenses, representing a 25% decrease from the second quarter of 2026 at $25 million. Excluding the $5.3 million of onetime nonrecurring sales-based milestones related to our Zelsuvmi license recorded in the second quarter of 2026, SG&A decreased 5% during the third quarter of 2026. One additional point I would like to call out with respect to SG&A.

Beginning this quarter, we have presented royalty expense associated with our licensing partners as a separate line item within operating expenses on our income statement. We made a slight change in presentation to provide a more disaggregated level of detail for OpEx on the face of our P&L. Please note that we provide a detailed breakdown of the components of SG&A within the MD&A section of our quarterly report on Form 10-Q for the period ending September 30, 2026, filed this morning. But in total, cash basis SG&A, defined as SG&A less milestones and stock-based compensation, was approximately $16.9 million for the third quarter of 2026 as compared to $17 million for the second quarter of 2026.

Net loss for the third quarter of 2026 was $7.9 million as compared to $23.4 million for the second quarter of 2026. Adjusted EBITDA for the third quarter of 2026 was a negative $5.6 million as compared to a negative $5.7 million for the second quarter of 2026. Turning now to our balance sheet. As of September 30, 2026, we had $17.7 million of cash and $13.4 million in accounts receivable. Our working capital at the end of the third quarter of 2026 was $24.6 million as compared to $31.4 million at the end of the second quarter of 2026.

As previously discussed, in January of this year, we entered into a $50 million senior secured term loan facility with Horizon, of which we drew $30 million at close. On October 30 of this year, we executed an amendment to this facility and borrowed an additional $10 million. In addition, this lending facility also provides for an additional $10 million in funding prior to December 31, 2027, subject to the lender's discretion and certain conditions, including the company achieving trailing 12-month net revenue of at least $70 million.

Based on our current projections, including forecasted cash flows related to net product sales of Zelsuvmi and Xepi and proceeds drawn from the Horizon facility to date, we believe we have the flexibility to advance our business plan. In summary, while we are pleased with our performance since the launch of Zelsuvmi in July of 2025, generating $57.5 million of net revenue, we look forward to continued growth. Scott Plesha: Thank you, John. However, we do expect to be able to provide more information once we file our S-4 in due course.

In the meantime, I'd like to direct you to our Form 8-K that was filed on October 30 for additional information until we are able to provide additional information. I want to thank you for joining us today to learn more about Pelthos story. We'll now turn the call over to the operator for any questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our first question comes from the line of David Amsellem with Piper Sandler.

David Amsellem: Just a couple for me. I know you can't say all that much just yet on the transaction, but nonetheless, wanted to get your thoughts on how you see D-Fi's points of differentiation versus VYJUVEK. So that's number one. Then, in terms of the base business on Zelsuvmi, can you talk through how you're thinking about the direction of the gross to net in 2027? And then a question on Xepi. This in terms of volumes, seems like a fairly large market, particularly with a lot of usage of Naprosyn ointments. I guess my question here is, with that in mind and bearing in mind that Naprosyn is fairly inexpensive, how do you see usage paradigms evolving here?

And how do you see the payer landscape for Xepi evolving?

Scott Plesha: Okay, David, I'll kick it off. I'll handle -- talk about Zelsuvmi first and Xepi and then maybe we can transition to the capsule-free transition. So first off, a little bit of a background here. But on the GTN side of things, we've always said that we would be strategic about our contracting going forward with the different plans. And we have the opportunity in the situation to unlock a PBM, remove PA process there. And if you look at the quarter, we would have been up modestly if we decided not to do that. But it's a long-term investment in the brand and long-term growth.

We still have very reasonable gross to net rate for a newly launched product at 31.5%, especially in the derm space. And the rebate that we were able to get this win at was very reasonable. It did not trip our best price with the government, really important. So for the quarter, we were up 4% on units. Prescribers were up 8%. So really -- and other underlying metrics, increase in prescribers, new prescribers coming in, we were strategic in being willing to kind of take this hit on GTNs, very modest hit. We would have had actually a positive revenue growth quarter-over-quarter if we hadn't done it.

But we believe it's going to accelerate growth going forward not only next quarter, but into 2027 and beyond. On the Xepi front, yes, we -- one of the things we really like about the market besides just the synergy with the call point there is that it is a large market, to your point, a little bit more skewed to pediatrician, just slightly more, maybe 60% versus 40% derm, p-derm. And to your point, there are products in the market like Naprosyn. So we are already having payer conversations. They're going quite well.

One of the things we keep hearing is that there's a need for this product in the market, mostly due to the resistance you're seeing with Naprosyn. It's been used at a very high level over many years. So as you know, with antibiotics, a lot of times, when you put that pressure on it, you end up with resistance. And in fact, that's been seen. We've actually pulled some data and done additional research and you're seeing multiple therapies being used a lot of times in impetigo because of that. Next, the question you had asked kind of transitioning to Castle Creek. You had mentioned about the differentiation between the products.

I think that's something right now that we're not really able to discuss what we will be doing. And I think once the S-4 is filed, we can start talking a little bit more about the profile of the products and how they compare in the marketplace. But we're -- just high level, we feel very comfortable based on the research we've done, diligence that it's going to fit very well in that treatment space and be sometimes complementary to VYJUVEK and maybe used in places it's not.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Jeff Jones with Oppenheimer.

Jeffrey Jones: Just if I could, a little more color -- ask for a little more color around the revenue trajectory on Zelsuvmi. We've talked in the past about the colder months and quarters trajectory being reduced prescriptions and diagnosis for molluscum. But revenues flattened somewhat noticeably over the spring as well. And just thinking about what you're seeing in the market with your sales force, what you're learning, how you're adapting your strategy? And then, in the context of SG&A spend, how that might change as you adapt your strategy to increase penetration there and also in preparation for the Xepi launch? And maybe just one quick follow-up on the Xepi question.

Do you have numbers around the resistance levels to Mupirocin at this point?

Scott Plesha: Okay. So a lot to unpack there. So first off, on the revenue trajectory, what -- we're just getting around like one year and going back and being able to see what we -- since launch, just through the fifth quarter and we're learning a lot about the market.
