#3235. How Do You Land on a Moon With Almost No Gravity?

Japan’s MMX mission aims to sample the Martian moon Phobos

Japan's MMX spacecraft will fire its engines to slow down and enter orbit around Mars.

Last August, looking up from the edge of an ancient river delta on Mars, the Perseverance rover’s electronic eye spied an oblong shadow crossing the distant, glowing Sun. Phobos, the Martian moon named for the Greek god of fear and panic, was transiting the solar disk. Too small to darken the pale, dust-tinged sky, but orbiting close enough to eclipse a significant fraction of the Sun, Phobos passed in less than a minute.

NASA’s Perseverance rover captured Phobos passing in front of the Sun from the surface of Mars.ASU/MSSS/SSI/JPL-Caltech/NASA

The tiny moon, with its murky origins, is an enigma, and one whose makeup and history could tell us much about Mars and the wider solar system. And now the international Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission, which successfully launched on 20 October, seeks to explore that mystery with an unprecedented series of landings on the unknown surface of Phobos.

This mission brings unusual challenges—for example, designing an orbit to study a microgravity moon orbiting a much larger planet. Engineers also had to figure out how to assess and land on this low-gravity pile of loosely assembled dirt and rock, how a rover might rove across it, and how the spacecraft might take samples and return them to Earth.

“I often say that landing on Phobos is like trying to land a balloon,” says Yasuhiro Kawakatsu, project manager of MMX at the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA). “It’s very difficult to drop a balloon to the ground and prevent it from tilting or bouncing.”

Phobos is one of two small Martian moons; the other is Deimos, named after the Greek god of dread and terror. Their cosmic origins are unknown, though there are two prevailing theories. One holds that the moons were once asteroids from the belt between Mars and Jupiter, captured by the smaller planet’s gravity. In the other theory, Phobos and Deimos formed when a large celestial body slammed into Mars, sending debris into orbit. Some models suggest the pair are the last survivors from a cluster of satellites.

The enormous Stickney crater, roughly 9 kilometers across, dominates this view of Phobos taken by NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter.University of Arizona/JPL-Caltech/NASA

Scientifically speaking, Phobos is considered a rubble pile, a loosely consolidated aggregate of rock and dust. Far too small to become spherical under its own mass, it’s shaped like a lumpy potato, roughly 27 kilometers in length, with only 1/1,800th of Earth’s gravity. On Phobos, a typical adult would weigh about as much as a tennis ball does on Earth.

More than 10 years in the making, MMX launched on Japan’s flagship H3 rocket from Tanegashima spaceport on 20 October local time. It will arrive at Mars in 2027 carrying scientific payloads from several space agencies, including NASA, and a new rover called Idefix developed by the French and German space agencies (CNES and DLR) in collaboration with JAXA.

Engineers assembled MMX’s modules at Japan’s Tanegashima Space Center before the spacecraft’s October 2026 launch.JAXA

MMX consists of three modules: a propulsion module to power its journey to Mars and apply the brakes to enter orbit around the red planet; an exploration module carrying the rover, sampling gear, and other scientific instruments; and a return module, attached to the exploration module, that harbors the capsule destined for a high-speed reentry into Earth’s atmosphere. After collecting samples on Phobos, the exploration and return modules will lift off together. The exploration module will then be jettisoned while the return module sets a course back home.

If all goes according to plan, MMX will deliver a 10-gram sample to Earth in the second half of 2031. But the mission will face a series of daunting challenges to reach that end point, including navigating complex orbits around Phobos and landing on its surface while Mars periodically blocks communications with Earth.

The MMX’s modular design includes the propulsion module [left] and the exploration and return modules [right].Kyodo News/Getty Images

“It’s the most complex mission I have ever seen,” says Patrick Michel, director of research at CNRS (the French National Center for Scientific Research) and co-principal investigator on Idefix.

An H3 rocket carried MMX into space on 20 October 2026, beginning the mission’s five-year journey to Phobos and back.The Asahi Shimbun/Getty Images

Once MMX reached low Earth orbit, its propulsion module’s engine fired, kicking off a nearly year-long deep-space cruise to Mars. On arrival, the spacecraft will need to fire its engines in an extended, carefully timed burn to slow down enough to be captured by Mars gravity. The propulsion module will then be jettisoned, leaving the exploration and return modules to orbit Mars.

“If something doesn’t go according to plan, MMX will fly by Mars and get catapulted into the solar system,” says Nicola Baresi, an astrodynamicist who coauthored a paper on specially designed orbits for MMX.

From that initial orbit, MMX will transition into a specially designed quasi-satellite orbit that allows it to keep pace with the small moon but also move around it. Since Phobos is too small to orbit in the conventional sense, the spacecraft will orbit Mars alongside the moon, following a clever egg-shaped path that slings MMX alternately ahead of and behind the moon. “When you’re closer to Mars, you’re accelerating with respect to Phobos, and when you’re farther from Mars, you’re decelerating. So you essentially go back and forth,” explains Baresi.

Martian Maneuvers To reach Phobos, MMX will execute three major maneuvers: MOI-1 will put the spacecraft into orbit around Mars, MOI-2 will transfer it toward Phobos, and MOI-3 will place it into its final orbit alongside the moon.Chris Philpot

To reach Phobos, MMX will execute three major maneuvers: MOI-1 will put the spacecraft into orbit around Mars, MOI-2 will transfer it toward Phobos, and MOI-3 will place it into its final orbit alongside the moon.

The best existing images of Phobos, from spacecraft such as NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter and ESA’s Mars Express, have resolutions of only a few meters per pixel. That’s larger than Idefix, the mission’s rover, itself about the size of a microwave oven. To map the surface in greater detail, MMX will loop in front of and behind Phobos at distances ranging from 200 kilometers to less than 20 km from the surface.

During its two-year remote sensing campaign, the exploration module will use several cameras and a laser altimeter to map the surface in high resolution and look for candidate landing sites. When Mars passes behind the Sun as seen from the Earth, causing a roughly two-week communications blackout, MMX will retreat into a larger, stable orbit. After communications resume, MMX will prepare to send its first visitor down to the surface.

Before the exploration and connected return modules attempt to land, Kawakatsu says, MMX will send a scout that in Japanese is called “the first penguin,” leaping into unknown waters. For this mission, the first to leap will be the Idefix rover, named for the canine companion to Obelix in the French comics series Asterix. The exploration module will release the rover during a low-altitude pass of between 40 and 100 meters above Phobos’s surface in 2028 or early 2029.

MMX will use its TENGOO camera [left] and LIDAR laser altimeter [right] to map Phobos’s terrain.JAXA

It will be a tense moment that calls back to 2005, during Japan’s Hayabusa mission to explore the asteroid Itokawa. In a similarly designed drop, the MINERVA rover was released from an orbiter, but erroneously at 200 meters instead of the intended 70 meters. The rover missed the asteroid and, without propulsion, drifted off into deep space.

Idefix will get a slight nudge out of the exploration module toward its negligible-gravity target, freefalling and likely tumbling as it goes. It’s expected to touch down with a velocity of less than 1 meter per second. Unlike rovers that have landed on other surfaces with airbags or dedicated landing legs, Idefix will land without protection, apart from some extra padding on the solar panels due to their critical nature. The barely-there gravity of Phobos should allow the 23-kilogram rover to land softly, though exactly how this landing will play out is hard to predict.

The Idefix rover will travel to Phobos with its wheels tucked in and solar panels folded.DLR

“It will bounce probably several times,” says Stephan Ulamec, Idefix’s co-principal investigator and project manager at DLR. “It will come to rest somehow in some position.” Once it’s still, four retracted legs will deploy to right the rover autonomously, regardless of its orientation. It will then unfold its solar panels to charge its batteries for exploration tasks ahead.

A simulation shows how Idefix is expected to tumble onto Phobos, right itself using its articulated legs, and begin exploring the moon’s surface. DLR

Once operational, Idefix will roll at a snail’s pace, topping out at one millimeter per second. Its metal wheels have protruding blades like a paddle wheel, designed to gain traction in Phobos’s microgravity. “If we were to drive our rover faster, then it would actually be more like we were swimming through instead of driving across the surface,” says Cecily Sunday, a doctoral student involved in testing Idefix’s WheelCams at the Institut Superieur de l’Aeronautique et de l’Espace (ISAE-Supaéro) in Toulouse, France.

The WheelCams, a pair of cameras placed on the underside of the rover, will observe the wheels and their tracks during Idefix’s planned 100-Earth-day primary mission. The images will help researchers study the size and distribution of grains in Phobos’s regolith and how cohesive they are. How much or how little the grains stick together will greatly impact how Idefix moves. Sunday likens this to the difference between driving on dry and wet sand. “Think of trying to build a sandcastle with dry sand,” she says. “You can’t. Add water, and suddenly you can.”

The Idefix rover was mounted between the MMX spacecraft’s landing legs for the journey to Phobos.DLR

The team tested the rover’s nine-bladed wheels on a variety of materials, including Phobos regolith simulants provided by JAXA and DLR, lunar simulants, glass beads, quartz sand, and clay pebbles. “We characterize the mechanical properties of each simulant precisely, then test across the full range, with varying grain size, angularity, and even color, so we can map what we see in the WheelCam images back to actual surface properties,” Sunday says.

Despite the microgravity and Phobos’s rubble-pile nature, Sunday says Earth-based tests can approximate the rover’s motion on the surface of the small moon fairly well. While Phobos’s reduced gravity lowers the rover’s effective weight, there is also reduced pressure between the grains beneath its wheels. “As long as you’re moving very, very slowly and using the same materials and the same weight of the system, they should be representative,” Sunday says.

With four paddle-like wheels and deployable solar panels, Idefix is designed to crawl across Phobos.Ardan Fuessmann/Imago/Alamy

Idefix’s interactions with its new home will offer “sub-millimeter resolution and information on porosity, on grain size, on surface strength, on how hard is the material,” Ulamec says. “It fills a gap between remote observations from orbit and detailed observations of the return samples back on Earth.”

What Idefix finds on this rocky, rugged world will help determine how and where JAXA attempts to land the main spacecraft. Michel says the touchdown will provide ground truth for understanding of Phobos. When NASA’s OSIRIS-REx spacecraft touched down on the asteroid Bennu to collect a sample, its sampling arm surprisingly sank nearly half a meter into the loose material. But Ulamec doesn’t think Idefix will sink deep into Phobos, noting that Bennu is very different and much smaller, with a diameter of 500 meters.

Once Idefix has investigated the surface, MMX will face an even greater challenge: landing its much larger exploration module on Phobos. The spacecraft will make a controlled descent to roughly 10 meters above the surface, then drop the remaining distance in free fall. With so little gravity to pull it downward, even a small sideways motion could cause the lander to tip or bounce away. A successful, upright landing would mark the start of up to two hours on Phobos for the crucial sampling phase.

The MMX mission draws on the experience and technologies of Japan’s two Hayabusa sample-return missions, which landed on the asteroids Itokawa and Ryugu. But this mission has many more moving parts. MMX’s exploration module will use two sampling devices—a coring sampler developed by JAXA and a pneumatic sampler provided by NASA and fabricated by Honeybee Robotics, a subsidiary of Blue Origin. Data from these tools, and those carried by the Idefix rover, could answer questions about the origin of Phobos and how the Mars system has evolved.

The coring sampler uses a robot arm and a cylindrical corer designed to reach at least 2 centimeters below the surface. The arm can maneuver to find the best site for digging. “That by itself is a challenge because we’ve never done it,” Michel says. “You never know what can happen at the very sampling site itself, where you might have a boulder and the arm cannot move.”

Probing beneath the top layer will be valuable because solar radiation, galactic cosmic rays, and micrometeorites have battered and weathered the surface. The material below should offer a better record of the moon’s origins, and JAXA aims to collect at least 10 grams of it.

MMX will carry both the Idefix rover [bottom] and a robotic coring sampler [top] designed to dig beneath Phobos’s weathered surface.JAXA

The pneumatic sampler takes a different approach. Mounted on one of the lander’s legs, it will inject pure, non-reactive nitrogen gas into the surface and capture the grains stirred up. This sample could illuminate the changes Mars and its moons have undergone over time. The dual system also adds redundancy in the face of Phobos’s unknowns. “If the surface of Phobos proves to be very hard, [the coring sampler] may struggle to penetrate the ground. [The pneumatic sampler] would not experience this issue and still be able to gather material,” Kawakatsu says.

One of the most intriguing aspects of MMX is the additional possibility of collecting material from the planet below. It’s likely that Phobos has been peppered by Martian ejecta thrown into space by meteor impacts, so MMX also provides an opportunity to return the first Martian samples to Earth. Michel estimates that the samples could contain “a few hundred grains coming from Mars.” Scientists can distinguish those grains from native Phobos material by analyzing their oxygen isotopes.

That possibility raises a planetary-protection question. A direct Mars sample-return mission would have to follow strict rules to ensure that potentially living biological material from Mars doesn’t contaminate Earth. But those protocols don’t apply to MMX, even if its sample does collect grains of Martian soil. A panel of experts concluded that any microbes blasted off Mars wouldn’t survive the violent impact and ejection or the intense radiation exposure on the way to Phobos. This saved MMX from implementing expensive and time-consuming quarantine and containment protocols for the returning sample.

After landing on Phobos, MMX will have roughly two hours to collect samples from the moon’s surface before lifting off again.JAXA

During the brief surface operation, the robotic arm will deposit the samples in a storage unit, from which they’ll be transferred into a capsule aboard the return module and sealed in a vacuum. After that, lift off.

Once back in Mars orbit, the exploration module will resume its observations of Phobos and make several flybys of Mars’s other diminutive moon, Deimos, to gather data on its surface, structure, and composition. In November 2030, during a favorable alignment of Mars and Earth, MMX will begin the homeward leg of its trip. The return module will separate from the exploration module and power the voyage home, its sole objective to bring the dust of Phobos to Earth.

MMX’s sample return capsule will carry material from Phobos through Earth’s atmosphere in 2031.JAXA

Finally, in 2031, the 60-centimeter-wide sample capsule will plunge into Earth’s atmosphere at roughly 12 kilometers per second. Assuming it survives the extreme heat of reentry and lands safely in Australia, scientists will begin to tease out clues about Phobos and the early solar system. JAXA’s Institute of Space and Astronautical Science will receive and curate the samples, which will also be shared with mission partners.

“We have macroscale measurements from the spacecraft, microscale measurements with the rover, and then sample analysis,” Michel says. “So we can relate the three kinds of scales together because we have all of them.” The insights gleaned from orbital images, close-up images of the regolith, and the chemical analysis of the samples could have wider implications for our understanding of our solar system.

“MMX is a mission to understand the Mars system and shed light onto how terrestrial planets like the Earth, and maybe Mars, develop a habitable environment,” Kawakatsu says. “We strongly suspect that our terrestrial planet region formed dry, and water and organics were scattered inwards from the icy-rich outer solar system.” Mars, he says, sits at the gateway between the inner and outer solar system, making its moons valuable witnesses to the processes that shaped potentially habitable worlds.

Andrew Jones is a freelance journalist based near Helsinki. He writes about the space industry and technology with a particular focus on China's activities.

#3233. Axle raises $9M to bring AI agents to Wall Street’s meeting-makers

The startup replaces spreadsheets that banks use to set up investor meetings with company bosses.

Axle has raised $9M led by Eniac and Bonfire Ventures. It makes software that helps investment banks arrange meetings between investors and company management, and will add more AI agents. It says some of North America’s biggest banks use it.

Axle, a startup that makes software for investment banks, has raised $9M in a round led by Eniac and Bonfire Ventures, it announced on Thursday. Teamworthy Ventures also joined.

Axle works on what banks call corporate access. Banks arrange meetings between big investors and company bosses, analysts and industry experts. Those meetings help investors decide where to put money, and they shape which banks get their trading business.

CEO Sam Shapiro says much of this work still runs on old software, spreadsheets and manual scheduling. He worked in corporate access at Goldman Sachs before starting Axle, according to the company’s 2024 pre-seed announcement.

Axle puts conferences, investor meetings, roadshows and expert calls into one system. Clients can request meetings and see schedules through portals that need no login.

The company says it works with some of North America’s largest investment banks but did not name them. One bank started using Axle earlier this year and, within months, dropped three other providers.

The new money will go into AI agents that help bank staff understand clients and spot opportunities. Axle is also building tools to show how much the meetings are worth to clients.

AI startups are moving fast into banking. Berlin’s Taktile raised $110M from Goldman Sachs to automate bank decisions, and Anthropic has launched ready-made finance agents for Claude, while OpenAI sells a ChatGPT for finance.

Looking for thriller movies to watch on Netflix this week? Then you’ve come to the right place. Every week I comb through the new arrivals on the world’s most popular streaming service to find the recently added thriller movies to bring some excitement to your watchlist.

This week, I’ve not been short on options. For starters, we’ve got a “Bonnie and Clyde” style crime drama that mixes a criminal spree with romance, and it stars Samara Weaving, who’s recently been confirmed for Marvel’s new “X-Men” team. Or how about the latest Netflix original, led by an Oscar winner, that explores the darker side of Music City. Finally, there’s the movie of 2026, which might be primarily a horror, but still has plenty of thrilling moments.

All three of my picks this week are worthy of your attention, so without further teasing, let’s dive into the Netflix thriller movies to watch this week.

Watching “Carolina Caroline” feels quite appropriate this week as the entertainment world turns its focus to a little video game called Grand Theft Auto VI. You might be wondering how the two are related; after all, one is a game set in a fictional version of Miami, the other a movie set in the ‘90s American South. Well, both are clearly inspired by “Bonnie and Clyde,” with each exploring a romance between two criminals caught up in a dangerous spree.

Caroline Daniels (Samara Weaving) is a gas station attendant in rural Texas, dissatisfied with her life; she impulsively decides to skip town with Oliver Anderson (Kyle Gallner), a charismatic con man. The two begin a criminal spree across the country, ranging from small cons to daring heists, all while falling madly in love. But much like the infamous misadventure of Bonnie and Clyde, this doomed relationship can surely only end one way.

Sorry, Tyler Perry, “The Gospel of Christmas” looks heart-warming enough, but Netflix’s most buzzy original this week is “Heartland.” This new mystery-thriller combines the always popular genre with the world of country music, which has enjoyed a resurgence in recent years. All signs point to a Netflix original that will rocket straight to the No. 1 spot in the streaming service’s top 10 most-watched list. Here’s hoping it’s good enough to deserve it.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

“Heartland” stars Oscar-winner Jessica Chastain as Misty Jones, once a country music megastar, now a reclusive figure who has stepped away from the Music City spotlight. However, when Misty’s niece, played by IRL country singer Carter Faith, goes missing, she returns to Nashville to investigate. This forces Misty to grapple with her own complicated past and also to delve into the city’s underbelly. Expect a twist or two to keep you hooked.

Watch "Heartland" on Netflix starting November 13

Okay, so “Obsession” is predominantly categorised as a horror flick, but I’m including it here because it’s an acclaimed movie that blends multiple genres. In this well-crafted mixture, you’ve got horror, comedy and thriller elements. A box-office juggernaut, made for less than $1 million and grossing more than $500m, it’s one of 2026’s biggest success stories, and with awards buzz growing, now is the time (re)watch it as it heads to Netflix on Nov. 16.

Written and directed by Curry Barker, now one of Hollywood’s hottest talents, “Obsession” focuses on a timid music store worker named Bear (Michael Johnston). Hopefully infatuated with his friend Nikki (Inde Navarrette), Bear makes a wish for his feelings to be returned, which actually comes true, and then spirals totally out of control. Anchored by Navarrette’s incredible performance, “Obsession’s” position as a modern classic is already secured.

Watch "Obsession" on Netflix starting November 16

#3231. Apple reportedly met with Thai officials over spyware alerts sent to politicians

Bloomberg reports that Apple has met with Thai government officials in the wake of its recent wave of iPhone alerts about mercenary spyware attacks. Here are the details.

Last week, The Financial Times and TechCrunch reported that Apple had sent a fresh wave of threat notifications to potential spyware targets in 99 countries, warning them that they may have been targeted by mercenary spyware attacks.

At the time, the FT focused on German lawmakers who had received the warnings, while TechCrunch highlighted recipients in other countries, including Beirut-based filmmaker Radwan Mortada.

Today, Bloomberg reported that “Thailand held meetings with Apple Inc. officials” over the notifications, adding that the warnings raised questions about “who may have targeted [Thai politicians] and why.”

Receiving an alert doesn’t necessarily mean a device was successfully compromised, Digital Economy and Society Minister Chaichanok Chidchob said after meeting Apple representatives Wednesday, Krungthep Turakij and other media reported. Thai authorities also have no evidence so far that the latest attempted attacks involved Pegasus, the spyware developed by Israel’s NSO Group, he said.

As Bloomberg explains, Pegasus was “allegedly used against pro-democracy campaigners in 2022.”

The recent wave of alerts, which were sent out on October 29, followed another round in August, when Apple notified potential targets in 110 countries. As always, Apple declined to disclose what triggers these notifications to prevent attackers from evading detection in the future, but recommended that recipients enable Lockdown Mode and seek expert security assistance.

Bloomberg added that Thai authorities are expected to meet with other technology companies on Thursday to discuss potential countermeasures, including risks to Android devices.

#3230. AI Agents Are Testing the Limits of Zero-Trust Security

As autonomous AI agents work together, verifying their actions, enforcing security policies, and maintaining accountability becomes increasingly difficult

Vishal Sharma is a Reader in the School of Electronics, Electrical Engineering, and Computer Science at Queen's University Belfast, Northern Ireland, United Kingdom.

In a de-authentication attack on an aerial vehicle using a human- and agent-in-the-loop approach, an AI agent can quickly scan the active channel and autonomously intercept traffic, thus reducing the time to react and regain control.

This article is brought to you by Queen’s University Belfast.

Several teams around the globe are leveraging AI by creating a task force of agents managed by an orchestrator and creating applications to support risk assessment, client profiling, match making, and information yield with a slight overview of decision making. One of the important components for these agents is to ensure that the logs are managed and historic relevance is not being used to avoid skewing towards same decision making. Thus, the system is expected to keep checkpoints in place where agents are prompted to delete such historic relevance.

However, despite such methodology in place, a future prompt could make the agents bring forward the information that was supposed to be deleted and can be tricked into revealing more information, which is a classic case of context recovery attack. So, the question raised here is: How can we trust that our instructions have been followed? And where is the proof?

There is an element of utilizing zero-trust architectures (ZTA) for orchestrating and managing agentic activity, which simply means all agentic interactions use the core principle of “never trust,” “always verify.” ZTA components include a policy enforcement point (PEP) that has to be trusted to maintain trust across the system, so the question that remains is where is the component of zero-trust, and shall we trust the policies enforced by PEP?

Having a pro-agentic approach and utilizing agents could be helpful with the right guardrails in place. Opening our systems to random agents that are being trained on off-the-shelf models and blindly relying on them can pose significant cyber risks. For example, vibe coding by using an AI model to help develop software, giving away the entire codebase to an untrusted entity outside the organization can lead to vulnerability sweeping across multiple surfaces.

Vibe coding by using an AI model to help develop software, giving away the entire codebase to an untrusted entity outside the organization can lead to vulnerability sweeping across multiple surfaces.

This opens critical discussions towards how vibe coding could interfere with the positioning and implementation of trusted execution of the agentic queries. Consider an autonomous web of agents that relies on agents’ inputs to drive the operations. When the system is operating under low tolerance of failure and with non-tracking based agentic workflows, it could be computationally expensive to trust and verify each query in real-time that leads to the common trade-offs of memory vs execution.

Another risk to consider is the zero-day attack. When it happens, how will the system react? Would such an event be manageable without a total infrastructure breakdown? The scale of impact can be observed from over reliance on agentic ecosystems with only one trusted layer. This could mean that when failure occurs, the entire ecosystem could be exposed, just like there will be no autonomy if the backbone network is not available, which essentially means no layer to place trust.

An in-house experiment done at Queen’s University Belfast (QUB) provided an initial understanding of how the scale of agentic attacks could mean a lower window of vulnerability. The team focused on very popular de-authentication attacks and with agentic orchestration, the swift rate to do de-authentication attacks could go as low as 2 to 3 seconds. This gives little to no time to react and decide on patching the system.

There is another aspect of the large-scale agentic system, which establishes trust under asynchronous autonomy. Trust serves as a critical foundation for traceability. How would you ensure that all the agents operating towards a common goal are aligned and understand the delays associated with their goals?

Our team worked around this space, which at first involved demonstrating that the problem exists, and its impact and scale can be huge when you must prove trust under boundaries of asynchronous autonomy. Solutions towards such problems can be simplified by keeping things like AI-bill of material or leveraging distributed ledger technology that can provide underlying infrastructure of trust via traceability and immutability and keep the agentic activity and associated trust vectors agnostic to the platform.

Within trust, another factor that is not well explored but needs a thorough investigation is the concept of horizontal anomalies. It defines how agents interact differently with various sources under different settings. As agents behave correctly and align themselves with the architectural expectations for one specific task or application, that does not necessarily mean these can be trusted for their operations across all associated components. How to identify such anomalies and what methods can be employed without complying with such agents remain open questions and topics for further exploration.

The critical aspect is that utility of agents with semi to low trust governance offer short-term high benefits, but the cost of recovery when the system fails is yet to be explored, and this will not be a contained issue. We are looking into the system where agents are already sweeping into different entities and may not allow complete recovery. For example, a mere supply chain issue because an agent going rogue is now not a containable small task but needs sweeping across all the touch points of those affected agents. This essentially means despite the number of agents and their ability to trigger proxy-agents, which may not be directly linked to the wider ecosystem, there is a need to ensure that computationally expensive trackers are in place for all the agents.

Other relevant PhD works carried out in our research group are towards sovereignty of AI, exploring aspects of trust and accountability. Our hypothesis is that sovereignty and trust need to be governed together as onus of provenance is high on the host of agents. Thus, it needs understanding of laws governing trust-based executions of AI. The important challenge here is that there is a vital difference between missed information and missed instructions, and both have different impacts when it comes to trusted accountability.

The real-world issue with these systems lies in the failure to adopt approaches that historically have relied on state-based modeling when governing trust. In stateless systems where agentic autonomy is high, the convergence and reliability towards trust-provenance decreases significantly. Thus, it brings us back to the original question – does a true zero-trust even exist?

Can policies be trusted? If so, how should these be managed without falling into the trap of policy-based accessibility and control issues? Despite the argument that PEP can help manage access between the agents, placing a single entity and expecting it to scale towards all agentic interactions is underestimating the problem space.

Formal verification of trust is another part of a trust-based agentic ecosystem. When dealing with AI models, understanding the robustness helps to put trust in place for these models.

To build our case and settle around the challenges of trust embeddings in Agentic AI, within Cyber AI hub, we are exploring opportunities to help companies scale up as well as build their pipeline of agentic applications for commercial viability. However, the element that governs our regular work and decision making are scale of problem and number of agentic deployments, anomaly detection across the agentic workflows, continuous evaluation of the attack surfaces and vulnerability assessment, exploring differences in the pure agentic AI and task-driven multi-agent system.

We are working with industries where trust is a pre-requisite, and these organizations put trust as a guardrail managed via internal policies with a pure focus on securing the systems through policies rather than trusting the third-party agentic service providers. Additionally, trust in services is presented by ensuring constraints around their service models where agentic activities are tracked and managed via logs including management of their token revocation list to avoid replay attacks depending on the type of application. Formal verification of trust is another part of a trust-based agentic ecosystem. When dealing with AI models, understanding the robustness helps to put trust in place for these models. Things like balancing the adversarial accuracy along with certified adversarial robustness can help to determine how much the model can be trusted.

But the question is, can we settle for anything less than foolproof when it comes to deployment of agents in the real world? And if so, how much impact can be controlled, and who is responsible for the remaining component?

#3229. Cellebrite (CLBT) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

New AI product debuted strongly while a U.S. redomicile move advances.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Cellebrite DI Ltd. (CLBT -14.25%) reported third-quarter results characterized by the accelerating adoption of its AI-powered investigative tools and a strategic initiative to redomicile in the United States. Management stated that the move to establish a U.S. parent company is intended to eliminate sales friction associated with its foreign entity status and qualify the company for major U.S. stock indices. The company reported that its newest product, Genesis, reached a revenue milestone in its first full quarter, with adoption primarily driven by law enforcement agencies seeking to automate evidence analysis and reduce investigative backlogs. Management indicated that the business model is shifting toward more ratable revenue as cloud and AI solutions become a larger portion of the mix, leading to an updated commercial structure that will consolidate multiple customer contracts into a single platform agreement starting in 2027.

Operator: Welcome, everyone, to the Cellebrite Q3 2026 Earnings Call. [Operator Instructions] I would now like to turn the call over to Andrew Kramer, Vice President of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

The deals we have won and those we expect to close in Q4 reflect customers so convinced of Genesis' value that they reprioritized spending to fund it. Customers continue to share the powerful impact that Genesis is making. Genesis surfaces evidence in minutes that would otherwise take hours or days of manual review. Its capabilities extend beyond mobile forensics, helping investigators synthesize video, audio calls, financial records, and other evidentiary artifacts to surface leads.

A Florida detective recently shared that Genesis helped analysts search 2 years of jail calls and in just 15 minutes, surface a murder confession and plans for a cover-up. For this detective, Genesis was the difference between evidence that exists and evidence that is found. Last week, we announced the appointment of Rogerio Rizzi as Executive Vice President of Corporate Strategy and Development, bringing substantial experience in AI, technology, and M&A to our company. In addition, we are making good progress on our search for a new leader of our product and technology organization, which we initiated when I became CEO.

Today, Cellebrite moves forward with a strong foundation that was built by delivering market-leading digital forensic solutions for a specialized, highly technical user community. In recent years, we have broadened our offerings to address the workflow, collaboration, and analytic needs of investigators, analysts, field agents, command staff, and prosecutors. From proprietary machine learning models to new agentic capabilities, AI is infused into every Cellebrite solution, maximizing the impact of our solutions across different customer segments and user constituencies.

In 2027, Genesis will evolve from a purpose-built agentic AI product into an AI-native platform that will collect digital evidence from devices, cloud services, and other sources, securely share and analyze vast volumes of relevant artifacts, facilitate mission-critical workflows, and rapidly deliver trusted, court-ready insight and decisive operational intelligence. We believe Genesis will become the standard for how our customers conduct investigations and advance intelligence-led operations. There are three primary things I'd like to emphasize. First, the roadmap. Over the next 12 months, we will bring proven market-leading solutions onto our Genesis platform and deliver it in the environment that best suits our customers, from air-gapped and on-premise, with an option for forward-deployed engineers, to cloud and hybrid.

Underpinning that flexibility will be innovations in collecting digital evidence, managing investigative workflows, and analyzing an ever-expanding range of artifacts, anchored by a new unified evidence format that is optimized for Cellebrite's platform and ecosystem. Executing on this roadmap involves reshaping how we build products. We're moving from a feature-focused structure to one where AI agents work alongside our engineers, product managers, and forensic experts to take ideas from discovery to validated release faster, without sacrificing quality or security. This is enabling us to integrate agents and capabilities on top of our forensic foundation with the provenance, verification, and human oversight that support our customers' chain of custody requirements, legal frameworks, and investigative protocols. Second, hardware.

Customers need faster access to more devices and faster insight from them. Our platform will be paired with advanced hardware for each setting, from a portable handheld with a small language AI model for the field, to next-generation data collection systems for the lab, and we'll keep supporting the hardware customers already use. Third, the business model. Genesis will be priced in tiers that reflect the capabilities an organization needs and its expected consumption of data, compute, and tokens. Customers will begin moving onto the platform next year, and we'll make that transition as straightforward and appealing as possible.

Shiven Ramji: Yes. I will start and then have Marcus and Dave weigh in. So currently, Genesis is priced to scale with the value customers get. And as we continue to roll out the platform next year, we are going to make sure that the pricing is kind of evolved with that. And we have different models today. We do a Genesis cloud version. We now have a Genesis on-prem version. And over time, we will probably have a platform pricing with a usage component on top of it.

Marcus Jewell: Yes, and I will add in. Obviously, consumption pricing into our segments is accepted at varying levels. In law enforcement, consumption pricing is a new thing. So all we are able to do is give what we call a surety. There is a number of people trying to break into this market, and if you go in with a pure token burn model, it is not accepted very well. In fact, the buying mechanisms often do not allow that. You need to be more of a term-based or subscription-based in order to get through the way that things are procured, especially in the U.S.

So what we have done is a couple of things there, is that we give a meter, and so people know what their usage is at any one time. That is unique in the market. Marcus Jewell: Yes, I will just add a little bit, Shiv. Look, it is true multimodal, and what I mean by multimodal is it is bringing in multiple data sources. #3228. Apple is closing its Support Community forum after 28 years

Users can still browse the Apple Support Community, but can no longer ask or answer. Apple told AppleInsider it will take the forums completely offline, old answers included.

Apple has stopped taking new posts on the Apple Support Community and will close the forum on 20 November. The site has been read-only since 10 November, according to a notice on its homepage.

“You can continue to find trusted guidance and support on the official Apple Support site,” the notice says.

9to5Mac’s Marcus Mendes first reported the notice on the evening of 10 November. The last post appears to have gone up at 5:49pm Pacific time that day, Joe Rossignol reported for MacRumors.

Apple told MacRumors it made the decision after a careful evaluation of strategy and customer needs.

The forum launched in 1998 as Apple Tech Exchange, according to MacRumors. It became Apple Discussions in 2000, Apple Support Communities in 2011 and Apple Support Community in 2022.

The notice does not say what happens to the old posts. Apple told AppleInsider it will take the forums completely offline, William Gallagher reported on 11 November.

Apple has not read the forums in at least five years, according to AppleInsider’s sources. The sign-in button now leads to an internal portal for Apple’s corporate employees, MacRumors reported.

MacRumors pointed users to Apple Support, its own forums and Reddit. Reddit is moving to login-only viewing, and it now uses AI to summarise product threads.

Customers can still contact Apple Support directly, MacRumors noted. Last month, Apple Support took on Apple’s offer to replace iPhone Duos with failing inner screens.

Electronic products now pack circuits, structures, thermal paths, and packaging into very small spaces. These physical domains interact with one another. A packaging choice can change how a shock load reaches a circuit board. Such interactions are hard to predict. Most are found during physical qualification, late in development. At that stage, the design is mostly fixed. A failure leads to redesign, rebuilds, and retesting. Physical tests give strong evidence of robustness, but they give limited insight into load paths and failure margins. Traditional simulation gives more detail, but it needs specialist skills and long manual setup. This white paper explains how guided virtual validation brings shock and drop assessment into the design phase. It reviews common test configurations, model inputs, and acceptance criteria. A packaged drop case study then shows how packaging can be optimized across all drop orientations and checked against physical test results.

Fall has settled around us now, and that couch is looking comfier and comfier as the days grow colder. That's why I've already done the hard work for you, and combed through everything new on Hulu in November to shine a spotlight on the best movies of the bunch. That includes:

Want to know more about my picks before you dedicate your precious streaming time? I don't blame you. Here's everything you need to know about which three new movies on Hulu deserve a spot on your watchlist.

Kicking things off with a good ol' dad movie, "Black Bag" is a cross between "Ocean’s Eleven" and "Mr. and Mrs. Smith" with some charming chemistry on display between co-leads Michael Fassbender and Cate Blanchett. Tightly crafted, smart, and with plenty of dark humor to spare, it stars the two as a married couple who are both spies for the British intelligence service.

He's a human lie detector, but when his wife is suspected of being a double agent, he’s forced to use his skills on the one person he thought he knew best. Clocking in at just 94 minutes, "Black Bag" checks all the boxes, nailing exactly the kind of ever-rising stakes that you're looking for in an action movie without overstaying its welcome. It's just the kind of thing to throw on in the background for a night on the couch.

My colleague plugged "Heart Eyes" in last week's column, but I have the wheel of your attention now, and I say it's worth a second shout-out. The premise is hokey but fun: Each year on Valentine's Day, a masked serial killer known as Heart Eyes hunts down couples — except this time, he messes with the wrong one. For starters, they're not even together. Not yet, anyway, though it won't be long given all the meet-cute romcom movie magic propelling them into each other's orbit with the subtlety of a sledgehammer.

Ally (Olivia Holt), a newly single ad designer, is stuck working with her hopeless romantic colleague Jay (Mason Gooding) on a big project when Heart Eyes mistakenly targets them as this year's victims. It's a fun watch with plenty of tongue-in-cheek humor and solid scares. The biggest jumpscare came at the end, though, when I saw Josh Ruben, a name any Dropout or College Humor fan will recognize, was in the director's chair. His love of romcoms and horror comes through loud and clear.

"The Secret Life of Walter Mitty" is one of my husband's comfort movies, and I include it on today's list for that fact alone. It's an epic about the whimsy in life we may always find if we look for it, with Ben Stiller at his peak as Walter Mitty — a lovable sap you can't help but root for. He's a lowly office drone toiling away for a decade and a half as a photo manager for Life magazine when he gets pushed into what becomes the sort of adventure he often daydreams about. It's "Forrest Gump" by way of "Cats," if you will.

"The Secret Life of Walter Mitty" is a bunch of short stories James Thurber wrote in 1939 cobbled together and given a 21st-century overhaul with Stiller at the helm. Kristen Wiig is also worth shouting out as Cheryl, his co-worker love interest he quietly pines for. Stiller brings an infectious sense of joy to this one that'll leave you feeling like you're walking on air.

#3224. Labcorp: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Tuck-in acquisitions and specialty testing momentum give Labcorp tools to offset a looming $125 million Medicare reimbursement hit.

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Oct. 28, 2026, Labcorp (LH +0.02%) announced 7% revenue growth to $3.8 billion alongside raised full-year guidance. Enterprise profit expansion and solid organic demand show how scale keeps driving long-term earnings leverage. Three things management said stand out.

Proposed fee schedule changes under PAMA, the Protecting Access to Medicare Act, will lower Medicare reimbursement rates across hundreds of tests starting in 2027. Management plans to counter the $125 million hit through volume growth, biopharma demand, and cost efficiencies.

High-growth specialty areas like oncology and neurology carry higher margins and pull routine volume along with them. Physicians ordering specialized diagnostic panels routinely send companion core testing to the same laboratory provider.

Agreements to buy assets from BioReference, Myriad Genetics' prenatal business, and Millennium Health target local market density. These acquisitions are expected to be accretive to adjusted EPS (earnings per share) in year one.

Operating efficiency and organic expansion continue to expand profitability, giving management the flexibility to absorb reimbursement regulatory shocks. Its global central laboratory footprint, proprietary specialty assay portfolio, and disciplined cost initiatives through Launchpad, its enterprise cost savings program, anchor long-term value creation. Management focuses on organic growth and pricing discipline to compound shareholder returns.

Integrating newly acquired assets into the core network while maintaining book-to-bill strength across biopharma services provides clear operational momentum as regulatory policy shifts unfold.

#3223. J.Crew launches an AI stylist built on Anthropic’s Claude

Style Advisor suggests full outfits from J.Crew's own photo shoots instead of single items.

J.Crew built its new Style Advisor with several of Anthropic’s Claude models.

J.Crew has launched Style Advisor, an AI stylist on its US website built with Anthropic’s Claude. Shoppers describe an occasion and get complete outfits from looks J.Crew’s stylists put together. Personal recommendations based on past purchases will come later.

J.Crew has launched Style Advisor, an AI stylist on its website built with Anthropic’s Claude, Anthropic announced on Thursday. It is available in the US for women’s and men’s clothing.

Instead of searching for a sweater, then trousers, then shoes, shoppers can describe what they need, such as an outfit for a beach wedding or a first job interview. Style Advisor replies with complete looks, and shoppers can keep refining them. They can also start from one item and ask what goes with it.

Every suggestion comes from outfits J.Crew’s own stylists put together for the brand’s catalogue shoots. The AI picks and shows those looks rather than inventing new ones, which keeps it in line with the brand’s style.

“We see an opportunity to fundamentally rethink the shopping experience,” said Libby Wadle, CEO of J.Crew Group.

J.Crew built the tool using several Claude models. In each conversation, the mid-sized Sonnet 5.5 acts as the stylist, while the smaller Haiku 5.5 handles quick tasks so answers come fast. For now, it does not tailor suggestions to each shopper’s past purchases, but J.Crew plans to add that and expand to more countries.

Retailers are racing to add AI stylists. Ralph Lauren launched its Ask Ralph assistant late last year, and Kate Spade uses Amazon’s shopping AI, while Zalando’s agent will shop other retailers from 2027. On Prime Day, shoppers sent by AI assistants were more likely to buy than those from search.

#3222. Binance warns iPhone crypto holders of security flaw researchers say remains unpatched

Crypto exchange Binance has warned iPhone users about an iOS vulnerability that could allow malicious apps to access sensitive data stored by other apps. Here are the details.

In a post published on X (via AppleInsider), Binance says that a vulnerability called worse_query could allow “malicious apps to read local files from other apps, putting seed phrases, private keys, and login credentials at risk across the entire ecosystem.”

Binance says the flaw affects iOS 26.7.1, iOS 27.0.1, and iOS 27.2. However, a Community Note points out that researchers describe the vulnerability as an unpatched zero-day and that Apple’s latest security updates, including iOS 27.2.1 (the current version at the time of writing), do not mention a fix.

A vulnerability (worse_query) affecting iOS 26.7.1, 27.0.1, and 27.2 allows malicious apps to read local files from other apps, putting seed phrases, private keys, and login credentials at risk across the entire ecosystem. This is an iOS-level issue, not unique to Binance.…

That said, in addition to updating their devices, Binance recommends that iPhone crypto holders take the following immediate actions:

The vulnerability was disclosed by security researchers @0xjohnny and @forcequitOS, who published a proof of concept on GitHub demonstrating how it can be used to bypass iOS sandbox protections, which normally prevent apps from accessing each other’s files.

Researcher @forcequitOS also noted that neither iOS 27.2.1 nor iOS 27.3 beta 1 patches the vulnerability.

Just as a general statement so there isn’t any confusion about it, worse_query is *not* patched in iOS 27.2.1 and 27.3 beta 1. I’ll update version support on the readme when it’s patched.

Although the researcher describes the code as intended for developers and not useful on its own, other developers have already built apps using it, including a file manager that can access, modify, and delete data belonging to other apps without requiring a jailbreak.

According to The Hacker News, neither Binance nor the researchers have reported any attacks or cryptocurrency thefts involving the vulnerability so far.

I won’t be putting up my Christmas tree just yet, but my home already looks festive thanks to my seasonal indoor plants. Aside from a pretty white cyclamen and bright red poinsettia, I also have a Christmas cactus.

Now that I have completed my winter houseplant collection, I’m wondering how I can help my Christmas cactus thrive and stay vibrant and healthy over the festive season and beyond.

It turns out there’s a natural fix, and it’s sitting in the compost caddy in my kitchen. Besides giving me a kick in the morning, coffee grounds are a natural fertilizer that can perk up your Christmas cactus.

But before you start adding all your spent coffee grounds to your Christmas cactus, take it easy. Although coffee grounds can be used as a mild fertilizer, there are other steps you can take to help your plant thrive.

What’s more, there are certain times of year when your Christmas cactus will appreciate a feed, and other times when it won’t.

The Christmas cactus grows in tropical rainforests of Brazil, and thrives in rich, organic compost, unlike the desert cacti that grow in arid, sandy ground. Coffee grounds can help mimic this rich environment, and their nitrogen content supports healthy new growth. They are also acidic, which this plant favors.

Beyond promoting lush growth, vibrant color and a strong root system, coffee grounds can enhance soil structure by improving aeration and water retention.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Beyond promoting lush growth, vibrant color and a strong root system, coffee grounds can enhance soil structure by improving aeration and water retention.

Although I’m happiest when I have a daily fix of coffee grounds, your Christmas cactus won’t appreciate a daily sprinkle of grounds. In fact, it only needs a coffee fix every four to six weeks in the spring and summer.

If you add coffee grounds to your plant’s soil over the festive season, it can stress the plant during its flowering season. Instead of adding nutrients to the soil, the extra nitrogen can disrupt the plant’s cycle, preventing buds from forming or causing flowers to fall early.

It’s best to dry the coffee grounds first and mix them into the soil or another compost before adding them to your plant.

Wet coffee grounds sitting on top of the soil can develop white mold and attract fungus gnats; drying them first eliminates this risk. Wet grounds are also likely to clump together and form a dense layer on the surface, hindering aeration. While, fresh or uncomposted grounds break down more slowly and take longer to work.

This set of three ceramic planters features a reactive beige glaze and includes drainage holes and saucers. They are the ideal gift for the plant lover in your life. You can place them together or spread them across different rooms in your home. The largest pot measures 6.5 inches in diameter, the medium pot 5 inches and the smallest container 4 inches.

1. Coffee grounds and potting soilSpread used coffee grounds on a plate and let them dry completely. Once dry, mix 1 to 2 tablespoons of the grounds with 1 cup of potting soil. Spread the blend over the top of your plant’s soil, repeating every four to six weeks during the spring and summer.

2. Make a liquid feedMix 1 teaspoon of used coffee grounds into 1 cup of warm water and let the solution steep overnight. Strain out the grounds and use the coffee-infused water to feed your plant, repeating monthly during the spring and summer.

3. Create a coffee compostAdd used coffee grounds to your compost bin. Once the compost has fully broken down and is ready to use, add a fresh layer to the top of your plant’s soil. While it takes the longest to prepare, composting is the safest and most effective way to fertilize your Christmas cactus with coffee grounds.

While it's best not to fertilize your Christmas cactus during its flowering season, you can help it thrive by providing the best conditions.LightPlace your Christmas cactus in a bright spot, such as near a window, but keep it out of direct sunlight, as harsh rays can scorch, bleach or weaken the plant. Because these plants are native to tropical rainforests, they thrive best in dappled shade.

TemperatureAim to keep the room temperature around 65-75°F during the day, while a cooler nighttime temperature will help trigger blooming.

WaterBecause it’s not a desert cactus, it needs to be watered, but don’t go overboard. I use a simple tool, like this Hathdia Soil Moisture Meter, $5 at Amazon, to check when my plants need a drink.

#3220. iPhone Duo one week later: The future, or not for me?

My iPhone Duo arrived last Thursday, so I’ve had a week to use it as my daily carry. My early experience has been mixed, so I keep asking myself an important question: is this the iPhone’s future and I just need to adapt, or is the Duo simply not for everyone?

After a week using the iPhone Duo, in some ways I have a lot of clarity about the product, and in other ways my thinking is very clouded.

To put it simply: I’m not having a great time with the Duo, which makes me wonder if the problem is me, not it.

I’ve seen countless social media posts from Duo owners proclaiming how much they love the product. And I absolutely believe them. The iPhone Duo is a remarkable innovation for the iPhone. It’s cool, weird, and wonderful in all sorts of ways. But for me and my needs (preferences?), it’s been more frustrating than enjoyable.

And that frustration mainly boils down to one thing: I almost never want to open it.

I’d estimate at least 90% of my iPhone Duo usage involves the front display. And when I unfold it the remaining 10% of the time, it’s often because I force myself to do it in the hopes of discovering what I’m missing out on. Like, I know I should be unfolding it more, so I do. But it doesn’t add any real value for me.

Because I rarely want to open the iPhone Duo, I’m left using the outer display all the time. In that mode, the Duo is too heavy for extended use, too wide to comfortably reach, and the UI in most apps is an adjustment.

Are these dealbreakers? No. I could live with the Duo’s outer display if I had to, but it’s definitely an inferior experience to my iPhone 18 Pro.

If I was opening the iPhone Duo more, and actually taking advantage of the key value proposition of foldables—that you can unfold them—I doubt the outer screen would bother me much.

But what I’ve found, at least so far, is that one-handed iPhone use is very important to me, which rules out using the inner display. I use my iPhone mostly for quick interactions, and often with a child in one hand (I have three very young kids). In situations when I do have two hands free to open the Duo, I’m probably sitting in front of my iPad Pro with a Magic Keyboard attached and would rather use the iPad instead.

So again: is the problem with the Duo, or with me?

I think foldables and slab phones will obviously coexist as there will be fans of each.

I’m absolutely already converted however and am loving my duo.

Considering the Air was my favourite phone up until this it’s surprised me. I love proper one handed use again on the outside screen and unfolded it’s much nicer than my old mini 7.

I get it’s not for everyone but those that click with it like myself have a superb device!

I think it’s the latter, but I’m not sure “problem” is the right word. I just don’t find myself using it the way it’s meant to be used. And that’s fine.

I want to love the iPhone Duo, because I see how much fun other people are having with it. And maybe given more time, something will click and I’ll start to use it “as intended.”

If iPhone Duo is the future of the iPhone, I’ll adapt and move on with my life. But one week in, I think it’s probably just not for me. And if it’s not for me, maybe there are a lot of people who will continue preferring non-foldable iPhones for many years to come.

What’s your iPhone Duo experience been like? Are you loving it or struggling? Let us know in the comments.
