#3199. The Dynamo-Electric Principle: 160 Years of Powering Industry

How a breakthrough in electromechanical energy conversion helped shape the motors and generators that drive modern industry

Innomotics is a global leader in electric motors and large drive systems, operating from its headquarters in Nuremberg, Germany.

The dynamo-electric principle: one idea, 160 years, millions of motors.

This article is brought to you by Innomotics.

In the annals of industrial history, few innovations have demonstrated such remarkable staying power as the dynamo-electric principle. Discovered by Werner von Siemens in 1866, this groundbreaking principle remains fundamental to modern electrical engineering more than a century and a half later – and continues to shape the technology portfolio of Innomotics, a globally leading provider of electric motors and large drive systems. What began as a breakthrough in electromechanical energy conversion has evolved into a cornerstone of global industry – powering everything from brewery operations in Qingdao to high-voltage drive systems in petrochemical plants.

The year 1866 marked a decisive turning point, not only in the broader arc of industrial transformation but specifically in the realm of electric motion. At a time when Europe was entering a new phase of industrial transformation, Werner von Siemens pioneered the dynamo-electric principle – a breakthrough that enabled electric machines to generate their own magnetic field through self-excitation. This innovation transformed electric machines from laboratory curiosities into practical power sources, enabling the widespread electrification of industry and infrastructure that defined the late 19th century.

This electric motor from Innomotics was installed in the early 1900s at the historic Tsingtao Brewery in China and supported production processes for more than 90 years, operating continuously under industrial conditions.Innomotics

The principle itself is elegantly simple: an iron core generates a stable magnetic field; a rotating coil is placed within this field; movement in the magnetic field induces an electric current; part of this current strengthens the magnetic field; and electrical energy is continuously converted into motion. This self-reinforcing cycle made efficient and reliable electric motion possible – and it remains the foundation of modern motors today.

More than 160 years later, the same fundamental idea continues to power industrial applications around the world. Millions of motors operate reliably under demanding conditions, keeping production running across generations. The dynamo-electric principle made it possible for electric machines to convert electrical energy into motion (and motion back into electrical energy), creating the technological foundation for modern electric motors and drive systems.

Active Vibration Control System (AVCS) enhances stability and reliability by actively reducing vibrations.Innomotics

Perhaps no example illustrates this longevity better than the electric motor from Innomotics at the historic Tsingtao Brewery in China. Installed in the early 1900s during the early electrification of industrial brewing, this motor supported production processes for more than 90 years, operating continuously under industrial conditions. It became a powerful example of long-term reliability in real-world applications – a testament to how engineering ensures reliable motion across decades.

Continuity, however, does not mean stagnation. Sixteen decades after the original breakthrough, innovations continue to emerge that build upon this proven foundation. Two recent developments – the Active Vibration Control System (AVCS) and oil-lubricated rolling bearings (OLRB) – carry this spirit of innovation and ingenuity forward, a commitment that has been recognized with the German Innovation Award.

Innomotics’ patented Oil-Lubricated Rolling Bearing (OLRB) technology enhances reliability and reduces maintenance requirements.Innomotics

AVCS helps optimize high-voltage motor performance by actively decoupling motors from their foundations to reduce vibration issues. OLRB helps prevent rolling bearing failures from the start with continuous lubrication, supporting higher availability, less downtime, and long-term cost savings. These innovations demonstrate how the basic principle of 1866 can be enhanced through modern engineering to meet contemporary demands for reliability and efficiency.

For three decades, with over 25,000 units driving performance globally, Innomotics’ Perfect Harmony GH180 medium-voltage drive platform has supported reliable operation across industries. Its modular architecture enables efficient power control, high availability, and long-term performance. With thousands of installations worldwide, Perfect Harmony GH180 continues to build on a proven technological foundation, minimizing downtime and ensuring stable production.

Keeping critical motors running requires the right expertise and innovation spirit throughout the entire lifecycle. With Innomotics Customer Services, operators and plant managers gain the insights they need to maintain reliability and optimize maintenance strategies. Winding Lifetime Analysis (WLA) combines operating history, machine measurements, and physics-based modeling to assess the condition of the winding insulation and estimate its remaining useful lifetime. This enables informed maintenance decisions, reduces uncertainty, and helps minimize the risk of unplanned downtime.

The Perfect Harmony GH180 delivers efficient, reliable and flexible medium-voltage drive performance.Innomotics

What began as a breakthrough in 1866 still brings its value to modern industry. The dynamo-electric principle made efficient and reliable electric motion possible – and it remains the foundation of modern motors today.

As industries worldwide grapple with challenges ranging from energy efficiency to operational resilience, this 160-year-old principle continues to prove its relevance.

For plant managers and engineers seeking long-term performance in demanding applications, the message is clear: the foundation laid in the 19th century remains as solid as ever. What has changed are the tools and services built upon it – from vibration control systems to predictive analytics – all designed to extract maximum value from a principle that has, quite literally, powered the modern world for a century and a half.

Innomotics, carrying forward a legacy that spans the full arc of this history, continues to move industry forward with innovations that create real progress. The dynamo-electric principle may be 160 years old, but as the company’s portfolio demonstrates, it is far from obsolete. It is, in every sense of the word, still running.

Discover how Innomotics is driving the future of industry: https://www.innomotics.com/hub/en/company/about-innomotics/dynamo-electric-principle

Innomotics is a global leader in electric motors and large drive systems, operating from its headquarters in Nuremberg, Germany.

#3196. Google’s Gemini 4 Hydrogen brings a fast, cheaper model to everyone

The model scores close to Google's flagship Argon, runs faster and costs less than half as much.

Google’s Gemini 4 Hydrogen costs $1.50 per million input tokens and is free in the Gemini app and Search.

Google has launched Gemini 4 Hydrogen, a fast, lower-cost model for coding and AI agents. It is available to everyone in the Gemini app and Search, and to developers at $1.50 per million input tokens. Google says it nearly matches its flagship Argon.

Google has launched Gemini 4 Hydrogen, a faster and cheaper model built for coding and AI agents, the company announced on Thursday. Unlike its more powerful Gemini 4 models, Hydrogen is open to everyone, including free users of the Gemini app and Google Search.

For developers, it costs $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output tokens. That is less than half the standard price of Google’s flagship Gemini 4 Argon. Hydrogen can handle up to 1 million tokens of input at once.

Google says Hydrogen finishes tasks 2.5 times faster than the older Gemini 3.8 Flash. On a ranking by independent tester Artificial Analysis, it scores one point higher than Argon at its default setting. Vals AI calls it the cheapest and fastest model in its top six.

Hydrogen is meant to do the everyday work while bigger models plan. Google also launched Orchestrator in its Antigravity coding tool, which switches between Hydrogen and its top model, Gemini 4 Carbon. Google says this gets close to Carbon’s results while using 24% less quota.

Google also says Hydrogen makes up facts five times less often than 3.8 Flash. In Search, it is meant to handle messy, multi-part questions and link to a wider range of websites.

Hydrogen still trails some rivals. Artificial Analysis puts its top setting one point behind Anthropic’s Claude Sonnet 5.5, and OpenAI recently cut GPT-6 prices with cheaper models of its own.

#3195. Forgent (FPS) Q1 2027 Earnings Call Transcript

Management says regulatory noise isn't dampening data center demand for its gear.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Forgent Power Solutions, Inc. (FPS -9.85%) reported record quarterly revenue of $479 million and raised its full-year 2027 financial outlook following a successful production ramp across new facilities. Management reported that high demand for electrical distribution infrastructure in data center and industrial markets persists despite evolving regulatory and permitting environments. The company indicated it is transitioning from platform establishment to performance optimization, with a focus on capturing operating leverage and improving manufacturing efficiency. Management stated that significant progress has been made in its direct sales strategy with hyperscalers and artificial intelligence labs, which is expected to support further growth in fiscal 2028.

Operator: Greetings, and welcome to the Forgent Power Solutions First Quarter 2027 Earnings Conference Call. [Operator Instructions] As a reminder, this conference is being recorded. It is now my pleasure to introduce Kate Africk, Vice President of Investor Relations. Thank you. You may begin.

Kate Africk: Thank you, operator, and thank you, everyone, for joining us today for Forgent Power Solutions Fiscal First Quarter 2027 Earnings Call. With me today are Gary Niederpruem, our Chief Executive Officer; and Amy Ard, our Chief Financial Officer. On this call, management will be making forward-looking statements based on current expectations and assumptions, which are subject to risks and uncertainties. Actual results could differ materially from our forward-looking statements if any of our key assumptions are incorrect because of various factors, including those in today's earnings release and during this conference call and in our latest filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission, each of which can be found on our website.

Today's presentation also includes references to non-GAAP financial measures, including adjusted EBITDA, adjusted EBITDA margin and adjusted earnings per share. You should refer to the information contained in the company's earnings release and presentation for definitional information and reconciliations of historical non-GAAP measures to the comparable GAAP financial measures. With that, let me turn the call over to Gary.

Gary Niederpruem: Thank you, Kate, and good morning, everyone. I'll begin with a summary of our first quarter results and a business update. I'll then turn the call over to our new Chief Financial Officer, Amy Ard, who will discuss the key initiatives our finance team is focused on, followed by a detailed overview of our results for the quarter and our updated outlook. But first, I want to address what I know is top of mind for many investors, whether the post-election policy environment could slow data center development and in turn, demand for the electrical equipment we provide. As CEO, one of the most important responsibilities I have is to anticipate and plan for a range of market scenarios.

That is something our senior leadership team does continuously. Following the election, we spoke directly with many of our customers, assessed the potential impact of a more restricted, regulatory and permitting environment and stress tested what that could mean for our business. We came away from that work with continued confidence in the outlook for our data center business, and there are 5 reasons for that. First, we do not see regulation changing the underlying demand for data center capacity. What we are hearing from our customers is that new regulation may affect where, when and how data centers get built, but they are not planning to build less capacity.

The underlying need for compute continues to grow, and our customers remain committed to developing the infrastructure required to support it. In fact, in recent weeks, we've actually seen a request for a few projects to be pulled in rather than pushed out. So point number one, regulation may change where, when and how capacity gets built, but based on our customer conversation, it has not changed how much capacity they ultimately expect to need. Second, the demand/supply imbalance for electrical equipment provides a significant buffer against potential demand reduction. Demand for medium voltage switchgear, transformers and other critical electrical equipment materially exceeds available industry capacity today.

That means demand does not need to remain at today's level for our order book to remain full. Now let's put that into context. Most industry forecasts have called for more than 100 gigawatts of incremental U.S. data center capacity from 2027 through 2031. Let's stress test that a bit. Let's just assume 20% of those projects don't get delayed or relocated, but disappear entirely because of regulatory constraints. That would still leave roughly 80 gigawatts of new capacity over 5 years in the U.S. That is more than 6x the amount of data center capacity expected to be added this year before considering retrofits expansion or replacement demand.

So point number two, even under a scenario with significant demand reduction, we believe there would still be more demand for our products than the industry has the capacity to supply. Third, the commitments already being made upstream give us additional confidence that this capacity ultimately gets built. The products we manufacture are among the later pieces of equipment ordered in the development of a data center. Long lead time equipment further upstream, particularly power generation is committed to much earlier. Turbines, fuel cell and other generation suppliers have multiyear backlogs and in many cases, have already put significant capital behind those orders. That's an important leading indicator for us.

Unless many developers are prepared to walk away from their commitments and deposits, we believe there is a high probability that generation capacity gets deployed. And when it does, it ultimately needs transformers, switchgear and power distribution equipment to connect that power to the data center itself. So point number three, we can see investment occurring several years upstream of us, and those commitments give us confidence in the downstream demand that should ultimately flow to our products. Fourth, we believe our customers are well equipped to navigate a more complex regulatory environment. These are some of the largest and most sophisticated companies in the world.

They have the financial resources, internal capabilities and experience to work through difficult permitting requirements. And where one jurisdiction becomes more challenging, they have the ability to evaluate alternative locations that can accommodate their requirements. So point number four, more regulation can make development more complicated, but we believe our customers have both the capability and the resources to adapt to it. Fifth and most importantly, for our near-term outlook, we already have substantial visibility through fiscal '27 and into fiscal '28. Our backlog extends through that period and a good portion of it is supported by nonrefundable deposits. Just as importantly, our position relatively late in the data center development cycle provides additional protection.

We generally do not receive a purchase order until the permitting process is complete. And in many cases, we do not receive that PO until the project is already under construction. In other words, the projects sitting in our backlog are generally not conceptual projects at the beginning of a development process. They are substantially further along, supported by customer commitments and in many cases, already under construction. So point number five, regardless of what ultimately happens with regulation, the quality, maturity and contractual support behind our existing backlog gives us a high degree of confidence in our outlook through fiscal '27 and into fiscal '28. Now let me bring those 5 points together.

We believe our customers continue to expect significant capacity growth. The electrical equipment market remains substantially supply constrained. We can see capital being committed upstream of us years in advance. We believe our customers have the resources to navigate a more challenging regulatory environment and our own backlog gives us substantial visibility. We will obviously continue to monitor the regulatory environment closely, and we recognize that policy could affect the timing and location of individual projects. But based on what we are seeing today, we believe the recent reaction to potential regulatory changes understates both the magnitude of the underlying demand and the degree of supply constraint in the markets we serve.

Now turning to our results for the quarter on Slide 5. We started fiscal '27 with strong first quarter results. Revenue increased 69% to $479 million, marking the highest quarterly revenue in our company's history. Adjusted EBITDA increased 61% to $105 million, representing our second highest quarterly adjusted EBITDA, just below the record achieved last quarter. And our adjusted EPS increased 83% to $0.24. Turning to Slide 6. There are 5 key takeaways from the quarter. First, we exceeded the high end of our first quarter guidance, reflecting disciplined execution of our production ramp. Our teams continue to scale production across our new facilities, increasing throughput and utilization while maintaining focus on quality, efficiency and cost control.

This progress directly supported revenue and earnings above our guidance ranges and demonstrates the organization's ability to execute. Second, orders grew substantially year-over-year. Data center was strongest, followed by industrial and other, partially offset by moderation in grid, which underscores the value of maintaining diversified exposure across 3 end markets. Third, our direct sales strategy with hyperscalers and AI labs is beginning to deliver tangible results. As we discussed last quarter, we already have exposure to these customers through intermediaries, but our goal is to deepen those relationships and capture a greater share of their demand by working directly with them as well.

In fiscal '27 to date, we secured a volume order from one AI lab and an initial order from a second. We also believe we are on track to receive direct orders from at least one and potentially another hyperscaler by the end of this fiscal year, providing another meaningful avenue for growth. Fourth, our plan to expand adjusted EBITDA margin sequentially through fiscal '27 is progressing as expected. We execute against the plan, we continue to identify opportunities to drive long-term margin expansion. We are laying the foundation now to capture those benefits in the coming years. Finally, we are raising our fiscal '27 guidance.

This increase reflects the successful execution of our production ramp in the first quarter, which we expect to continue supporting performance in subsequent quarters as well as the strength of our backlog, which now fully covers our updated outlook. Turning to Slide 7. I want to spend a few minutes on what we're seeing across our 3 primary end markets: data center, industrial and grid. Starting with data center, demand remains very strong. Data center was the largest contributor to our year-over-year order growth in the first quarter and the signals we are seeing from customers remain positive.

As I discussed earlier, policy may affect where and how certain data centers get built, but we don't believe it changes the underlying demand for capacity. And importantly, our backlog is well protected because customers generally don't place orders with us until critical milestones such as financing, tenants, power and permitting are already in place. Turning to industrial. We're seeing demand both accelerate and broaden. Over the last 2 years, growth was heavily influenced by large mega projects. Those projects remain an important driver, but we are increasingly seeing demand from smaller projects, facility expansions and follow-on investments across many verticals.

We saw that broadening in our own results this quarter with strong industrial orders and a meaningful increase in the number of customers placing orders with us. Finally, in grid, underlying utility demand remains steady, while renewables and battery storage have seen some near-term softness, primarily driven by policy and project timing. There are 2 factors at work here. First, some wind and solar developers pulled orders forward to safe harbor projects ahead of the July deadline, creating a tougher comparison this quarter. Second, new restrictions on foreign produced grid equipment have caused some developers, particularly in battery storage, to pause projects while they wait for greater clarity.

That moderated our grid orders in the first quarter, but we view it primarily as a timing issue rather than a demand issue. As that uncertainty clears, we expect activity to improve. And longer term, policies designed to strengthen domestic grid security and encouraging U.S. manufacturing should be supportive for a domestic manufacturer like Forgent. So stepping back, we feel very good about the health of our end markets. Data center remains very strong. Industrial is accelerating and becoming more diversified. And in grid, we see upside as near-term policy uncertainty clears. Turning to Slide 8.

Last quarter, I talked about how Forgent is moving upmarket in data centers from primarily selling point products through intermediaries to engineering direct solutions for some of the most technically demanding customers in the market, including hyperscalers and Frontier AI labs. At that time, we had received our first direct order from a Frontier AI lab and had signed our first master service agreement with a hyperscaler. Since then, we have continued to make meaningful progress across both customer groups, and this slide lays out where those relationships stand today. The important point is that direct selling into these customers is not transactional.

It requires a rigorous qualification process that can include technical engagement, competitive bidding, factory audits, master service agreements and specific product agreements, and that's even before an initial purchase order is issued. We think about that progression in 3 stages: crawl, walk, run. Crawl is the initial order, typically smaller in size, but strategically important because it validates the customers' confidence in our engineering, quality and execution. Walk is when strong performance on those initial orders leads to larger volume opportunities. Run is when those relationships evolve into a program level orders or longer-term supply agreements. We are now seeing that progression taking shape. Our first Frontier AI lab customer is a great example.

We executed well on the initial order, and that has already led to a volume order. A second AI lab has now placed its first direct order with Forgent, expanding our direct engagement within that customer category. On the hyperscaler side, 2 customers have moved beyond the MSA stage and signed specific product agreements, which is typically the final commercial step before an initial order. A third hyperscaler has also entered the qualification process, which further expands the pipeline of potential direct end-user relationships. These are customers that purchase electrical infrastructure at very large scale.

Our initial orders are only the starting point, but they are important because they establish Forgent as a qualified direct supplier and create the opportunity to expand over time as we execute. Looking ahead, we expect orders from AI labs on a direct basis in the first half of fiscal '27 and from hyperscalers on a direct basis in the second half. Over time, as these relationships progress from crawl to walk, to run, we believe they can become a meaningful driver of growth in fiscal '28 and beyond. Moving to Slide 9. Over roughly the last 30 months, we have built the platform Forgent needs to compete and win at scale.

That includes a broader product portfolio, a differentiated offer built around customization at scale and short lead times, vertically integrated manufacturing capacity, deep engineering capabilities and experienced commercial leadership. Just as important, we have built customer credibility through consistent execution and proven delivery. That last point is critical. The capabilities we have built matter because we have been able to execute against them. By delivering for customers, we have earned trust and that trust is what's opening the door to larger, more strategic opportunities with some of the most sophisticated buyers in the market.

As a result, we are now a full year ahead of our IPO plan on revenue, but we also recognize that there is still significant value to unlock. The next phase for Forgent is about shifting from platform creation to performance optimization. In practical terms, that means improving execution consistency, standardizing processes, sourcing smarter, optimizing capacity across our manufacturing footprint and reducing cycle times while continuing to improve quality and delivery. It also means taking what is working in one part of the business and replicating those best practices across our sites and functions. The goal is straightforward: convert the scale we have built into greater operating leverage.

This work is being driven by an increasingly experienced operational and finance leadership team. Juan Macias joined us in August as President of Solutions & Service, bringing more than 30 years of leadership experience at Schneider Electric, GE and other industrial businesses. Jamie Brown joined us in September as President of Transformers with 25 years of manufacturing and operations leadership at Legrand and CommScope. Together, they bring deep experience scaling industrial operations, improving execution and institutionalizing the operating discipline required to drive margin expansion. This is also a natural point to turn the call over to Amy Ard, our new Chief Financial Officer.

Amy has been instrumental in building the financial infrastructure to support the platform we have created and she is now helping leverage that infrastructure to optimize performance as we scale. She and her team are playing an important role in improving visibility, strengthening cost discipline and converting our growth into greater operating leverage. With that, I'm pleased to turn the call over to Amy. Amy?

Amy Ard: Thank you, Gary, and good morning, everyone. As I get to know many of you in the months ahead, you'll find my approach is straightforward: run the business with discipline, communicate with clarity and build credibility through execution. I'll briefly cover my background and priorities as CFO. I've spent more than 25 years in finance and accounting leadership, primarily in manufacturing and industrial businesses. I've served as CFO of several growth companies and have helped scale organizations through periods of rapid expansion. Across those experiences, one lesson has been consistent, financial discipline and operational execution must be tightly connected. That is the operating mindset I bring to Forgent. I also know this business well.

I joined as CFO of PwrQ, one of the companies that became part of Forgent and then served as Executive Vice President of Finance for the combined company. In that role, my focus was building the finance platform required to support a larger, faster-growing public company. That work included strengthening our reporting, controls and governance, establishing the foundation for forecasting and investor communications, scaling our systems and building plant level margin analytics across the business. Those analytics are now an important part of how we manage pricing, sourcing, labor and operational performance. As CFO, my priorities are clear: first, ensure a seamless transition and continue building trust with the market through consistent execution and clear communication.

Second, help lead the shift from platform creation to performance optimization. For finance, that means applying the infrastructure that we have built to improve decision-making, drive margin expansion and strengthen working capital and cash conversion. Turning to Slide 12. Every leader has an area where they feel most at home. For me, it's operational finance and driving continuous improvement, and that's what this slide is about. Over the past several months, I've worked with our operations team to develop a detailed set of priorities across the 6 areas you see on the left side of the slide. overhead and SG&A, working capital, labor productivity, material costs, manufacturing efficiency and logistics.

For each area, we've identified specific actions to improve financial performance. That means putting the right people in place, improving processes and systems, establishing clear accountability and then measuring the results. That's the operating discipline we're building across Forgent. The priorities toward the top of the slide are generally the ones we can address more quickly, while the opportunities further down require more time and operational work across our manufacturing footprint. Our first near-term priority is SG&A efficiency. The objective is straightforward: scale engineering, sales and our corporate functions more slowly than revenue. That operating leverage is an important driver of the year-over-year adjusted EBITDA margin expansion embedded in our fiscal 2027 guidance.

And you can see an early example on the right. We've identified functions in supply chain, project management and finance where it made more sense to build the capability internally. By bringing those roles in-house, we've reduced our reliance on outside professional services and generated more than $5 million of annualized savings while building an organization that can scale more effectively. Our second near-term priority is working capital efficiency. We took a systematic look across our supplier base and renegotiated payment terms with vendors representing more than 80% of our material spend. That has already generated more than $30 million of working capital improvement.

Then as you move further down the slide, you get into some of the larger operational opportunities, labor productivity, material costs, manufacturing efficiency and logistics. These take longer because the improvements have to be embedded into how we operate across multiple facilities. But the opportunity is significant, and we're already making progress. Labor is a good example. We've identified areas where we were relying on higher cost contract labor and replaced those positions with full-time employees. That has generated approximately $5 million of additional annualized savings while giving us a more consistent workforce to support the business as we grow. So when I look at this slide, the important takeaway is that we're still early.

We already have tangible results across all 3 of the early wins highlighted here, more than $5 million from professional services, more than $30 million of working capital improvement from supplier terms and approximately $5 million from reducing contract labor. The initiatives towards the top of the slide are contributing to the margin improvement we expect in fiscal '27. But some of the bigger opportunities in labor productivity, materials, manufacturing and logistics are still ahead of us. And we believe those opportunities provide runway for margin and cash flow improvement beyond fiscal 2027.

This is the kind of work I know well, and it's work I really enjoy, building the right organization, putting better processes and systems in place, establishing accountability and then translating those changes into measurable improvements in margins and cash flow. With that, let me walk through our first quarter results, starting on Slide 14. First quarter revenues were $479 million, an increase of 69% year-over-year and all organic. Revenues exceeded the high end of our guidance range and were approximately $24 million above the midpoint. The upside was driven by higher throughput and strong execution on our production ramp. Growth continued to reflect robust demand and our scaling capacity. Revenues increased across each of our offerings.

Custom products grew 73% to $354 million. Powertrain Solutions grew 62% to $106 million. Standard products grew 18% to $11 million and Services more than doubled to $8 million. The mix of revenue by offering in the quarter was as expected, reflecting delivery dates requested by our customers. Looking ahead, we expect growth to accelerate in the second quarter, particularly in Powertrain Solutions. Moving to adjusted EBITDA and adjusted EPS on Slide 15. Adjusted EBITDA was $105 million, up 61% year-over-year. Gross profit increased 62% on volume growth. SG&A increased in absolute dollars, reflecting continued investment across sales, operations and engineering to support our growth.

Adjusted EBITDA also exceeded the high end of our guidance, driven by higher throughput and better cost absorption. Adjusted EBITDA margin of 21.9% was ahead of our expectations. As we indicated in September, we expect the first quarter to be our lowest margin quarter of the year. It reflects onetime costs to support our second quarter production ramp, primarily under absorbed labor, which we did not add back. Adjusted EPS was $0.24, an increase of 83% year-over-year, outpacing adjusted EBITDA growth on operating leverage and lower net interest expense. With that context on the first quarter, let's turn to our outlook. Our guidance philosophy remains unchanged.

I've been part of shaping it since before our IPO, and you can expect the same approach going forward. On Slide 17, I'll start with our full year fiscal 2027 guidance, which we are raising. We now expect revenues of $2.45 billion to $2.65 billion, $50 million higher than our prior guidance and representing 80% growth at the midpoint. We expect adjusted EBITDA of $587 million to $637 million, $12 million higher than our prior guidance, representing 90% growth and implying an adjusted EBITDA margin of 24%. And we expect adjusted EPS of $1.30 to $1.44, $0.04 higher than our prior guidance and representing 101% growth at the midpoint. A few points on how to think about our updated guidance.

First, the increase is driven by our strong production ramp execution to date, which gives us incremental confidence in the year ahead. Second, as production continues to ramp, we are unlocking additional book and ship capacity, which allows us to take more orders for delivery in the current fiscal year. Third, with the incremental orders we've received, our backlog now fully covers our updated guidance. Given that, I want to offer a few reminders about the quality of our backlog. It consists of firm purchase orders often secured with deposits and milestone payments that help protect against cancellations. Because of those provisions and other contractual protections, we have historically experienced minimal cancellations.

Finally, we continue to expect revenue and adjusted EBITDA to increase sequentially throughout the year with margins expanding as production ramps. Turning to Slide 18 and our outlook for the second quarter. The production ramp is gaining momentum, supported by the investments we made in the first quarter. For the second quarter of fiscal 2027, we expect revenues of $560 million to $590 million, representing 94% growth year-over-year and approximately 20% growth versus the first quarter at the midpoint. We expect adjusted EBITDA of $127 million to $137 million, representing 119% growth year-over-year and approximately 26% growth versus the first quarter at the midpoint.

That implies an adjusted EBITDA margin of approximately 23%, up roughly 260 basis points year-over-year and roughly 110 basis points sequentially as operating leverage builds with higher volumes. With that, I'll turn it back to Gary for closing remarks.

Gary Niederpruem: Thanks, Amy. Turning to Slide 19. Before we open the call for questions, I want to leave you with our key takeaways for the quarter. First, we delivered. We exceeded the high end of our first quarter guidance, executed well against our production ramp and are raising our fiscal '27 outlook. We now expect revenue growth of 80% and adjusted EBITDA growth of 90% for the year. Second, order momentum remains strong. Demand was led by data center and industrial, and our customer base continues to diversify. Our strategy of serving 3 distinct end markets is providing multiple avenues for growth. Third, we are gaining traction with some of the most demanding customers in the market.

The initial orders we're receiving from Frontier AI Labs and hyperscalers are important milestones, but they represent only the beginning of what we believe the relationships can become. Fourth, our fiscal '27 adjusted EBITDA margin plan remains on track with stronger operating discipline, better financial infrastructure and seasoned leaders in place, we see runway for further margin expansion in the years ahead. And fifth, our outlook is well supported. Our backlog fully covers our updated guidance. And as our production continues to progress, we are also creating additional book and ship capacity. Overall, this was a very strong start to the year commercially, operationally and financially.

I want to thank Team Forgent for their continued execution and focus as it is truly this team working every day to make Forgent better for our customers, better for our coworkers and better for our investors. With that, we're happy to take your questions. Operator?

Gary Niederpruem: Yes. Julian, Gary here. Yes, I think there's a couple of things to note. Nigel Coe: And again, I appreciate all the detail here, Gary. And are you aware of any kind of projects in the funnel that are maybe just getting put on pause because of kind of uncertainties around the go-forward regulatory environment and where data center capacity needs to be constructed going forward given the changes with the election?

Gary Niederpruem: Yes, for sure. Nigel, a couple of different dimensions to that one here. So you're right. Just like we talked about in our prepared remarks, we've canvassed almost all of our large customers over the last 4 or 5 days and the definitive answer comes back and continues to say no change. And so I think that's consistent with what other people are talking about, and we went right to the ground with good old-fashioned voice of the customer, and that's what came back. That's number one.

Number two, I think it is also important to remind everybody that the fundamentals of the market is the demand side of this, and there is clearly no abating on the demand side of it. That's number two. Number three, in terms of our engagement, 2-part answer here. So we'll get engaged early in the process. So when people are thinking about building a data center in a certain location, we'll get engaged with design engineering upfront and early -- very early in that process. But that's when it sort of sits in our pipeline. And those things always ebb and flow will move around. So that's very natural.

That isn't any different today than it would have been a year ago. But I think more importantly is when we get that purchase order then. Amy Ard: Andrew, I'll take that one. I'd say, first and foremost, no, we haven't had any significant changes in our policies around down payments. So there's no difference that you're seeing from a contractual perspective. It is a timing-related change in the deferred revenue balance. And so the way to think about it, our accounting policies have us recording deferred revenue when cash comes in the door. So we had a very strong Q4 in terms of orders. We told you it was $1.5 billion of orders in Q4. The way it works is we book an order, then we invoice the deposit and then the cash comes in, and that timing is not the same week, right?

So there's some delay between when the invoice gets issued and then when we get payment from that. So some of what you're seeing in the Q1 deferred revenue balance is cash receipts from some of the order book that happened in Q4. #3194. Jensen Huang resigns as CEO of Nvidia

Jensen Huang has resigned as the CEO of Nvidia following recent reports of extramarital affairs, including one involving a woman suspected of spying for China. Here are the details.

In late October, The New York Times reported on Jensen Huang’s “close relationship” with Alice Huang, a former managing director at Singapore-based Megaspeed, whom US intelligence officials reportedly identified as a Chinese intelligence asset suspected of passing information to Beijing.

According to subsequent reports, Chinese intelligence allegedly recruited her to gather information about Jensen Huang and influence his position on selling advanced AI chips to Chinese companies. China disputes the espionage allegations, dismissing them as groundless speculation intended to smear the country.

That said, while Nvidia previously denied any impropriety in their relationship, Huang admitted last weekend to having an extramarital affair in a message to employees, saying, “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did.” He did not mention Alice Huang directly.

In the following days, concerns grew over the potential national security implications of the relationship, in addition to Nvidia seeing its stock plummet.

And while Huang remained CEO as Nvidia’s board commissioned an independent investigation into the allegations, The New York Times reported on Wednesday that he had a second extramarital affair, this time with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of healthcare, who reports directly to him.

In the hours that followed, The Wall Street Journal reported that Nvidia’s board was preparing to meet to decide Huang’s future. Soon after, Semafor reported that some board members favored Nvidia CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO, while other reports suggested that Huang’s daughter, Madison Huang, could eventually succeed him. Madison Huang works at Nvidia as senior director of product marketing.

Semafor also named Apple’s chief hardware officer, Johny Srouji, as a potential successor, while Bloomberg reported that Nvidia had hired an outside firm to identify candidates.

Now, Nvidia has officially announced that Huang “has resigned as President, Chief Executive Officer, and a member of the Board, effective immediately.”

The company confirmed that Kress has been appointed interim CEO, while retaining her current responsibilities, until a permanent successor is named. The company is considering both internal and external candidates.

Nvidia also announced that Harvey C. Jones, a longtime technology executive and venture investor, has been appointed the company’s first-ever board chair.

In a statement, Jones said the board has “full confidence in Colette and the leadership team,” adding that Nvidia expects its operations, customer commitments, and product roadmap to continue without interruption.

The shareholder lawsuits over the broad-spectrum mismanagement are going to be incredible.

No succession plan. Lying to investors to cover up the CEO’s unethical and foolish behavior. Having a super-weak board of directors absent anyone with high-level relevant experience.

Nvidia did not directly address the allegations surrounding Huang in its announcement, instead thanking him for his contributions to the company over the past 33 years.

Following the Times’ Wednesday report, Nvidia shares plunged in after-hours trading, erasing the day’s 2.9% gain after two consecutive sessions of losses.

The stock continued to fall following today’s announcement, dropping more than 10% at the time of writing from Wednesday’s closing price of $173.73, bringing its total decline to approximately 35% from its October 6 record close.

How Nvidia’s stock will behave when the market opens today and in the days that follow is anyone’s guess, especially with the company scheduled to report its quarterly earnings next Tuesday, November 17.

#3192. Mount Thor raises $45 million to build Mac data centers for AI agents

Apple @ Work is exclusively brought to you by Mosyle, the only Apple Unified Platform. Mosyle is the only solution that integrates in a single professional-grade platform all the solutions necessary to seamlessly and automatically deploy, manage & protect Apple devices at work. Over 45,000 organizations trust Mosyle to make millions of Apple devices work-ready with no effort and at an affordable cost. Request your EXTENDED TRIAL today and understand why Mosyle is everything you need to work with Apple.

Mount Thor, a Bay Area startup building cloud infrastructure on Apple silicon, announced today that it has raised $45 million across Seed and Series A rounds. The pitch to its investors was simple: AI agents are incredible on Apple silicon, and nobody is renting them at data-center scale.

About Apple @ Work: Bradley Chambers managed an enterprise IT network from 2009 to 2021. Through his experience deploying and managing firewalls, switches, a mobile device management system, enterprise grade Wi-Fi, 1000s of Macs, and 1000s of iPads, Bradley will highlight ways in which Apple IT managers deploy Apple devices, build networks to support them, train users, stories from the trenches of IT management, and ways Apple could improve its products for IT departments.

CRV and Conviction co-led the Series A. Chad Byers and Offline Ventures co-led the Seed. CSC Leasing, Enea Capital, Long Journey Ventures, and Upper90 participated, along with angel investors from OpenAI, Meta, Cognition, Together AI, and Vercel. The company also raised separate non-dilutive financing for new hardware as well.

Mount Thor runs macOS on Apple silicon as elastic compute instances, just as a cloud provider rents Linux VMs. Customers get on-demand fleets of Macs for work that only happens on macOS: training computer-use models in reinforcement learning environments, running secure macOS sandboxes for agents, long-running instances that let an agent work across a user’s devices under one Apple ID, and build and test farms for Apple software.

There are two ways to use its solution. With managed compute, customers pick a machine class and image, and get either a full bare-metal Mac or an isolated macOS VM with administrator access, provisioned through a web portal, a command-line tool, Kubernetes, or the API, and billed per Mac on a 24-hour basis. With customer-managed compute, an organization runs its own Macs at a Mount Thor site using its own MDM, while Mount Thor operates the facility and provides inventory by serial number, problem reporting, and event notifications.

The argument is that agents are becoming macOS users, and the demand for Apple’s platform now scales with the number of agents rather than the number of people.

“Making Apple’s operating system and silicon available at datacenter-scale is a massive untapped opportunity in AI infrastructure,” said Peter Voell, Founder and CEO of Mount Thor. “Decades of investment in accessibility and human-computer interaction make macOS the best place for agents to work and for humans to hold them accountable. And with chips like the M5 Ultra, Apple silicon is becoming a high performance, more power- and cost- efficient platform for production inference.”

The other half of its pitch is inference. The M5 Ultra Mac Studio shipped in August with up to 512GB of unified memory, which puts large open-weight models within reach of a single machine at a fraction of the power draw of a traditional GPU-based server. Mount Thor says a focus of the new funding is building what it calls the best inference lab for open-source models on Apple silicon.

“Mount Thor sits at the intersection of two important shifts: the rapidly expanding capabilities of autonomous agents and the increasing demand for compute that can support both local and cloud workloads,” said Brittany Walker, General Partner at CRV. “We’re thrilled to back Peter and the team as they make it easier to use Apple’s platforms at scale for agentic AI.”

The team comes from Cerebras, CoreWeave, Fluidstack, Nebius, OpenAI, and xAI. The company was founded this year and deployed its first data center in under six months.

Macs in the cloud are not new as AWS has rented Mac instances for a few years, and MacStadium has been doing so longer than AWS. Mount Thor’s pitch is that the larger customer is an AI agent that needs a Mac to do its job, and that demand grows with the number of agents rather than the number of developers.

The company says the funding will go toward expanding its compute footprint and building out the team, and that it plans to add capacity quickly to keep up with customer demand.

#3191. How AI security failures are endangering your supply chain – and what you can do

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

New research provides a stark look at the AI supply chain and the risks it brings to businesses.

Artificial intelligence companies worldwide are bringing a new wave of vulnerabilities and security issues to the digital supply chain, researchers warn.

According to a new report published by Black Kite on Tuesday, there now exists a “widespread cybersecurity weakness” across the “rapidly expanding ecosystem of companies developing, deploying, and supporting artificial intelligence.”

AI and smart solutions don’t automatically equate with safe solutions. In a study titled “2026 AI Supply Chain Report: The Risks Behind Your AI Relationships,” Black Kite says that many AI suppliers — the companies that develop and deploy AI services to today’s businesses — are struggling with “basic security practices.”

Also: Rogue AI incidents hit ‘tens of thousands’: Can businesses trust these tools?

According to the research, after examining the companies themselves, along with their software, integrations, and components, researchers found failures to patch critical vulnerabilities, protect credentials, authenticate users and email, and address network security issues.

The study analyzes 18,160 AI companies worldwide, ranging from 0-10 employees to more than 1,000 employees. A company’s AI involvement was determined through reviews of company products and services and primary business activities, covering six broad groups: everyday application development; AI development and implementation; AI applications in specialized sectors such as healthcare, IT, and finance; industrial organizations; and AI foundations working on data, compute, and modeling.

A small percentage of assessed companies are considered “unclassified,” and the study excluded businesses that use AI only incidentally.

In addition, unusual network activity was detected at 44.3% of organizations, and botnet-related activity was recorded at 41.8% of AI companies.

AI’s main business appeal is its ability to integrate with existing software and platforms to handle manual tasks, heavy lifting, and tedious, time-consuming work, freeing employees to focus on work that requires human oversight.

Enterprises are investing billions of dollars in AI. Menlo’s 2026 research estimates that enterprise AI spend reached $37 billion in 2025, with half of overall spend going to AI apps. In total, 76% of enterprise AI solutions are purchased rather than built internally.

However, the moment an AI or automated component is introduced into a corporate ecosystem or operational platform, any security problems it has impact the user — and each additional integration, such as software components or open-source tooling, may also increase the attack surface.

In an accompanying analysis of AI firms’ use of Model Context Protocol (MCP) components, which can link AI apps to business systems, 48.8% of 1,732 logged security findings were rated High or Critical, including code and command injection vulnerabilities.

Also: The new enterprise AI expert every company needs

It’s not just the AI application itself. As noted by Black Kite, AI suppliers often have access to customer data, developer environments, business infrastructure, and enterprise platforms. If the supplier’s credentials are stolen, this could expose its customers to a range of cyberattacks.

The researchers found, for example, that 19.9% of AI companies offering solutions for enterprise AI deployment had corporate login information in infostealer records, and that stolen corporate logins, overall, were linked to 6.8% of AI suppliers in the study.

Visibility matters, too, for businesses that should be monitoring their digital supply chains. However, 33.2% of AI companies assessed have a “limited” digital footprint, including their domains, subdomains, and IP addresses.

The same principles for protecting the digital supply chain apply to AI suppliers, where continual monitoring and assessment are among the best protections businesses have.

Staying informed and aware of the risks to your own business makes all the difference. As recommended by Black Kite, it takes more than a single point-in-time security assessment — frequent monitoring and engaging with suppliers to understand their technologies and dependencies can reveal potential security issues.

Also: Do you need AI agent liability insurance?

If you find weaknesses, manage them by priority, handling ransomware-related exposures and vulnerabilities actively exploited in the wild first.

Also audit an AI tool’s integrations and components, access, what data it can reach, and the potential impact of exploitation. Once you’re armed with this information, it’s possible to weigh risk and reward — and whether the AI tool is worth the potential attack exposure it brings. If you decide to keep it, limit its permissions and access to what it requires.

#3190. Apple TV 4K review: The best streamer comes at a cost

It’s been four years since Apple last updated the Apple TV 4K, but a new version is here. There’s Siri AI support, a faster chip, an improved remote, and more.

Here’s everything that’s changed, what’s better, and whether the new Apple TV 4K justifies its new $299 price.

The Apple TV 4K’s overall design is largely unchanged. It’s still the same familiar black box that sits underneath your television. The only visual change is that the front status light has moved from the right side to the center.

Inside, Apple has upgraded the A15 Bionic to the A19 chip, touting 50% faster CPU performance and twice the GPU performance.

Those are great improvements on paper. In practice, I’m not doing anything on my Apple TV that really stresses the performance. Compared to my third-generation Apple TV 4K, I’ve occasionally noticed slightly smoother animations and faster performance in apps that handle more processing locally, like Infuse.

I think the biggest advantage of the A19 chip is future-proofing. People tend to buy and keep these devices for years. In fact, I’m still using a first-generation Apple TV 4K from 2017 in my bedroom, and it still works just fine nearly a decade later. The A19 gives the new Apple TV plenty of performance headroom for future tvOS updates and more demanding apps, even if those advantages aren’t particularly noticeable today.

The Siri Remote looks the same as before, but it now supports Precision Finding in the Find My app, making it easier to track down when misplaced. You can also play a sound on the remote to help locate it. I lose my Siri Remote all the time, so this honestly might be the change I’ve noticed and appreciated most in my 10 days testing the new Apple TV.

It’s worth noting Apple also sells the new Siri Remote separately for $59, and it’s compatible with every previous Apple TV 4K generation. You do, however, need a newer iPhone model to use Precision Finding.

One of the more interesting new features is support for a four-HomePod surround sound system. You need four HomePod (2nd generation) or HomePod mini 2 speakers, arranged in matching pairs at the front and rear of the room. Apple TV automatically calibrates the speakers based on their positions in the room.

For context, I typically use my Apple TV with a stereo pair of full-size HomePod (2nd generation) speakers. I’ve spent some time testing the new four-speaker surround sound setup by adding a pair of HomePod mini 2 speakers.

My house’s layout isn’t particularly well-suited for a traditional surround sound setup, but to my admittedly untrained ears, this sounds great. I can’t speak to how it compares to a dedicated surround sound system, but I appreciate Apple continuing to expand what’s possible with HomePods and Apple TV.

One of the biggest changes with the new Apple TV 4K is the addition of three far-field microphones. This means you can now interact with Siri without picking up the Siri Remote. In conjunction with this, Siri AI is also coming to Apple TV.

Siri AI brings the same broad world knowledge and personal-context capabilities you’ve experienced on iPhone and HomeView, but adapts them to finding and watching content on your television. Siri AI on Apple TV requires the owner of your Apple Home setup to have an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad.

Personal context requests also require a paired compatible device connected to the same Wi-Fi network as Apple TV.

What was that TV show Lily recommended a few weeks ago?

What are some baseball movies I might like?

What did the vet say after Blake’s vet appointment?

For each example, tvOS responded with a dedicated interface on Apple TV, showing the answer along with poster art, cast information, and more. It also offers built-in contextual suggestions when you ask for recommendations, so you can refine the results further.

You can also ask Siri contextual questions about the show or movie you’re watching. This includes things like “where was this show filmed?” and “when is the next season coming out?”

I’ve found Siri AI’s responses to those contextual questions less accurate. It struggles to accurately identify the show or movie that’s playing, leading to completely inaccurate responses to those types of questions.

It’s worth noting that Siri AI is also coming to the second-generation Apple TV 4K from 2021 and the third-generation model from 2022. The far-field microphones are what’s exclusive to the new hardware. This lets you shout Siri commands into the air without talking directly into the Siri Remote.

In my testing, hands-free Siri works relatively well, and it’s convenient to control Apple TV without reaching for the remote. It does a good job at picking up commands

I can’t go any further in this review without talking about the price. The Apple TV 4K (4th generation) costs $299. That’s a huge increase over previous Apple TV models. Here’s a brief history of Apple TV 4K pricing over the years to set the stage:

After Apple introduced the $129 Apple TV model in October 2022, I started to notice a change. More and more people had Apple TVs when I would visit. Friends and family who had previously bought an Amazon or Roku box, or just used their TV’s built-in software, had purchased an Apple TV.

At $299, I worry that type of adoption is going to come to a screeching halt. And it’s unfortunate because the Apple TV is so much better than anything else out there. tvOS is fast, clean, and relatively free of the clutter and advertisements you find on competing platforms. The Siri Remote is excellent, and the integration with the rest of Apple’s ecosystem is hard to beat.

I could justify the $299 price for the Apple TV 4K (4th generation) if it were just one option available in a broader lineup. If there were lower-priced options for people who don’t need all the bells and whistles. That’s not the case, though. In fact, this is the first Apple TV 4K generation to be sold in just one configuration. There’s no cheaper version with less storage or fewer features.

To Apple’s credit, these are devices that can last for years. The fact that I’m still using an Apple TV 4K from 2017 makes the $299 price a tiny bit easier to swallow, but it doesn’t really change my frustration.

Apple seems serious about its new smart home strategy. There’s the HomeView smart display, a new HomePod mini, and the Apple Home Collection family of smart home accessories launching later this year. One of the best ways to get deeper into people’s homes is by controlling how they watch TV. I can’t help but think pricing the Apple TV 4K out of reach for so many people will hinder those ambitions.

Don’t get me wrong, I love the Apple TV. I have three of them in my house. If one of them broke, I would reluctantly pay $299 for a new one. Whether you fall into that category is for you to decide. All I can say is that the new Apple TV 4K is the best streamer on the market.

#3188. Why Mobility Global Stock Gained Today

CARFAX is an increasingly valuable information source for the auto industry.

Shares of Mobility Global (MBGL +16.11%) jumped 16% on Thursday after the automotive analytics provider delivered stronger-than-expected profits for the third quarter.

Mobility Global's revenue rose 7.4% year-over-year to $478 million.

The company's flagship CARFAX business, which provides comprehensive vehicle history reports to consumers and car dealerships, saw sales rise 8% to $313 million.

Mobility Global continues to extend its reach and strengthen its information-gathering network. "CARFAX receives data from more than 100,000 service shops through relationships we've built over decades, one shop at a time," Bill Eager said during a conference call with analysts.

All told, Mobility Global's earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) grew 2% to $195 million. And its adjusted earnings per share checked in at $0.40, topping Wall Street's estimates of $0.38.

Mobility Global also generated $186 million in free cash flow, up 37% from the year-ago quarter. This robust cash flow production enabled the company to announce an $800 million stock buyback program.

Mobility Global also recently began paying a $0.06 per-share quarterly dividend. Its shares now yield a bit more than 1%.

Mobility Global expects roughly $1.88 billion in full-year revenue in 2026. Management also lifted the low end of its adjusted EBITDA guidance to $750 million, up from a prior forecast of $745 million.

"As more vehicle shopping moves online, the demand for trusted independent information continues to grow," Eager said.

#3187. Ring’s new drone patrols your home to keep an eye on things – even upstairs

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Home & Office > Smart Home > Home Security

Alongside the Ring Drone Cam, Ring introduced the Rover Cam for businesses. It investigates disturbances and streams 4K footage.

Today, Ring announced the launch of a new subbrand, Ring Robotics, with two new products: the $249 Ring Drone Cam, an indoor “mobile security camera” drone that shoots 2K video, and the $999 Ring Rover Cam, a security robot for businesses that patrols autonomously and investigates disturbances.

Also: Amazon’s new Echo Studio gives Alexa+ an AI camera to see inside your home

Both devices use Ring’s custom navigation software, “AI Pilot,” to autonomously navigate interior spaces and move between set points along a patrol, rather than being controlled directly by the user. AI Pilot leverages the devices’ cameras, sensors, and vision models, along with cloud processing, to create interior maps, then move the devices between predesignated patrol points such as a side door or a window.

I recently saw both new robots in person at a showcase in New York hosted by Ring’s founder and chief inventor, Jamie Siminoff. They certainly do what they advertise but come with some significant limitations. The drone, for example, can only stay in the air for about 8 minutes before it needs to dock and recharge, while the Ring Rover Cam is slow and deliberate, seemingly ideal for routine surveillance rather than rapid response to an event.

The Ring Drone Cam moves around predetermined patrol points in your home, sending you a live 2K video feed whether you’re just in another room or out of town. The user doesn’t actually fly the drone; instead, it moves around autonomously using Ring’s custom “AI Pilot” navigation technology, leveraging its cameras, sensors, and cloud processing to create a map of its surroundings. This allows it to fly through the air at an appropriate height, going from room to room, even up stairs.

In the Ring app, the user creates patrol points they want the drone to move between — likely a window, doorway, or high-traffic room — creating a set path that is both predictable (so you always know where the drone will go) and relevant, so it’s only monitoring the areas you want it to. But here is where its limitations come into play: It needs a finite path to navigate because its flight time is limited to just five to eight minutes in the air before it has to return to its charging dock.

That makes the dock both the start and end point for the drone’s routine trips, and it’s designed with this in mind. When it goes to land, the drone hovers over the dock and lowers itself down, dropping into place so it can start charging automatically. I asked about its potential to land elsewhere, and Ring told me it would only make an emergency landing outside of its dock in case it didn’t have enough power to get home.

Also: Amazon’s new Echo Dot can turn into a Wi-Fi extender – how it works

There’s one other very important caveat: This thing is loud. There’s no sneaking up on anyone with the Ring Drone Cam, as the entire household is likely to hear it the second it undocks. The four propellers emit a constant, high-pitched whirring while in the air that’s loud enough to announce its presence to anyone in the vicinity: intruder or resident.

During the product briefing, Siminoff insinuated that this was part of its design to dissuade home intruders snooping around your house at night (especially when paired with the drone’s front-facing spotlight), but it’s likely just the result of its engineering, especially considering this is a first-gen product. It’s so loud that it makes me think it’s better suited to navigating the home when no one’s home (although whether or not your pets go bonkers trying to catch it is a whole other issue).

The Ring Drone is designed to work out of the box with the existing Ring ecosystem, including the 2K Video Doorbell and Indoor Cam, and is also compatible with Amazon’s Map View.

The Ring Drone Cam will start shipping on Jan. 27, 2027, and will cost $249.

The other product Ring announced is the Rover Cam, a mobile robot with a 4K camera designed to monitor large spaces like warehouses, offices, or businesses. Ring calls it a “security guard that never clocks out,” but it’s more like a slow-moving droid that goes on set patrol paths. It leverages the same AI Pilot technology as the Ring Drone to map its surroundings and navigate around shelving, furniture, and obstacles in real time.

It’s much quieter than its airborne sibling, traveling at low speeds and offering mobile surveillance instead of wiring every square inch of a large space. If the technology here looks familiar, it’s because it resembles the Amazon Astra, a smaller robot designed for home monitoring but with a very similar build.

The idea here is to deploy the robot to certain areas of a workplace via the app, then get 360-degree views once it’s there. Like the drone, it can also set out on automated routes at select timing intervals — like right after a business closes or before it opens. During working hours, it chugs along with its camera, capturing everything in its view.

Also: The 4 biggest Amazon smart home announcements from today

If another Ring device is triggered, the Rover Cam autonomously goes to investigate the disturbance, providing 4K footage in real time via the app. It also features a periscope camera that can extend to see over obstacles like shelving, counters, or furniture, providing a high-level view if needed. In case you lose it in a large warehouse or office, it has a “light tower” that projects light upward onto the ceiling, notifying users of its location.

Even when docked, it uses motion-sensing technology to start recording the second it senses any kind of movement, just like Ring doorbell cameras. In case of an emergency, the Rover features a siren and red flashing lights to dissuade intruders.

The Ring Rover Cam is available for preorder now and will start shipping on Dec. 16, 2026. It will cost $999.
