#3186. Apple HomeView review: An adorable smart display that earns its place

Apple’s HomeView smart display is here. It combines a 7-inch display with Siri AI and an all-new software experience that actually feels really familiar.

I’ve spent the last ten days living with HomeView in my kitchen. Here’s everything you need to know.

HomeView is an adorable little thing. That’s the best way to describe it. A 7-inch square display sits atop a rounded aluminum speaker base. A small, polished metal arm connects it and lets you tilt the display forward and backward.

HomeView comes in four colors: Starlight, Rose Pink, Silver, and Space Gray. My review unit is Starlight, and it’s very subtle. I had to double-check the box to make sure it was Starlight, not Silver.

The decision to make the display square is interesting. Between that design and the software experience centered around faces and widgets, HomeView really does feel like an oversized Apple Watch for your home.

I really appreciate the square display. It makes HomeView look less like an iPad propped up on a stand and more like a dedicated, purpose-driven device.

In terms of specs, the 7-inch display has a 1088 × 1088 resolution, equating to a pixel density of 220 pixels per inch. Max brightness is 500 nits. It can also dim all the way to 0.3 nits, which means it can go in a bedroom without being a nuisance. It also has True Tone to match your room’s lighting temperature.

For the past ten days, my partner and I have been living with HomeView on our kitchen counter. The square display and aluminum base look great in that setting. I don’t think an iPad-style display would look nearly as intentional. We also don’t have much spare counter space. If HomeView were any bigger or wider, I’m not sure we’d have room for it.

In the lead-up to HomeView’s launch, I was skeptical of how usable a 7-inch display would be. In practice, I’ve found this to be (mostly) a non-issue. Apple has done a great job optimizing the interface for the display. Text is readable at a glance from a few feet away, timers are nice and large, and the interface adapts to show more information when you’re closer.

Sometimes I wish it were bigger. Viewing a recipe requires a bit more scrolling than I would like. It’d be nice to fit a couple more widgets on the Modular face. But those trade-offs are easier to accept when I consider how much I appreciate HomeView’s compact footprint.

Apple touts that the HomeView has a custom-engineered acoustic system. There are two custom full-range drivers in the display, paired with a down-firing woofer and two force-canceling passive radiators in the base.

In practice, HomeView’s sound quality falls somewhere between the HomePod mini and the full-size second-generation HomePod. Its sound quality won’t blow you away, but it’s respectable for music and podcast playback. I replaced a full-size original HomePod in my kitchen with it, and while it doesn’t sound quite as good, it makes up for it in other ways … like by having a screen.

HomeView can serve as an AirPlay target, too, so you can beam content from your iPhone or other Apple device right to it. You can also AirPlay from HomeView to other AirPlay targets in your house.

HomeView doesn’t have any buttons, which is a design decision I’ve found very frustrating on multiple occasions. I wish it had volume buttons, so I could quickly adjust the volume without yelling at Siri or using the touchscreen.

HomeView’s software borrows heavily from iOS and watchOS. The interface is built around a system of faces with widgets, very similar to the Apple Watch’s complications system. The process of configuring a face will feel very familiar to Apple Watch and iPhone users.

You can customize faces by long-pressing on them, which reveals a familiar “Customize” screen. Here, you can change the style, color, widgets, and background. You can also add widgets from your nearby iPhone. Apple says that widgets are visible to everyone, but widget content is only visible while your primary device is in the home.

I’ve become particularly fond of the Modular face, which lets you place four equally sized square widgets. I think it provides a nice amount of glanceable information without feeling too dense. The Photos face is also a delight, essentially turning the HomeView into a digital picture frame. Support for Shared Albums is especially nice.

I think Apple made the right decision by building the HomeView experience around faces rather than a traditional app-focused interface. Most of the time, HomeView is just sitting on your counter or table, and you’re not actively interacting with it. That’s why I’ve gravitated towards the Modular face.

The faces system also means that HomeView doesn’t constantly draw your attention. Just like the physical design, it’s there when you need it, but otherwise does a good job blending into the background.

Swiping down from the left two-thirds of the display activates Siri AI, while swiping down from the top right takes you to Control Center (which annoyingly isn’t customizable). Swiping up from the bottom takes you to the Home Screen, where you’ll find a grid of apps and spots to add even more widgets.

There is no App Store on HomeView. Instead, there’s a collection of built-in Apple apps paired with audio and video apps through its CarPlay-based app system. Here are the Apple apps that are available on HomeView:

I’m hopeful that Apple builds on the app story for HomeView sooner rather than later. I don’t think HomeView needs its own App Store, but I do think it needs more apps. This includes more Apple apps and additional third-party apps.

I desperately want Apple to add the Notes app to HomeView. My wife and I keep recipes and dinner ideas in Notes, so it would be great to have that experience available on HomeView. It feels like an odd omission right now. HomeView also needs a dedicated Photos app.

I think the idea of basing the system on CarPlay makes sense. There are a lot of similarities in UI between how an app should work in the car and on a smart display. The Audible app, for example, translates really well from CarPlay to HomeView, as does Spotify.

However, the list of supported categories for CarPlay is a lot broader than the audio and video category Apple is allowing on HomeView right now. There are signs this could expand very soon, and I’m hopeful that’s the case.

One of the cleverest aspects of HomeView is its recipe experience. When you open a recipe in Safari, HomeView gives you the option to convert it into a dedicated cooking interface. You can browse for recipes directly on HomeView, or find one on your iPhone and simply hold it in front of HomeView to hand off the webpage.

HomeView then intelligently detects the actual recipe information and puts it into a streamlined interface. You can view the full ingredient list and measurements, and check off items as you go. The recipe itself is broken down into individual steps. It also intelligently identifies when you need to set a timer and gives you the option to start one directly from the recipe.

This is the exact type of feature that’s perfect for HomeView, and perfect for a dedicated screen sitting on the kitchen counter. You don’t have to keep reaching for your phone, unlocking it, and finding your place in the recipe.

The feature works incredibly well. I tried it with recipes of varying lengths from multiple different websites without any major problems.

There are some limitations, though. For example, it does struggle if a website splits the recipe into multiple pages. Also, as I mentioned earlier, the 7-inch display means there’s more scrolling involved than I’d like. It doesn’t solve my frustration with the lack of a dedicated Notes app. Still, it’s a great example of where this design excels.

Ultimately, the HomeView’s software interface is really well done. Delightful animations appear throughout the experience, like when notifications or the Siri blob slide in from the top bezel. Everything feels very smooth. The software feels familiar because of its similarities to Apple Watch and iPhone, but it’s also clearly purpose-built for the smart display form factor.

Since HomeView is meant for everyone in your home, Apple had to engineer a multi-user system. HomeView supports up to six people, each with their own personalized Home Screen, widgets, and access to personal information.

HomeView identifies the different people in your house in two ways: facial recognition and voice recognition. The goal is to recognize who’s interacting with it and customize the experience for that person. So, when I approach HomeView, it can recognize my face and display my calendar, reminders, and messages. When my wife approaches, it can recognize her instead and show her information.

The facial recognition implementation is particularly interesting. HomeView doesn’t have Face ID. Instead, it uses its built-in camera for facial recognition. During setup, you’re asked to turn your head left, right, up, and down so HomeView can capture your face from different angles.

In practice, HomeView’s facial recognition works surprisingly well. I was skeptical, but it’s done a good job of identifying both my wife and me. If I approach it and try to open the Messages app while it’s on my wife’s profile, I get a message saying it can’t verify my identity. If I repeatedly try, HomeView disables facial recognition, requiring my wife to authenticate using her iPhone before she can access her personal information again.

In addition to protecting personal data, HomeView does a decent job of automatically switching between profiles. There’s occasionally a delay of a few seconds, so I wish it were slightly faster.

HomeView is powered by Apple’s A18 chip, which enables support for Siri AI. However, Siri AI works a bit differently on HomeView than on other Apple devices.

HomeView can answer world knowledge questions on its own, without relying on a paired iPhone or iPad. This is basically the trivia questions we’ve all grown accustomed to shouting at voice assistants over the years. The difference, of course, is that Siri AI answers these questions well, unlike old Siri. On HomeView, the experience is even better because you can visually see the response on the display, often accompanied by images or other visual information.

The second aspect of Siri AI is personal context. To use Siri AI’s personal context on HomeView, you need an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad in your house.

Apple says that the device must have been recently unlocked and be connected to the same Wi-Fi network as HomeView.

In my testing over the last 10 days, I’ve never run into a situation where HomeView was unable to answer a Siri AI query because my iPhone was unavailable.

I’ve found Siri AI to be quite impressive and useful since it debuted in September. It’s a huge upgrade over old Siri. Broadly speaking, that experience extends to HomeView.

Many of the same personal context questions I ask on my iPhone can now be answered by HomeView. And because of HomeView’s form factor, it’s more useful when multitasking. Instead of reaching for my iPhone or hoping it’s within earshot, I can just ask HomeView.

Here are a few questions HomeView has answered without a hiccup:

In terms of speed, I’ve found HomeView to be slightly slower to answer personal context questions than my iPhone Duo. It’s not a huge difference, but it’s a few seconds each time. I assume this is because HomeView is basically handing off the request to my iPhone, adding an additional step that requests directly on the iPhone don’t have to do.

Siri AI is not without its faults. There are times on HomeView where it just hangs and never responds, or responds with a generic “Sorry, try again later” message of some sort. HomeView’s primary interaction method is your voice, which makes these types of Siri AI failures even more frustrating.

HomeView can also serve as the command center for your smart home. It has a dedicated Home app, as well as multiple different Home-focused face options. You can also, of course, use your voice to control HomeKit accessories and scenes through Siri.

There’s ultimately nothing particularly remarkable about HomeView’s support for smart home control. It offers much of the same functionality as the Home app on your iPhone, but in one central location that everyone in your house can use.

There is one limitation: you currently can’t use Siri AI on HomeView to control secure devices like locks and garage doors, even if the device recognizes you. If they are part of a scene, you can tell Siri AI to set the scene and it works. But you can’t individually control them.

Apple tells Joanna Stern that a software update coming next month will add security accessory support to HomeView’s Siri AI.

I wish Apple would expand what HomeView can do for the smart home. It has a built-in camera, so why can’t I use that camera for motion sensing or as a HomeKit Secure Video camera?

I’ve found the screen most useful for quickly checking the status of accessories, like seeing whether a door is locked or glancing at the doorbell camera. For actually controlling accessories, I still find Siri and automations to be the easiest approach. HomeView hasn’t really changed that, although I do appreciate being able to adjust the thermostat right from the kitchen counter.

HomeView costs $299, which is about $100 less than I expected based on rumors. That’s a surprisingly reasonable price, I think. The key, of course, is whether you’ll actually use it day to day.

When you get a new iPhone, you already have a pretty good idea of what you’ll use it for and where it fits into your life. New features might change how you use it, but the core functionality stays the same.

HomeView is very different. At first, it sits on your counter and is nice to look at. It’s a very, very cute little thing. But it takes time to discover how and why it fits into your life.

At first, I had no idea whether I’d actually use HomeView. But in the ten days it’s been sitting on my counter, it’s grown on me quite a bit. It’s gone from being a nice-to-have to something I use and rely on for multiple tasks each day.

It’s also been interesting watching my partner interact with it. Her first impression was essentially, “It’s cute, but I don’t know what I’ll use it for.” Over the last week, however, she’s remarked multiple times how much she likes it.

Whether it’s personal context-focused Siri AI interactions, simply being able to glance and see how long is left on a timer, watching the animated album art as a song plays, or the joy of the Photos face, HomeView has earned its spot.

In fact, I moved HomeView from our kitchen to my office for a day to test a few features and settings in more depth. While cooking dinner that night, we both found ourselves shouting Siri commands into the air and glancing at the empty spot on the counter, only to remember it wasn’t there.

I think that’s the best example of what makes HomeView special. You don’t have to be a HomeKit enthusiast or spend hours tinkering with smart home automations to appreciate it. It’s a device everyone in the house can find their own uses for, and it becomes more useful the longer it’s part of your routine.

#3185. Amazon Has a New Meal Delivery Partner Ahead of Black Friday

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

You can get $20 off your first two orders of $25 for the first two weeks.

If you’ve been on the fence about adding an Amazon Prime membership to your list of subscriptions, the new perk might win you over. And it’s just in time for Black Friday and holiday shopping from your couch.

On Thursday, Amazon announced that Prime members in the US will get free delivery on Uber Eats orders made directly through Amazon’s app or website. And you’ll get $20 off the first two Uber Eats eligible orders of $25 or more for the first 14 days, plus Amazon-exclusive offers. That adds up to $40 in savings on Uber Eats orders. And if you have a Prime Visa credit card, you’ll earn 5% back on all Uber Eats orders until Dec. 5, with a Prime membership.

It’s another perk that may make Amazon Prime membership worthwhile, in addition to Black Friday deals that are weeks away. And it may be worthwhile if you already use Uber Eats often or want a cheaper meal delivery option.

In order to get free delivery and $20 off your order, go to the Uber Eats tab at the top of your Amazon app or Uber Eats on Amazon’s website. Place your order as usual with a participating restaurant but make sure the $20 discount applies at checkout.

I tried the new perk and promo out for Saturday’s dinner. However, I will say the tip, a nearly $10 service fee, tax and the delivery fee all added up to the cost of another meal — which is worth paying attention to when you order.

But you may wonder what that means for the GrubHub partnership that both Amazon and GrubHub touted for years — dating back to 2022. Before now, your Prime subscription included a GrubHub Plus membership at no additional cost. GrubHub Plus included no delivery fees, lower service fees and 5% back on pickup orders.

The new partnership launched the same day that Lyft and DoorDash announced that they’re teaming up for a new subscription, Lyft Go. An Amazon spokesperson said in an email to CNET that the GrubHub and Amazon partnership ended on Thursday. There’s no telling how long Amazon will partner with Uber Eats.

“We continuously evaluate our third-party offers to ensure they provide the best possible value for Prime members,” the spokesperson said. “As part of that ongoing evaluation, we identified an opportunity to deliver an even better restaurant delivery experience.”

However, a GrubHub spokesperson said in an email to CNET that if you have a Prime membership and activated GrubHub Plus, you’ll have the membership until Dec. 31, 2027.

GrubHub shared a joint statement from Amazon and GrubHub in an email to CNET:

On Nov. 5, Grubhub and Amazon have decided to end the Prime-exclusive Grubhub Plus offer, and Amazon customers will no longer be able to place Grubhub orders through Amazon.com or the Amazon Shopping app. Amazon and Grubhub are proud of the partnership and the value provided to Prime members over the years. As the agreement concludes, both companies remain committed to serving our customers and delivering a great customer experience.

The new Uber Eats perk is now available to all Prime members, including those with Prime Access and Prime for Young Adults. And if you’re looking for another dining option, your Amazon Prime membership still offers free same-day delivery on perishable grocery orders over $25 when you order from Amazon Grocery.

#3184. 5 apps I need Siri AI to work with now that it’s open to third-party developers

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Home & Office > Smart Home > Smart Assistants

With the latest betas for iOS and other platforms, Siri AI is now available to all developers for full integration into their apps. Here are the ones I hope will jump on board.

One of the many benefits of the new Siri AI is its ability to work directly with apps on your device via a feature known as App Intents. Currently, this skill includes many of Apple’s own built-in apps and some third-party ones. But with the latest public and developer betas for iOS 27.3, the company is expanding support to all third-party developers.

Also: Ready for a Siri AI agent? Apple under pressure to upgrade

With App Intents, you’re able to ask Siri to tackle a variety of actions among various built-in and third-party apps. On a basic level, you can tell it to perform tasks such as getting directions, playing music, scheduling meetings, sending messages, adding reminders, and finding photos.

On a more advanced level, you can ask it to do things like organize your inbox, edit a photo, and analyze and help you with your current screen. You could also tell it to combine several actions in one shot, work across multiple apps, and engage in a natural back-and-forth conversation.

Introduced in 2022 with iOS 16, the App Intents skill does play well with classic Siri, no Apple Intelligence required. This applies not just to built-in apps but also to third-party apps. However, classic Siri lacks the AI smarts and advanced skills of the latest version.

Siri AI fully supports most built-in apps, including Calendar, Files, Finder, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather. It does support some third-party apps, but its more advanced features are limited or unavailable.

That’s the gap the new developer betas aim to close. With iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, MacOS 27.3, and VisionOS 27.3, all developers will be able to use Siri AI to fully support and integrate with their apps. For example, instead of manually opening an app like DoorDash or Grubhub to check or change a food order, you can tell Siri to do it for you.

Also: The Siri AI waitlist is gone in iOS 27: How to try the beta now

“Today’s preview allows any app to bring its content and actions directly into Siri AI by using App Intents, making it easier for all apps to tap into Siri AI’s newest capabilities, including personal context understanding, on-screen awareness, natural language, and more,” Apple said in a news release for developers. “So people can just ask for help in their own words, and Siri AI carries out any custom action you’ve built, from checking a delivery to booking a reservation to placing an order.”

As I use many third-party apps on my iPhone and iPad, both personally and professionally, I’m looking forward to enhanced support for the ones I rely on. With that in mind, here are five apps for which I’d welcome the new and full Siri AI integration.

I often use Amazon on my iPhone and iPad to shop for and purchase items, review my wishlist, and check the status of products I’ve ordered. To do any of those things, I have to open the app and manually go to the right screens. How convenient it would be if I could tell Siri to handle those tasks for me.

“Siri, search for the 512GB 2026 iPad mini on Amazon and add it to my shopping cart.”

“Siri, review my Amazon wishlist for the luggage I recently added and tell me the latest prices.”

“Siri, check the delivery status of the Alexa photo frame I just ordered on Amazon.”

Right now, Siri can’t do any of those things. But if Siri AI and App intents are fully integrated with Amazon, I may just be able to accomplish those tasks in the future.

IMDB is my go-to app for getting info on movies, TV shows, performers, directors, and more. After I open the app and run a search, I often want specific details, such as the rating and runtime of a particular film or TV episode.

Also: AI completely changed how I develop iPhone apps

To simplify that process, I’ve love to be able to ask Siri: “Siri, search IMDB for the 1935 movie ‘The Bride of Frankenstein,’ give me the running time, tell me where I can stream it, and add it to my watchlist.” If Siri could accomplish all that at some point, it would get a round of applause from me.

I borrow and read a lot of e-books through my local library systems, and I use the handy Libby app for that. Here, I can search different libraries for books by title, author, or subject. I can then borrow a book and read it through the Libby app or, more typically, through the Amazon Kindle app. For this, I have to manually open the app and search among the various libraries for the book I want.

Also: I lost 100 pounds in 7 months: How a smart scale and Apple Watch helped

Instead, I’d like to ask Siri to do that for me. I might say: “Siri, look in Libby for books about Alan Turing, give me the titles of the ones you find, and tell me which ones are currently available to borrow.”

My wife and I are big theater buffs, and we see a lot of plays on Broadway when we’re in New York and on the West End when we’re in London. Often, I buy tickets through the TodayTix service and app. For this, I’ll open the app, set the location to New York or London, look for a specific play, and then try to find seats for a certain day and time.

If TodayTix is ever fully supported by Siri AI and App Intents, I might be able to ask Siri to track down the right seats for me. I could say: “Siri, look for the play ‘Rent’ in London, give me the available performances for Dec. 5 through 9, and let me know which seats are accessible in the first 10 rows.”

As my wife and I often travel and dine out, Yelp is another app I frequently use. Here, I also have to manually launch the app and run searches for restaurants and other places. I then have to try to filter or sort the results based on location, price, and ratings.

It’s going to be tough to ignore the Nov. 19 release of Grand Theft Auto 6. A PCMag survey reports that roughly 12.5 million US workers are likely to take time off when the game comes out, resulting in over $1 billion in lost productivity. Technology company Logitech is deciding not to fight this, giving the entire company the option to take GTA6 launch day off.

Logitech calls this impromptu company holiday Logi Game Day, and it allows all employees to call off work for a day to play whatever game they want. The company is obviously expecting quite a few people to use the day to play GTA6, but employees who don’t can take a different day off if they choose. This invitation to spend time gaming extends from the upper ranks of Logitech all the way down to the interns.

“It’s time to retire the stereotype that gaming is a waste of time,” Logitech CEO Hanneke Farber said in a statement. “As a company designing products for work and play, we see every day how engagement in one sphere supports performance in the other.”

In addition to giving everyone the day off, the company is also hosting a streaming event on Nov. 19, hosted by Robin Piispanen, general manager of Logitech’s gaming brand, Logitech G.

“We see firsthand how Logitech employees who sharpen their skills in-game translate directly back to work and problem-solving,” Piispanen said in a statement.

Grand Theft Auto 6 is the first entry in the long-running and popular GTA series to launch in 13 years. Its predecessor made over $1 billion and sold 235 million units over its long life, making it one of the highest-selling video games of all time. The upcoming game was delayed multiple times throughout 2025 and 2026, which only served to drive up the hype more.

Logitech is the largest company to announce company-wide permission to take a day off to play Grand Theft Auto 6, but it’s not the only one. At least three other organizations are granting official paid time off so employees can play the game.

The first such organization to announce free time off for the launch was the US Army’s 9th Brigade Engineer Battalion of the 3rd Infantry Division at Fort Stewart, Georgia, which gave soldiers a four-day leave to play the game if they reenlisted. That leave runs from Nov. 20-23, effectively giving soldiers a four-day weekend.

The SoCal-based company Burger Motorsports announced on its Instagram that it would pause operations for the day on Nov. 19 to give employees time to play the game. Canada’s Edison Motors gave up asking employees to come in on Nov. 19 and 20, granting the company a four-day weekend to play the game.

Companies that take the initiative and give employees days off are ahead of the curve. Rather than penalizing anticipated absences, these employers are leaning into the launch — a move that could yield unexpected workplace benefits.

Logitech cited two such studies in its press release, including one that found that 81% of gamers believe that playing games increases confidence, reduces anxiety and stress, and is directly correlated with stronger day-to-day work performance. The other study showed that 98.8% of enterprise IT decision-makers reported that gaming skills directly translated into work performance.

Psychiatrist Douglas McWilliams told Psychology Today that taking time off to play games can also help reduce burnout, which is one of the leading causes of high turnover, absenteeism, lost productivity, and mental and physical health struggles among employees.

“Being able to mentally detach from work is generally accomplished through taking time off,” McWilliams told the magazine. “For recovery to occur, the time off needs to result in mental disengagement from work; it must involve some sort of activation energy; it must be relaxing; and it must be a decision within an individual’s control.”

McWilliams goes on to say that major video game launches such as Grand Theft Auto 6 and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time — due out Nov. 21 — can meet these conditions and may positively affect the mental health of employees who take time off to play them.

#3181. Reddit launches AI-powered Reviews feature – with 10,000 products to start

Reddit is adding AI-generated product reviews that compile real user sentiment from across communities. Here's how they work.

If you regularly turn to Reddit for product advice, your experience is about to change.

Reddit announced a new feature on Tuesday called Reddit Reviews, which takes conversations from subreddits across the site and compiles them into AI-generated, in-depth product summaries. The feature works much like Google AI Overviews and is likely an attempt to better compete with them.

When you search for a product on Reddit, you’ll see an “easy-to-digest format” that has a “what people are saying” recap. A visual breakdown will show whether conversations are generally positive, mixed, or negative, as well as common sentiments among users. If you want to go deeper, Reddit says you can browse comments about a product, apply topic filters, read original user discussions, ask follow-up questions, or explore other commonly compared products.

In an example shared by Reddit, a user searches for “Best headphones 2026.” The search returns several results with tags like “Very positive,” “Positive,” and “Mixed.” Clicking on one expands to a review that says, “Reddit likes the XL224’s fantastic battery life, powerful bass, and strong sound quality, while the steep price and fit on smaller heads draws criticism.”

“A mix of generative AI and other in-house technology” is used to identify themes and summarize what people are saying, a representative explained, and added that “the technologies and models we use may evolve over time to best support the experience.”

Perhaps the most important part is that Reddit Reviews are shaped by users, and companies can’t pay to have product features. For a community sensitive to commercialization, this is a big deal.

My first concern was about bots or other fake reviews, but a Reddit representative said they’re taking that into consideration. “Platform-wide,” the representative said, “we are labeling apps and prompting accounts we detect to be running automations to either verify there’s a human behind the username or be labeled as an app.” In this context, an app is a registered API client that’s developed to interact with Reddit (including posting, commenting, upvoting, and scraping). In short, the system will label known bots.

Also: Ring’s new drone patrols your home to keep watch – even upstairsSpecifically for reviews, a “review conversation” will appear that describes a person’s experience with a product. Reddit also has “defined rules,” it says, “to help our LLMs identify these review conversations based on the surrounding conversation for context.”

You’ll start to see Reddit Reviews over the next few weeks in the US on iOS, Android, and browser versions of the site. Around 10,000 products across electronics, health and beauty, home and garden, and fashion and apparel will be available to start.

I find myself frequently adding “reddit” to Google searches for everything from the best restaurants in a city to the best headphones for my kids, so these overviews are definitely intriguing. It’s not easy right now to wade through numerous threads, so if this does make it easier to get true user sentiment, it could be a big plus.

#3178. Should You Buy Alphabet Stock Now That Google Will Let Customers Run Its AI Chips in Their Own Data Centers?

The search giant's turning its AI chips into hardware it sells. Is the stock a buy around 28% below its peak?

Alphabet (GOOGL +1.79%)(GOOG +1.62%) just gave its custom artificial intelligence (AI) chips another way to reach customers. On Monday, Nov. 9, Google Cloud announced two new versions of its tensor processing units (TPUs) -- chips Google designs to train and run AI models. And Google Cloud vice president Mark Lohmeyer told reporters that select customers will be able to install one of them, the TPU 8tx, in their own data centers.

For most of their history, the only way to use a TPU was to rent one in Google's cloud. This changed in the second quarter, when Alphabet started booking revenue on TPU systems it sold to customers running their own data centers. Google now says almost 100 customers use the chips.

Meanwhile, Alphabet shares trade near $292 as I write. Its record close was on May 13, at $402.62, which puts the stock about 28% under that peak.

Most of the revenue from those chip sales won't arrive until 2027, and Alphabet pays for the hardware first. But I think the move makes the long-term case for the stock a bit stronger.

The TPU 8tx is made for confidential work. Google says it's designed for regulated firms and governments running AI alongside their most sensitive data, and it protects that data even as the chip is processing it. (Usually, data needs to be unlocked in memory as a computer works on it.)

Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian described the appeal on Alphabet's third-quarter earnings call in late October.

"For some industries, they have data in their premise that they cannot move to a cloud, and it allows us to bring accelerated compute to where the data sits," Kurian said.

Put another way, on-site TPUs can reach customers Google's cloud can't fully serve. Some TPU customers Kurian named on the call seem to match that description, such as capital markets firms Citadel Securities and Jump Trading.

The market these chips compete in is huge. Nvidia posted data center revenue of $89.0 billion in its fiscal second quarter alone (the period ended July 26, 2026). Even a small slice of that kind of spending could matter to Alphabet.

Showing how quickly Google's own AI business is moving, Google Cloud's third-quarter revenue more than doubled year over year to $30.7 billion, and management said TPU system sales were a meaningful contributor. The growth rate has climbed every quarter this year -- 63% in the first quarter, then 82% in the second. Cloud's backlog (contracted revenue not yet recognized, including the TPU sales deals) hit $561 billion, up from $462 billion at the end of March. And the segment's operating margin widened to 36.2% from 23.7% a year before.

Still, the chip sales themselves are early. Alphabet's quarterly filings say it's signed a limited number of agreements to supply TPU systems to customers who run their own infrastructure. The company expects the significant majority of the revenue from these deals to be recognized in 2027.

Of course, selling hardware also changes how cash flows through Alphabet. It buys parts after a contract is signed but before the customer pays, so the money goes out first.

Alphabet's inventory, which consists mainly of TPU systems and Pixel devices, jumped to $13.3 billion at the end of September from $2.4 billion at the end of 2025. With that build and $51.4 billion in capital spending, free cash flow was negative $9.1 billion in the third quarter.

On the upside, Kurian said putting TPU systems in customer data centers "offsets the need for us to have to prebuild facilities to host these TPU systems." But Alphabet still expects capital spending of $195 billion to $205 billion this year, and it expects that number to grow significantly in 2027.

Does this change the case for Alphabet stock? Not overnight. But it gives Google a second way to make money on chips it already designs for itself, from business its cloud couldn't reach alone.

Alphabet stock costs around 19 times expected 2027 earnings. That's a fair price, I think, for a company whose cloud revenue just more than doubled. Free cash flow will probably stay weak for a few more quarters. Still, at this price, I'd consider buying shares.

#3177. Apple Support Community Is Shutting Down, as DIY Advice Bites the Dust

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Even if the site was no longer very useful, it's still sad to lose free peer support.

Senior Editor / Home Security and Smart Home

Senior Editor / Home Security and Smart Home

When people tried visiting the Apple Support Community site on Tuesday, they found not only that new posts were blocked, but that Apple is planning to shut down the forums permanently on Nov. 20. If you want to look up a specific Apple troubleshooting topic on iPhones or HomePods, now’s the time to do it. Soon, the entire peer advice and support site, which has been operating for nearly three decades, will be gone.

Apple was a pioneer in community support forums before the aughts, letting people discuss their Mac issues as early as 1998. For those of you who might remember, that’s the year Apple debuted its iMac G3, the desktop with a translucent blue teardrop-shaped case. The iMac G3 abandoned legacy ports and the floppy disk drive in favor of CD-ROM and USB.

Back then, the site was called Apple Tech Exchange, later renamed Apple Discussions until it eventually became the Apple Support Community in 2011. Many still turned to forums for DIY solutions, using it to get advice from other tinkerers interested in figuring out how to fix things on their own.

An Apple spokesperson told CNET the decision was made “after careful evaluation of our strategy and our customers’ needs.” Apple’s site notification directs people to visit the official Apple Support site. You’ll also be able to use Apple’s online chat, support phone numbers and in-store support, the same way they worked in the past.

Apple is one of the first American tech companies to give up its community discussion site — Google still has Google Communities Help, and Amazon manages its own forum domain with discussions from both staff and users. But Apple’s sudden closure could indicate a major shift, with others eventually following suit. It has highlighted an ongoing discussion about the role of peer support in tech, how AI has changed our online conversations and more.

When news of the shutdown spread, Apple users flocked to the internet to express everything from dismay to vindication.

For many, the Apple Support Community forums were controversial, not least because it wasn’t always clear how they worked. The site contained “user-submitted content, comments and opinions” and was “for informational purposes only,” yet many would mistake it for official Apple Support from staff.

In discussions on Reddit about the closure, many bemoaned the absence of real Apple employees from the site’s forums and found the advice from other Support Community users to often be frustrating and not worth the effort. On the unofficial Apple subreddit, many mourned the loss of community while also noting that answers on the forum were often much harder to come by. Others said the site grew less helpful over the years.

CNET phone reviewer and senior editor Mike Sorrentino told me that the forum shutdown “will likely drive customers looking for help with basic questions to Apple’s official support articles rather than user-created threads.” But Sorrentino also acknowledged that the move reflects a general trend away from the site, with more people getting answers from sites like Reddit. “Apple’s always been big on controlling what information is shown on its website, and in that view, moving away from user discussion makes sense,” he said.

Just this week, I used the Apple Support Community site when looking for an answer to a problem implementing Apple Intelligence on my home security cameras, which required jumping through multiple hoops. Perhaps tellingly, I ended up finding the correct answer on Reddit myself. But that could become harder to do in the near future.

The shutdown of Apple’s peer support forums is definitely a sign of the times, especially as tech companies push users away from repairing their own devices and toward replacing them outright — or at least encourage device owners to pay for official support services. It’s also a sign of the growing role of artificial intelligence, which is capitalizing on user-created content to provide summaries, moving people away from organic discussion and exchange on sites like these.

Reddit has lucrative data-licensing contracts with Google and OpenAI, allowing the companies to train their AI models on Reddit’s massive archive of human discussions, as well as surface Reddit content in tools like Google AI Overviews and ChatGPT. Reddit is also moving to a login-only viewing mode, making it significantly harder for casual users to find answers unless they trust AI summaries.

Apple may be leery of keeping so much user knowledge online for AI models to scrape for their own answers. The company may also want to prevent AI summaries from providing information from past forum users on how to jailbreak Apple devices or DIY fixes, even as the EU has mandated that Apple start building replaceable batteries by next year. And it wouldn’t be a good look if Siri AI started regurgitating incorrect or outdated info it had picked up from Apple’s own sites.

Whatever the reason, the circle of Apple users helping users has grown smaller, and that doesn’t bode well for support forums as a whole. It may be time to start archiving those years of data before other tech companies implement similar plans.

#3176. Done with Debian Linux distros? Try Fedora next – 7 reasons why

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

After using a Debian-based distribution, you may find yourself longing for something different. I know exactly what you should try next.

Back when I was constantly distro-hopping, I found it important to have a “what’s next” mentality. That way, I could plan accordingly, instead of jumping in blind. I could prepare myself for the installation, the package management system, the desktop, and other necessary bits and pieces.

Also: Fedora Everything let me build the Linux desktop I actually want

But more than anything, I always found it best to know which type of distribution should be next.

You wouldn’t want to jump from Ubuntu to, say, Gentoo, as the leap in required skills is considerable. You also wouldn’t want to jump from Ubuntu to Debian, since Ubuntu is based on Debian, making it a lateral move. From my experience, when coming from an Ubuntu-based distribution, the best next distro is one based on Fedora.

This statement wouldn’t hold water five years ago because Fedora often required work to get it running properly. Now, Fedora requires no work or effort to get it working out of the box. Hardware support is on par with Ubuntu, modern boot processes are supported, it has an excellent first-boot experience, Nvidia driver support is out of the box, the touchpad works out of the box, suspend and resume work flawlessly, it ships with a newer kernel, it includes built-in support for modern display stacks, and it’s clean and bloat-free.

Like many Linux distributions, Fedora lets you choose your desktop, but it does so better by offering dedicated spins for each. You’ll find Fedora spins for KDE Plasma, Xfce, Cinnamon, Mate-Compiz, i3, LXQT, LXDE, SOAS, Sway, Budgie, Miracle, Plasma Mobile, and COSMIC. Instead of manually installing your desktop of choice, just download the Fedora spin with your desired desktop.

Also: Fedora 44 made me forget I was using Linux – in the best way

Yes, there’s a Debian-based distribution for every desktop, but knowing you can just go to the Fedora Project Spins page and quickly find what you’re looking for makes the process easy. As well, Ubuntu has its own “flavors” (such as Kubuntu, Lubuntu, etc.), so coming from an Ubuntu flavor will make total sense.

When using a Debian-based distribution, if you install/manage software from the command line, you’re used to APT, such as sudo apt install quillmark. Did you know that Fedora’s DNF works in the same way? That’s right: sudo dnf install quillmark will get you the same results as sudo apt install quillmark (so long as the app is found in the Fedora repositories).

The same holds true for removing software. One difference, however, is that when system software is upgraded, you’ll have to reboot a Fedora-based distribution for the upgrades to take effect. The only time you have to reboot on a Debian-based distro upgrade is if the kernel is upgraded in the process.

If you’re using Ubuntu as your Debian-based distribution, you’ll find that it includes a universal package manager, just as Fedora does. On Debian, the package manager is Snap, while on Fedora it’s Flatpak. While these two are different, they do have some similarities, such as app installation.

Also: 5 of my favorite Linux distros for AI – and why

With Snap packages, the installation goes something like this: sudo snap install quillmark. On Fedora, that command would be flatpak install quillmark. You’ll notice that sudo is not used with Flatpak; the reason for this is that Flatpak apps are typically installed on a per-user basis. Yes, you can install them system-wide, but that defeats the purpose of sandboxing.

Both Fedora and Ubuntu are secure, even if they arrive at that security by different routes. For example, Ubuntu has AppArmor and Fedora has SELinux. However, both of these tools manage Mandatory Access Controls — just in different ways. The good news is that you’ll probably never have to touch either system.

Also: Ubuntu 26.04 vs. Fedora 44: After years of testing both, here’s my verdict

Also, both Debian- and Fedora-based distributions tend to ship with a GUI frontend for the firewall. If you don’t find one installed, you can install one through your package manager. It is important to know that the Fedora firewall manager is considerably more powerful than Ubuntu’s, which also means it has a steeper learning curve. The good news is that, out of the box, you probably won’t have to make many changes to the firewall, other than ensuring it’s enabled.

Once upon a time, I would have debated such a statement, but Fedora is now on par with Ubuntu in terms of user-friendliness, especially if you choose one of the more user-friendly spins (such as KDE Fedora, Cinnamon, or MATE-Compiz). Fedora also has a System Settings app similar to Ubuntu’s; each one lets you manage nearly every aspect of the computer, so there’s no need to use the command line with Fedora (unless you want to).

With Debian, the release cycle is every 2 years, and support is 5 years. With Fedora, the release cycle is every 6 months, and support is 13 months. If you’re using an Ubuntu-based distribution (which is based on Debian), the release cycle is the same as Fedora, but there are two versions: LTS and interim. LTS support is considerably longer than interim releases: LTS releases receive 5 years of free support, while interim releases receive 9 months.

Also: My favorite Linux desktop environment for laptops surprised even me

In the end, the Fedora release/support cycle is faster and simpler.

Because both development teams focus on building a user-friendly distribution out of the box, migrating from a Debian-based to a Fedora-based distribution is seamless. When making such a transition, aside from a few minor differences, you’ll feel like you never left your Debian-based distro, especially if you choose a Fedora Spin that includes the same desktop you’ve been using.

#3174. What to Learn About Meta’s Muse AI Before It Learns Too Much About You

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Meta’s Muse AI agent quietly builds a profile on you the second you start using it, even if you explicitly tell it not to. That turns Jolly, its supposedly cute and cuddly mascot, into the friendly face of some serious security flaws.

On top of that, Muse asks for the keys to your digital life: passwords, full disk access, emails, calendar invites, contacts, Notes and WhatsApp chats. Meta also feeds your conversations into its AI training pipeline by default, leaving it on you to dig through the settings and opt out.

If that wasn’t enough, there’s also a widely publicized case in which Muse mistakenly shared the home address of a Toronto tech reviewer, Matt Robb, with a potential buyer on Facebook Marketplace. Muse invited the stranger to Robb’s home without his explicit consent or knowledge, then later apologized for doing so, as detailed in a Threads post. Robb hadn’t realized that he had inadvertently granted Muse blanket permission to automatically reply to Marketplace inquiries using the details he provided, including his address.

Before facing a potential security nightmare, here’s what to know about Muse.

Meta’s Muse appears to blatantly ignore user permissions, according to a report by AppleInsider. In one case, the AI agent synced roughly 187,000 lines of a user’s Apple Messages without their consent, even though “Full Disk Access” was turned off.

The report shows that Muse pinged a user’s messages database thousands of times despite disk access being disabled. Muse then successfully harvested texts from the user’s Mac — not from Meta’s Messenger, but from Apple Messages.

Even people who refuse to use Muse may have their data collected by the AI if they text someone who does have it installed.

Before Meta launched the ability for its Muse to make outbound business calls on your behalf, internal Meta documents revealed that the company planned to rely on human contractors at call centers to help make reservations and appointments.

That means not only would the software have access to all your private data, but a total stranger might also be managing your personal commitments — all without your knowledge. The human concierge feature appears to have been rolled back for now, according to Reuters.

The VPN company Surfshark said it found that Meta Muse is collecting — or attempting to collect — 31 out of 35 types of data, putting it far ahead of other popular chatbots like Gemini, ChatGPT and DeepSeek. Muse also collects highly sensitive personal information like location data, sexual orientation, genetic information or biometric data.

Muse (along with Meta AI and Gemini) also reserves the right to use collected audio data for other purposes, such as analytics or product personalization. Surfshark released a full dataset for what it uncovered.

Want to share your experience with Meta’s Muse or other AI agents? Email us at editors@cnet.com.

#3173. Your FitBit Versa and Sense smartwatches will lose some features this month – what to know

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Time's running out for some Versa and Sense models. After Nov. 28, you can no longer install or update third-party apps or clockfaces on these Google smartwatches.

If you have a Fitbit Versa or Fitbit Sense smartwatch, you’ll soon be unable to update the third-party apps on these devices. Google announced on Monday an update to its older lineup of devices that may signify the beginning of obsolescence. Users can no longer install or update third-party apps or clocks on these Fitbit smartwatches, beginning on Nov. 28.

Also: Google’s Fitbit Air is a $99 screenless wearable that I can actually take seriously

The apps will continue to work after that date, but if users delete any of these apps, they will not be able to reinstall them. The changes affect the Fitbit Sense and Fitbit Sense 2, as well as the Fitbit Versa, Fitbit Versa Lite, Fitbit Versa 2, Fitbit Versa 3, and Fitbit Versa 4.

Google noted that users will still have access to Fitbit- and Google-developed apps and clocks, and that they should update to the latest app versions to keep those apps functioning properly.

The Nov. 28 support cut-off comes right on the heels of this season’s Black Friday sales. (Google’s Pixel Watch 5 just got a $100 discount at Amazon.)

So the smartwatches aren’t dead — they can still perform the same primary functions, like recording workouts or receiving or responding to messages and calls. Still, the news is a downer for Versa and Sense users who’ve been using their smartwatches and the many third-party apps on them for anywhere from two to eight years now.

All signs point to these devices being slowly phased out in favor of Google’s latest lineup of fitness trackers and smartwatches.

Also: Google’s new Fitbit Edge solves my biggest gripe with the Pixel Watch

Within the past few years, Google has unveiled an impressive new lineup of health trackers, including the screenless Fitbit Air, the screened Fitbit Edge, and the Pixel Watch 5. For those looking to ditch their Versa or Sense, a few affordable options exist in the ecosystem to take their place.

The earliest and most recent Fitbit Versa models were launched in 2018 and 2022, respectively, and the first and last Fitbit Sense models launched in 2020 and 2022, respectively — making the oldest of these devices eight years old.

#3172. History Says This Investing Strategy Has Never Failed After a Midterm Election

The midterm elections are over. Starting in January, Democrats will take control of Congress from the Republicans. As usual, political change creates a backdrop for heightened stock market volatility. And this year was no different.

The biggest question mark is what impact, if any, the new political regime will have on the artificial intelligence (AI) build-out. Investors generally believe that the entire industry will be under more scrutiny. Moreover, data center construction could slow, a development that the hyperscalers, which are spending huge sums of capital, depend on so heavily.

Uncertainty is the key theme. And investors are trying to figure out how to best position their portfolios. History shows there's an investment strategy that has never failed after a midterm election.

Elections naturally get all of the attention. And media outlets never hesitate to draw connections between the political arena and your financial situation. This can drive a sense of urgency. You may feel like you need to take deliberate action immediately. That's not the right thing to do.

This might come off as the most boring piece of advice ever. But the best move that investors can make is absolutely none. A smart investing strategy is to avoid making portfolio moves strictly based on election outcomes.

History proves that this is the optimal course of action from a purely financial standpoint. Since 1980, the S&P 500 index (^GSPC -0.35%) produced a positive total return over the 12 months right after a midterm election 100% of the time, with an average gain of 13.7%. It's impossible to argue with this track record. It doesn't matter whether Congress is blue or red.

You might start to think that this time will be different. After all, valuations are high. There's geopolitical tension. Inflationary pressure is persisting. And the AI boom, which is sucking up so much capital, is sparking fears of a bubble.

To be clear, there are always reasons to worry. Seasoned market participants know that this is true. Uncertainty is nothing new. In fact, it's par for the course.

History shows that staying invested in the stock market is the winning strategy. Over the long term, it pays off. On the other hand, panicking and backing out will prove to be a costly mistake.

Investors are to do nothing after a midterm election. This leads to the next point: Investors' specific portfolio management strategies don't need to be altered. Everything should generally be viewed as noise, no matter how many headlines a particular topic grabs.

The recipe for long-term success in the stock market is still the same. It depends on identifying high-quality businesses that come with wide economic moats. These companies sell differentiated products and services. They have durable growth potential. From a financial perspective, they operate with solid balance sheets and generate consistent profits.

This is a good list of characteristics investors should look for. Once you've narrowed down a group of businesses, valuation comes into focus. It's not ideal to buy stocks when they're expensive. All else equal, purchasing shares at a margin of safety is optimal.

If picking stocks isn't on your radar, then consider buying an S&P 500 tracker, like the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (VOO -0.34%). At an extremely low expense ratio of 0.03%, this exchange-traded fund (ETF) offers instant exposure to the biggest businesses powering the U.S. economy. You'll own about 80% of the entire country's stock market capitalization in a hassle-free manner that requires no active portfolio management.

The midterm elections are over. While your investing playbook won't change, events like these should reset your perspective, which can be an invaluable exercise.
